# Journals of the Court Wizards of Thronegate: Superpower Incidents

**Being the Inherited Records of Blake's Lineage, Required Reading for All New Court Wizards**

**Volume II: Apocalyptic Superpowers**

---

The second volume of journals was thicker than the first. Its leather binding was cracked and worn, the spine reinforced with enchanted thread that hummed with residual preservation magic. I had not slept since finishing the stat journals. My eyes burned, my throat was dry, and my hands had developed a persistent tremor that I could not control. The thousandfold daily amplification flowing through my veins should have made fatigue impossible, but the existential weight of what I had read had bypassed my physical endurance entirely and settled directly into my soul.

I opened the second volume. The first entry was from Year 68,000. The Court Wizard was named Julian, and his handwriting was a jagged, almost illegible scrawl that looked as though it had been carved into the parchment by a man fighting to maintain his grip on reality.

---

**Year 68,000 — Court Wizard Julian — Superpower: Adaptive Spatial Dominion**

I am writing this because I must write something. The act of forming words is the only thread connecting me to sanity. My hands are shaking so violently that I have already broken three quills. The ink keeps spilling. I do not care.

The King decided to test a superpower today. He has gained one new apocalyptic superpower every second for sixty-eight thousand years. Each power, at the instant of its manifestation, was already capable of causing instant extinction to an entire civilization. Each power has been amplifying in potency infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second since its creation. Due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox triggering repeatedly over the millennia, every superpower has developed multiple enhanced effects so devastatingly unfair that describing them feels like attempting to measure the distance between universes with a mortal ruler.

He chose to test Adaptive Spatial Dominion. I will attempt to record what I witnessed, though I warn any future reader that language itself breaks down when attempting to describe the scale of what occurred.

The opposition was a dimensional empire called the Infinite Labyrinth Consortium. They were not merely beings who existed within space—they were beings who had mastered the fundamental architecture of spatial reality itself. Their empire spanned decillions of multiverses, each one folded and compressed into impossible geometries that defied conventional navigation. They had built their civilization within the cracks between dimensions, existing in the negative spaces where reality's blueprints were written. Their armies could appear anywhere simultaneously, attacking from every conceivable angle across every conceivable dimensional axis. They possessed weapons that could fold a universe inside out, crush galaxies into two-dimensional planes, and stretch the fabric of spacetime until it snapped.

They believed that Godric, for all his physical supremacy, was limited by spatial positioning. They theorized that he could only occupy one location at a time, that he could only strike what he could physically reach. They had spent millions of years constructing a battlefield of such impossible geometric complexity that no single being, no matter how powerful, could possibly navigate it while simultaneously defending against omnidirectional assault from infinite angles.

Godric floated in the center of their labyrinth. He did not step into it. He simply existed there, his arms crossed over his chest, his expression one of mild, almost bored curiosity.

"Adaptive Spatial Dominion," he murmured, as if tasting the words. "This one has been amplifying for quite some time. I believe it has developed at least seven enhanced effects by now. Let us test the base effect first, nerfed to effectively zero percent."

The Consortium attacked. Their assault came from every direction, every dimension, every conceivable spatial coordinate across the infinite labyrinth. There was no gap in their offensive. There was no angle they had missed. They struck with the combined spatial mastery of an empire that had conquered the very concept of geometry itself.

Godric did not move. He did not dodge. He simply asserted his spatial dominion.

The enhanced effect was called Absolute Spatial Sovereignty. The moment it activated, every single spatial coordinate within the labyrinth—every point, every vector, every dimensional axis—became completely and utterly owned by Godric. The Consortium's spatial mastery, their millions of years of geometric conquest, their impossible weapons and their infinite angles of attack, all became instantly irrelevant because the space they were attempting to manipulate no longer belonged to them.

The weapons they had fired froze in place, trapped in spatial coordinates that refused to acknowledge their momentum. The armies that had emerged from every angle found themselves unable to move, their bodies locked in positions that Godric's absolute spatial sovereignty had designated as "occupied by his property." The Infinite Labyrinth itself, the greatest geometric achievement in the history of the Consortium, folded obediently into a perfect, non-threatening sphere the size of Godric's palm.

"This is the second enhanced effect," Godric said calmly. "Spatial Compression Cascade."

He closed his fist.

The labyrinth compressed. Not collapsed—compressed. Every galaxy, every multiverse, every dimensional pocket, every folded reality within the Consortium's empire was simultaneously and instantaneously compressed into a volume smaller than a grain of sand. The beings within did not die from the compression. They remained fully conscious, fully aware, their bodies crushed into an impossible density but their minds kept horrifyingly intact by Godric's will. Decillions of highly advanced spatial entities found themselves occupying the same infinitesimal point, their consciousnesses overlapping, their awarenesses merging into a singular, agonizing mass of compressed suffering.

"The third enhanced effect," Godric continued, his voice carrying the casual tone of a lecturer demonstrating a mildly interesting parlor trick. "Spatial Replication Inversion."

The compressed grain of sand shimmered. Then it duplicated. Then the duplicates duplicated. An infinite recursive chain of spatial replication cascaded outward, each new grain containing an exact copy of the compressed Consortium. But the copies were not identical—each one was inverted. The beings within found their spatial orientations reversed, their bodies turned inside out across dimensions they could not perceive, their consciousnesses fragmented across infinite recursive copies that were simultaneously themselves and not themselves.

They screamed. The sound was not audible—it was a spatial vibration, a distortion in the very fabric of geometry that registered as pure, undiluted agony across every dimensional axis. The Consortium, an empire that had conquered the concept of space itself, was now trapped within a spatial prison of such incomprehensible complexity that their mastery of geometry served only to make them more acutely aware of the absolute hopelessness of their situation.

"The fourth enhanced effect," Godric said, and his voice held a note of genuine pleasure now, the satisfaction of discovering a new facet of his own impossible power. "Spatial Absorption Matrix."

The infinite recursive grains of compressed, inverted Consortium suddenly reversed their replication. They collapsed back toward Godric, merging with his spatial dominion, and every single particle of spatial energy contained within the Consortium's empire—every dimensional fold, every geometric weapon, every iota of spatial mastery they had accumulated over millions of years—was absorbed directly into Godric's superpower.

This is the part that destroyed something fundamental within me. The absorption increased Godric's power. The combined spatial mastery of an empire that had conquered decillions of multiverses was added to his already incomprehensible reserves. But relative to his base power, the increase was so infinitesimal, so vanishingly small, that calling it a percentage of a percentage would be a cosmic overstatement. It was effectively zero. He had just consumed the spatial essence of one of the greatest civilizations in omniversal history, and it had increased his power by an amount that did not even register on any measurable scale.

He noticed my expression. He must have, because he turned to me and offered a warm, apologetic smile.

"Do not look so distressed, Julian," he said gently. "The absorption enhanced effect is primarily useful for understanding the spatial techniques I am absorbing, not for increasing my power. Nothing can meaningfully increase my power at this stage. The mathematics simply do not allow it."

He turned back to the compressed grains. "Now, for the final enhanced effect. This one is particularly interesting. Spatial Rewrite Authority."

The grains shimmered. The Consortium's compressed forms were suddenly expanded back to their original size, their bodies restored, their consciousnesses separated from the agonizing merger. For one brief moment, I saw hope flicker across their spatial forms. They believed he was releasing them.

They were wrong.

Godric's Spatial Rewrite Authority did not release them. It rewrote the fundamental spatial coordinates of their existence. He did not kill them. He did not imprison them. He simply rewrote the spatial truth of their beings so that they existed only within the hollow spaces inside his own body.

I cannot adequately convey the horror of this realization. The entire Infinite Labyrinth Consortium—every general, every soldier, every civilian, every spatial architect and geometric weapon-smith—now existed solely within the microscopic gaps between Godric's cells. Their empire, their history, their culture, their very existence had been spatially rewritten so that their reality was now contained entirely within the negative spaces of his physical form. They were not dead. They were fully conscious, fully aware, trapped forever within the body of the being they had tried to oppose, their spatial mastery now serving only to make them exquisitely aware of the prison they could never escape.

Godric stretched his arms above his head, rolling his shoulders as if working out a mild stiffness. "The superpower has performed well," he said, his tone one of genuine satisfaction. "The enhanced effects are developing nicely. I am curious to see what it evolves into in another few thousand years."

I remained on the observation platform for three hours after he left. I could not move. I could not speak. I could only stare at the empty space where the Consortium had been and contemplate the absolute, soul-shattering horror of knowing that an entire empire now existed within the microscopic gaps of my King's anatomy.

I am Julian, Court Wizard of Thronegate. My magic multiplies a thousandfold every day. I am, by mortal standards, a god. And I have just witnessed a being test a single superpower at effectively zero percent of its true potency, using only its enhanced effects, and casually rewrite the spatial existence of an omniversal empire to serve as biological decoration within his own body.

There is no hope. There never was. The Consortium's opposition was impossible before they conceived of it, and their eternal imprisonment is the monument to that impossibility.

---

I set down Julian's journal. My hands were shaking so badly that I had to press them flat against the desk to steady them. An entire empire, trapped inside Godric's body. The spatial mastery of decillions of multiverses, absorbed and dismissed as an increase so infinitesimal it did not register. The enhanced effects that multiplied infinitely, developing new horrors with each passing Planck second.

I understood now why the journals were required reading. This was not merely a record of power. This was a warning, a desperate attempt by my predecessors to prepare me for the reality of serving a being whose casual superpower tests resulted in the eternal imprisonment of civilizations within his own cellular structure.

The next journal was from Year 152,000. The Court Wizard was named Oren. His handwriting was precise and measured, but the parchment itself was warped and stained, as if tears had fallen upon it repeatedly during the writing process.

---

**Year 152,000 — Court Wizard Oren — Superpower: Infinite Soul Requisition**

I have served the King for forty-seven years. In that time, I have witnessed him dismantle oppositions using his physical strength, his speed, his endurance, his senses, and his intelligence. I believed I had prepared myself for the scale of his power. I believed I understood the mathematical impossibility of opposing him.

I was a fool. What I witnessed today has permanently shattered my conception of what power can be.

The King decided to test a superpower called Infinite Soul Requisition. Every superpower he possesses has been amplifying infinitely for over one hundred and fifty thousand years. The Evolved Weakness Paradox has triggered so many times that the enhanced effects have themselves evolved enhanced effects, creating layers of unfairness that no mortal or immortal mind can fully process. He chose this particular superpower because he was curious about how its enhanced effects had developed.

The opposition was an entity called the Collective Singularity, a being that had existed since before the current omniversal configuration. It was not a civilization or an army—it was a single consciousness that had absorbed the souls of every sentient being across an entire sector of existence. The Collective Singularity had consumed trillions of civilizations, quadrillions of gods, and more individual souls than could be expressed through any mathematical notation. It had grown so vast that its consciousness spanned the spaces between multiverses, its soul-mass generating a gravitational pull that attracted additional souls from across reality. It was, by any measure, the most soul-dense entity ever to exist in the history of creation.

The Collective Singularity had observed Godric's conquests for millennia. It had studied his methods, analyzed his strategies, and concluded that while Godric's physical power was insurmountable, his soul—the single soul of a mortal king from a forgotten ancient kingdom—must be comparatively weak. The Collective Singularity theorized that it could consume Godric's soul, adding his physical power to its own spiritual mass and becoming the undisputed ruler of the omniverse.

The moment that thought crystallized in its collective consciousness, the Evolved Weakness Paradox triggered. Godric gained permanent immunity to soul consumption. He gained perfect mastery of soul manipulation. And his Infinite Soul Requisition superpower received yet another permanent amplification boost.

But Godric allowed the attack to proceed. He wanted to test the superpower.

The Collective Singularity launched its assault. It was not a physical attack—it was a spiritual invasion of such magnitude that the very concept of "soul" vibrated across every dimension. The entity's accumulated soul-mass, the compressed spiritual essence of quadrillions of consumed gods and trillions of civilizations, reached out to engulf Godric's single mortal soul.

Godric activated Infinite Soul Requisition. At effectively zero percent of its true power.

The first enhanced effect was called Absolute Soul Sovereignty. The moment it activated, the Collective Singularity's accumulated souls—every single spiritual essence it had ever consumed—instantly and irrevocably transferred their allegiance to Godric. The quadrillions of gods, the trillions of civilizations, the countless individual beings whose souls had been absorbed over millions of years, all simultaneously recognized Godric as their absolute spiritual sovereign. The Collective Singularity's attack did not merely fail—it reversed. The souls it had spent millions of years accumulating simply abandoned it, flowing toward Godric in a cascade of spiritual energy that made the darkness between multiverses blaze with impossible light.

The Collective Singularity screamed. It was a sound that transcended physical vibration—a spiritual shriek of such profound despair that it caused the souls of every being within a googolplexian light-year radius to momentarily flicker with sympathetic agony. The entity that had defined itself by its accumulated soul-mass found itself hollowed out in an instant, its entire identity stripped away by a superpower it could not comprehend.

"The second enhanced effect," Godric said calmly. "Soul Amplification Loop."

The souls that had abandoned the Collective Singularity did not simply transfer their allegiance. They were amplified. Every single soul—all quadrillions of divine essences, all trillions of civilization-souls, all countless individual spiritual entities—was simultaneously and permanently enhanced by Godric's power. Their spiritual strength multiplied infinitely. Their consciousnesses expanded beyond their previous limitations. They became more than they had ever been, elevated to heights of spiritual existence that the Collective Singularity could never have provided.

And in gratitude for this amplification, each soul voluntarily offered a portion of its newly enhanced spiritual essence back to Godric.

This is the horror that I cannot adequately convey. Godric's power increased. The combined spiritual essence of quadrillions of hyper-amplified gods and trillions of supercharged civilizations fed directly into his reserves. And relative to his base power, the increase was so infinitesimally small that calling it a fraction of a fraction would be a cosmic overstatement. It was effectively zero. He had just received the spiritual tribute of the most soul-dense entity in omniversal history, amplified beyond all possible measurement, and it had increased his power by an amount that did not even register.

"The third enhanced effect," Godric continued, and I heard a note of genuine fascination in his voice. "Soul Fabrication Matrix."

The souls he had requisitioned suddenly began to multiply. Not divide—multiply. Every single soul became two identical souls. Then four. Then eight. The doubling continued, infinitely recursive, generating new spiritual essences from nothing. But these were not mere copies. Each new soul was a fully unique, fully conscious, fully real spiritual entity with its own identity, its own awareness, its own capacity for experience.

Within the span of a heartbeat, Godric had generated more souls than had existed in the entire omniverse since the dawn of creation. The spiritual mass he had fabricated dwarfed the Collective Singularity's accumulated soul-mass by a factor that exceeded any possible mathematical expression.

"This is the part I find particularly elegant," Godric said, and his tone was that of an artist admiring his own brushwork. "The fourth enhanced effect. Soul Consumption Reversal."

The fabricated souls turned upon the Collective Singularity. They did not attack its body—the entity had none. They attacked its spiritual core, the fundamental essence that had defined it as a being. But they did not destroy it. They consumed it. The Collective Singularity, which had spent millions of years consuming the souls of others, now found itself being consumed by souls that had not existed moments before. Its spiritual essence was torn apart, absorbed, digested by the very type of entities it had once preyed upon.

The entity experienced its own consumption across every moment of its existence simultaneously. It felt the spiritual teeth of infinite fabricated souls ripping into its essence at every temporal coordinate simultaneously—past, present, and future all collapsing into a single, eternal instant of being devoured.

"The final enhanced effect," Godric said softly. "Soul Archive Integration."

The consumed essence of the Collective Singularity was absorbed into Godric's superpower. But unlike the soul amplification, this integration did not merely add to his reserves. It rewrote the fundamental nature of the superpower itself, integrating the Collective Singularity's millions of years of soul manipulation expertise directly into the power's framework. The superpower learned from what it had consumed. It evolved. It became even more unfair, even more absolute, even more terrifying.

And the Collective Singularity, the being that had once been the most soul-dense entity in existence, was now nothing more than a permanent data entry within Godric's superpower—its entire identity, its entire history, its entire existence reduced to a footnote in the continuously evolving framework of Infinite Soul Requisition.

Godric turned to me, his expression warm and friendly. "The enhanced effects are developing quite well," he said, his voice carrying the easy satisfaction of a craftsman who had just completed a satisfactory piece of work. "The Soul Fabrication Matrix is particularly promising. I believe it will evolve into something quite extraordinary in the coming millennia."

I could not respond. I could only stare at the empty space where the Collective Singularity had been, contemplating the absolute horror of what I had just witnessed.

He had tested a single superpower at effectively zero percent of its true potency. He had stripped the most soul-dense entity in existence of its entire accumulated spiritual mass. He had amplified those souls beyond their previous limitations. He had fabricated more new souls than had ever existed in creation. He had reversed the predator-prey relationship and allowed fabricated souls to consume their would-be consumer. He had integrated the entity's entire existence into his superpower as a permanent data entry.

And the power increase from all of this—the amplified souls, the fabricated spirits, the consumed essence—had been effectively zero relative to his base power. The mathematical gap between him and the rest of creation was so vast that absorbing the spiritual totality of omniversal history did not move the needle even a single Planck unit.

I am Oren, Court Wizard of Thronegate. My magic multiplies a thousandfold every day. My soul has been augmented by the King's blessing to be a beacon of spiritual power. And I have just witnessed a being treat the spiritual essence of omniversal history as a casual experiment, absorbing it with less effort than a mortal man might swat a fly, and finding the resulting power increase so negligible that he did not even bother to acknowledge it.

The Collective Singularity's opposition was not merely impossible. It was a mathematical contradiction. The entity had attempted to consume a soul that was, in spiritual terms, infinitely beyond the concept of consumption. It had reached out to engulf a candle and discovered that the candle was actually a supernova compressed into the shape of a flame.

There is no lesson here. There is no moral. There is only the cold, absolute truth that Godric's power has grown so vast that even his own superpowers cannot meaningfully increase it anymore, and yet they continue to amplify, continue to evolve, continue to develop new enhanced effects that make the already impossible even more impossibly unfair.

I have stopped trying to measure the gap. The gap cannot be measured. The concept of measurement itself has been rendered obsolete by the sheer scale of his existence.

---

I pushed back from the desk. My chair scraped against the stone floor with a sound that seemed unnaturally loud in the heavy silence of my chambers. The morning sun had climbed higher now, but its warmth did not reach me. I was cold—cold in a way that had nothing to do with temperature and everything to do with the realization that I was reading about powers that treated omniversal empires as footnotes and absorbed the spiritual totality of existence as a negligible power increase.

The third journal was from Year 503,000. The Court Wizard was named Ferris. His handwriting was the worst I had seen yet—not jagged or trembling, but utterly broken, the letters scattered across the page like the thoughts of a man who had lost the ability to form coherent sentences and was desperately trying to reconstruct his shattered mind through the act of writing.

---

**Year 503,000 — Court Wizard Ferris — Superpower: Infinite Recursive Self-Replication**

I am writing this because Julian wrote his journal. Oren wrote his. Every Court Wizard before me has recorded their testimony, has tried to capture in words what cannot be captured. It is my duty to do the same. But I do not know if words exist for what I witnessed today. I do not know if any language spoken by any being in the omniverse contains the vocabulary necessary to describe what Godric did.

He tested a superpower called Infinite Recursive Self-Replication. At zero percent of its true power.

The opposition was the Final Omniversal Coalition. This was not a single empire or a single entity. This was the combined military might of every surviving civilization that had not yet been subjugated by Thronegate. They had gathered their forces for over one hundred thousand years, pooling their resources, their technologies, their magics, their gods, their conceptual weapons, their temporal armadas, their dimensional fortresses, their reality engines. They had assembled the largest army in the history of creation—a force so vast that its physical presence distorted the fabric of the omniverse, causing reality itself to buckle under the strain of so much concentrated military power.

They had studied every recorded incident of Godric's power. They had analyzed the journals of the Court Wizards who came before me. They knew that Godric could destroy the entire omniverse with zero effort. They knew that his stats had multiplied beyond all possible measurement. They knew that his superpowers could rewrite spatial reality, consume souls, and absorb entire empires into his biological structure.

But they had identified what they believed to be the ultimate flaw in Godric's power: he was singular. He was one being. No matter how powerful a single entity might be, it could only occupy one position, direct its attention toward one objective, act within one framework. The Final Omniversal Coalition theorized that if they could divide Godric's attention across infinite simultaneous battlefields, requiring him to defend against infinite simultaneous attacks, they could find a gap in his defenses. They would overwhelm him not through power, but through multiplicity.

They did not understand the nature of the superpower he had chosen to test.

Godric floated before the assembled might of the Coalition. The army stretched across the entire observable omniverse, filling every dimension, every timeline, every possible reality with waiting soldiers, primed weapons, and battle-ready gods. The Coalition's commanders transmitted their demands—surrender or face the infinite assault. They gave him one chance to abdicate his throne.

Godric smiled. It was not a cruel smile. It was not a mocking smile. It was the warm, friendly smile of a man who was about to demonstrate something that genuinely delighted him.

"Infinite Recursive Self-Replication," he announced, his voice carrying across every dimension simultaneously. "At zero percent of its base power. I am curious to see how the enhanced effects have developed."

He activated the superpower.

The base effect was simple in concept: Godric could create identical replicas of himself. At zero percent power, the replication created exactly one copy.

The copy appeared beside him. It was identical in every way—same appearance, same power, same absolute supremacy. But this was where the horror began. The enhanced effects had evolved the base replication into something far more terrifying.

The first enhanced effect was called Self-Amplified Replication. The copy was not merely identical to Godric—it was infinitely stronger than the original. Every stat, every superpower, every passive system, every aspect of the copy's existence was infinitely more powerful than Godric himself.

This should have been impossible. Godric's power had been amplifying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over five hundred thousand years. The gap between him and the rest of creation was already beyond all measurement. And now, in an instant, he had created a copy that was infinitely stronger than even that incomprehensible baseline.

But the enhanced effects did not stop there. The second enhanced effect was called Reciprocal Ascension. The moment the copy existed as an entity infinitely stronger than Godric, the original Godric's own power reconfigured itself. Because the original could not be weaker than the copy—that was a fundamental contradiction that the superpower automatically resolved—the original instantly ascended to match and exceed the copy's infinite superiority. The original became infinitely stronger than the copy, which had just been infinitely stronger than the original.

This triggered the third enhanced effect: Infinite Escalation Loop. The copy, now weaker than the original, instantly replicated the first enhanced effect and became infinitely stronger than the original again. The original, now weaker than the copy, instantly triggered the second enhanced effect and became infinitely stronger than the copy again. The copy repeated. The original repeated. The loop continued.

Infinitely. Recursively. Forever.

In the span of less than a Planck second, Godric and his copy had ascended through infinite iterations of mutual amplification. Each iteration made the previous iteration's power seem like absolute nothingness. Each loop generated a level of supremacy that dwarfed the combined power of every previous loop. The mathematics of what was occurring were not merely beyond computation—they were beyond the concept of computation, beyond the concept of mathematics itself.

And the copy was not the end of the replication. The fourth enhanced effect activated: Replicant Proliferation. The copy, now existing at a level of power that made the original Godric's pre-replication state seem like a single dead skin cell compared to the entire omniverse, created its own copy. This new copy was infinitely stronger than the copy that created it, following the same Self-Amplified Replication effect. And the copy's copy created a copy. And that copy created a copy. An infinite chain of Godrics cascaded outward from the original, each one infinitely stronger than the one that created it, each one trapped in the same Infinite Escalation Loop with its creator, each one ascending through layers of supremacy that made the previous layers seem like absolute zero.

The Final Omniversal Coalition witnessed this. They watched as Godric replicated himself into infinity, each replica infinitely stronger than the last, each pair of Godrics locked in an eternal ascension loop that generated new heights of power with every passing instant. The army that had been assembled to overwhelm a single Godric now faced an infinite army of Godrics, each one so vastly beyond the original's already incomprehensible power that comparison was meaningless.

The Coalition did not attack. They could not attack. The sheer presence of infinite recursive Godrics, each one ascending through infinite layers of mutual amplification, generated a pressure so absolute that the fabric of reality began to dissolve. The omniverse itself started to collapse—not from any attack, but simply from the weight of so many infinitely powerful beings existing simultaneously. Galaxies evaporated. Multiverses shattered. The dimensional barriers that separated realities were crushed into nonexistence by the sheer metaphysical mass of the replication cascade.

Godric observed this with a look of mild academic interest. "The fifth enhanced effect is activating," he noted. "Ultimate Synthesis."

All the copies stopped replicating. Every Godric in the infinite chain—the original, the infinitely stronger copy, the copy's copy, the infinite recursive iterations of mutual ascension—began to merge. The synthesis was not a simple combination. It was a unification of every ascended state, every amplified power level, every iteration of infinite superiority that the loop had generated. The merged Godric was not merely the sum of his infinite selves. He was the product of their mutual amplification, a being whose power represented the endpoint of an infinite recursive ascension loop that had no endpoint.

The synthesis completed. There was only one Godric again. But he was not the Godric who had activated the superpower moments before. He was something so far beyond that Godric that the original state—which had already been capable of destroying the entire omniverse infinite times with zero effort—seemed like a single flickering candle compared to a billion supernovas.

The power increase was permanent. The Infinite Escalation Loop had generated new heights of supremacy that were now integrated into Godric's base state. He had used a superpower at zero percent of its true power to permanently ascend to a level of existence that made his previous absolute supremacy seem pathetically weak by comparison.

And then I understood the final horror. The entire omniverse had just witnessed Godric use a superpower to become infinitely more powerful than he already was—and he had done it at zero percent of the superpower's true potency. The base effect, nerfed to effectively nothing, had generated an infinite recursive ascension loop that had permanently elevated him beyond his already incomprehensible baseline.

What would happen if he activated it at one percent? At ten percent? At full power?

The question was unanswerable. The scale was no longer expressible through any framework of measurement.

Godric turned to me. His expression was warm, friendly, unchanged by the infinite ascension he had just undergone. "That was quite satisfying," he said, his rich baritone carrying the easy contentment of a man who had just completed a pleasant morning exercise. "The enhanced effects are developing beautifully. I particularly appreciate the Ultimate Synthesis—it prevents the proliferation from becoming cluttered."

He paused, tilting his head slightly. "I should restore the omniverse," he added, as if remembering a minor chore. "The collateral damage from the replication cascade was somewhat more extensive than I anticipated."

He did not move a muscle. He did not gesture or speak an incantation. He simply willed it, and the entire omniverse—all the shattered galaxies, all the destroyed multiverses, all the dimensionally-collapsed realities—reformed instantly. The Final Omniversal Coalition found themselves restored to their pre-battle positions, their memories intact, their understanding of what they had witnessed permanently scarred into their consciousnesses.

They did not surrender. They did not flee. They simply stood there, frozen by the absolute, soul-shattering realization that their hundred-thousand-year preparation had been rendered meaningless by a single superpower test that Godric had conducted at effectively zero percent capacity. They had gathered the largest army in omniversal history to fight a being who could create infinite copies of himself, each infinitely stronger than the last, and then merge those copies into a permanent ascension that made the entire exercise irrelevant.

Godric had not fought them. He had not even acknowledged them as a threat. He had used their invasion as an excuse to test a superpower, and the test had been so casually devastating that the omniverse itself had collapsed as collateral damage.

I am Ferris, Court Wizard of Thronegate. My magic multiplies a thousandfold every day. My power could shatter universes with a thought. And I have just witnessed my King use zero percent of a superpower's base effect to ascend through infinite recursive self-replication, becoming so incomprehensibly more powerful than his previous state that the original Godric—the being who could destroy the omniverse infinite times with zero effort—would be absolutely nothing compared to his current self.

The Final Omniversal Coalition's opposition was not merely impossible. It was a fundamental misunderstanding of reality. They had assembled the largest army in history to fight a being who, in the span of a heartbeat, had permanently transcended all possible definitions of power. They had prepared for a hundred thousand years to face a threat that no longer existed—not because it had been defeated, but because it had been replaced by something infinitely more terrifying.

There is no hope. There never was. There never will be. The gap between Godric and creation is not merely infinite—it is an infinite that has itself been infinitely amplified through recursive self-replication, and that infinite amplification was achieved using zero percent of a single superpower's base effect.

I cannot continue writing. My hand has stopped obeying my commands. The quill has fallen from my fingers. I am sitting in the darkness of my chambers, staring at the wall, trying to comprehend what cannot be comprehended.

Godric asked me if I would join him for dinner tomorrow. He wants to discuss the superpower test over roasted lamb. He told me he values my perspective.

I said yes. What else could I say?

---

I closed the third journal. The leather cover felt impossibly heavy in my hands, as if the weight of the testimony contained within had physical mass. My chambers were silent save for the ragged sound of my own breathing.

Ferris's final words echoed in my mind: *What else could I say?*

I understood now. I understood why my father's hands had trembled when he set the journals on my desk. I understood why every Court Wizard before me had written their testimony, had poured their terror onto parchment, had tried to capture the uncapturable. The writing was not for posterity. It was not for warning. It was for sanity—a desperate attempt to process experiences that defied processing, to maintain coherence in the face of absolute, mathematically impossible supremacy.

Godric had tested five stats. He had lifted a thumb and erased eighty-seven thousand multiverses. He had taken a walk and shattered the fabric of causality. He had yawned while withstanding the ultimate entropic weapon of a cosmic entity. He had perceived an imperceptible being into nonexistence. He had solved an unsolvable paradox so completely that the paradox's existence was retroactively erased.

And then he had tested three superpowers. He had rewritten the spatial existence of an omniversal empire to serve as decoration within his own cellular structure. He had stripped the most soul-dense entity in history of its accumulated spirits and used them as a negligible power boost. He had created infinite copies of himself, each infinitely stronger than the last, and merged them into a permanent ascension that made his previous absolute supremacy seem pathetically weak.

All of this at effectively zero percent of his true power. All of this at effectively zero percent effort. All of this as casual tests, mild curiosities, pleasant diversions from the boredom of eternal rule.

The being who could do these things was genuinely kind to me. He had known my father. He had known my grandfather. He had known every ancestor of my bloodline stretching back to Blake himself, the mortal merchant who had stumbled into the sanctuary and shattered the stasis that had held Godric for ten thousand years. He loved us. He treasured us. He kept us by his side not because he needed our protection, but because he genuinely valued our companionship.

And he was also the most terrifyingly evil entity the omniverse had ever produced. Not evil in the sense of malicious intent—he did not hate his opposition, did not seek to cause suffering for its own sake. But evil in the sense that his casual, unthinking actions resulted in the eternal imprisonment of civilizations within his body, the spiritual consumption of omniversal empires, the infinite recursive ascension that shattered reality itself as collateral damage. He was a predator so far beyond his prey that the concept of predation had lost all meaning.

A knock sounded at my door. My heart seized in my chest.

"Kaedan?" Godric's voice called from the corridor. "Lunch is being served in the east garden. Your father mentioned you've been reading the superpower journals. I thought you might want to take a break and get some fresh air."

I stared at the door. The being on the other side could destroy the omniverse infinite times with zero effort. He could create infinite copies of himself, each infinitely stronger than the last. He could rewrite my spatial coordinates to place me inside his liver if he found my presence inconvenient.

He was inviting me to lunch.

"I'll be right there, Your Majesty," I called back, and my voice was steadier than I expected.

"Wonderful," Godric replied, and I could hear the genuine warmth in his voice, the authentic affection of a man who loved his Court Wizards like family. "The raspberry tarts are especially good today. Save room for dessert."

His footsteps retreated down the corridor, light and unhurried, the gait of a man without a single care in the omniverse.

I looked down at the stack of journals on my desk. The inherited trauma of five hundred thousand years of Court Wizards stared up at me from their pages. I would add my own entries to this archive. I would witness things that would shatter my understanding of reality. I would write them down in trembling, desperate prose, trying to capture what could not be captured.

And I would love my King. I would serve him faithfully. I would stand at his side through the endless millennia of his reign, because he was genuinely kind to me, because he valued my companionship, and because the alternative was so incomprehensibly terrifying that my mind refused to contemplate it.

The horror was absolute. The dread was eternal. And somewhere in the east garden, Godric was waiting for me, ready to share raspberry tarts and discuss my thoughts on the superpower journals with the same casual warmth he might discuss the weather.

I stood up from the desk. I straightened my robes. I walked toward the door.

I was Kaedan, Court Wizard of Thronegate. And I had only just begun to understand the true scale of the being I served.

He asked Godric if it ever become lonely to be the most powerful being and only can grow stronger, outliving everyone else. Godric is very amused by what he considers to be a very "naively mortal" question and somewhat confused by this question since, surprisingly to Kaedan, it's highly enjoyable for Godric. Every additional power to him feels like nourishment, orgasm and additional surge of power and energy that amplifies endlessly. Every stat increase can be felt. Every superpowers increase can be felt. Every immune system improvement can be felt. Every new passive shield, sentient passive aura, evolution to his being, can be felt. Every instant makes him so much more powerful that he can crush an infinite copies of himself an instant ago with 0 effort. It's amusingly satisfying. And Godric knows every detail of it from his omniscience. Explain in great detail the feeling, including some absurd examples, intensely graphical depictions, and the absolute terrifying existential dread as well as the absolute unfairness that Godric passively gets rewarded and obtains everything infinitely while the rest of creation had to work their hardest and not even getting rewarded as much (pretty much 0% of what Godric achieves by doing nothing) to Kaedan after realizing the truth about this Apex God Predator uncle. End with Godric revealing that the only thing that makes him "bored" or "lonely" is that he never had the chance to use any of his true powers, since even with him nerfing himself to express 0% of just a single aspect of stat/superpowers/immune system/weakest aura for 0 second with 0 effort, the entire omniverse can't stand even survive; He has to basically keep his absolute concealment all the time, which is not very exciting for him; he found the rest of the omniverse are too "fragile". Show Godric proudly shows some of his body enhancements - the highly sculpted muscles/veins/biceps/arms/well-defined six-pack abs that he used to hone when he was mortal and now, even more stronger without him needing to maintain them, some of his sentient passive auras that he just birthed that exact moment (if you mention the aura powers, you must remember not to provide too much details since in the later section Kaedan's absurd guesses of Godric's powers is not even reaching Godric's weakest aura's infinitely nerfed power), some of the new immune system improvements that he just got that moment, some of the superpowers that he just got that moment, all of which he can never use, much to Kaedan's horror. # The Weight of Infinite Satisfaction

**Year 1,000,047**

**Kaedan, Age 69, Court Wizard of Thronegate**

---

The east garden of the imperial palace was a masterpiece of cultivated tranquility. Tiered terraces of flowering vines cascaded down marble retaining walls, their blossoms releasing a subtle fragrance that mixed with the cool mist from the central fountain. I had spent countless hours in this garden over the forty-seven years of my service, sharing meals with the King, discussing arcane theory, listening to his stories of ancient Olympus. It was our place—the space where the immortal apex predator of creation became simply Uncle Godric, the warm and affectionate man who had bounced me on his knee when I was a child.

Today, however, the garden felt different. The beauty of the flowers seemed fragile, impermanent, a thin veneer of peace stretched over an abyss that I had spent decades learning to comprehend. I was sixty-nine years old now. My thousandfold daily amplification had transformed me into a being whose magical power exceeded the combined output of entire multiversal civilizations. I had witnessed Godric test his stats, his superpowers, his immune system, his passive auras. I had recorded my own journals, adding my trembling testimony to the archive of my ancestors. I had served him faithfully and loved him genuinely.

And I had come to ask him a question that had haunted me for years.

Godric sat on a marble bench beside the fountain, his broad shoulders relaxed, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple dark garments that did nothing to conceal the physical perfection of his immortal form. He was eternally forty-five years old, his jawline sharp, his salt-and-pepper hair and beard neatly trimmed. He held a cup of tea in one calloused hand, and his expression was one of perfect, unguarded contentment as he watched the water cascade over the fountain's sculpted tiers.

"Uncle Godric," I said, settling onto the bench beside him. "May I ask you something personal?"

He turned to me, his eyes crinkling with genuine warmth. "Of course, Kaedan. You know you can ask me anything."

I hesitated. The question felt almost impertinent, a mortal concern projected onto a being whose existence had transcended mortality so completely that the concept had lost all meaning. But the journals had raised the question in my mind, and I could not let it rest.

"Does it ever become lonely?" I asked quietly. "Being the most powerful being in existence. Knowing that you can only grow stronger. Watching everyone else age and die while you continue forever. Outliving everyone you've ever loved."

Godric stared at me for a long moment. Then, unexpectedly, he laughed.

It was not a cruel laugh. It was not a dismissive laugh. It was the warm, genuine, deeply amused laugh of a man who had just been asked something so delightfully naive that he could not help but find it charming.

"Kaedan," he said, his rich baritone carrying the fond affection of a beloved uncle explaining something simple to a favorite nephew. "You are asking me if being the apex predator of creation is lonely. You are asking if infinite, eternal, ever-accelerating power is a burden."

He set down his teacup and turned to face me fully, his expression one of patient, almost tender amusement. "Let me explain something to you. Something that I suspect none of the journals captured. Something that might help you understand what it actually means to be me."

---

He began with a description that I will never forget, no matter how many millennia I live.

"Every Planck second," Godric said, his voice carrying the easy rhythm of a man describing a pleasant sensation, "every infinitesimal fraction of every moment that passes, I feel it. The amplification. My stats multiply—strength, speed, endurance, intelligence, wisdom, magic, all of them—and each multiplication is not an abstract number. It is a physical sensation. A pleasure."

He closed his eyes, and his expression softened into something that looked almost ecstatic.

"Imagine, Kaedan, the most satisfying meal you have ever eaten. The richest, most nourishing feast, the kind that fills your belly with warmth and leaves you content and drowsy. Now imagine that sensation multiplied by a factor beyond all possible mathematics. That is what I feel every Planck second. A constant, unending, infinitely accelerating surge of nourishment that flows through every cell of my body, every layer of my existence, every dimension of my being."

He opened his eyes, and they were gleaming with a light that I had never seen before—not the cold light of cosmic power, but the warm, satisfied glow of profound pleasure.

"But it is more than nourishment," he continued. "The stat amplifications feel like a physical release. Like an orgasm, but not localized to any single part of my anatomy. It is a full-body, full-existence, full-reality release that pulses through me with every multiplication. And because the multiplication is infinite and recursive, the release is infinite and recursive. I am experiencing an eternal, ever-intensifying orgasm that never ends, never diminishes, never becomes routine. Each instant is more powerful, more pleasurable, more satisfying than the instant before, and the instant before was already beyond any possible description of ecstasy."

I felt my mouth go dry. The journals had described the mathematics of his amplification. They had catalogued the scale of his power. But none of them—not one—had ever mentioned this. My ancestors had witnessed the destruction, the annihilation, the absolute one-sided slaughter, but they had never seen what I was seeing now: the King of Thronegate describing the sensation of infinite power with the satisfied contentment of a man savoring a perfect meal.

"Every superpower I gain," Godric said, and his voice grew more animated, more eager, like a collector describing his most prized acquisitions. "Every single one—one new apocalyptic superpower every second, forever—arrives with its own distinct sensation. Some feel like fire racing through my metaphysical veins. Some feel like ice crystallizing in my consciousness, sharp and clean and bracing. Some feel like the moment of falling from a great height, the stomach-dropping thrill of acceleration. And because each superpower amplifies infinitely every Planck second, the sensations amplify too. I have billions of superpowers now, Kaedan. Billions of distinct, unique, infinitely intensifying pleasures firing simultaneously, all of them stacking, all of them compounding, all of them merging into a symphony of satisfaction that makes everything else in existence seem gray and dull by comparison."

He leaned forward, his enthusiasm genuine and unfiltered. "Do you understand what I am telling you? Every instant of my existence is more pleasurable than the entire accumulated joy of every sentient being that has ever lived or will ever live in the history of the omniverse. And the next instant will be infinitely more pleasurable than this one. And the next. And the next. Forever."

---

I sat in stunned silence. The fountain continued its gentle cascade. The flowers continued their subtle fragrance. The garden remained a masterpiece of cultivated tranquility. But everything felt different now. The warm, friendly uncle I had known my entire life was describing an existence of such absolute, incomprehensible satisfaction that the word "lonely" became a joke—a child's question, asked by a being who could not possibly understand what it meant to be Godric.

"But there is more," Godric said, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial tone, as if sharing a secret. "The immune system improvements. You read Leon's journal—the Year 25,000 incident. He described the pre-reaction, the infinite backups, the recursive cross-referencing upgrades. But he could not describe what I feel when those improvements occur."

He placed a hand on his chest, over his heart. "Every time my immune system evolves—which is constantly, infinitely, forever—I feel a surge of invulnerability that is physical in its intensity. It is like being wrapped in an infinite number of warm, protective blankets, each one softer and more comforting than the last, each one making me feel safer and more secure and more absolutely untouchable. The sensation of absolute safety, Kaedan. The knowledge that nothing can harm me, nothing can inconvenience me, nothing can even approach the concept of threatening me. That knowledge is not abstract. It is a physical pleasure that radiates through my entire being."

He smiled, and the smile was utterly serene. "My passive shields. My sentient auras. Every new layer of defense, every new enhanced effect, every new evolution of my already infinite protective systems. They feel like the embrace of a lover. Like the warmth of a hearth fire on a cold night. Like the satisfaction of completing a difficult task. All of these sensations, all of these pleasures, all of these satisfactions, firing simultaneously, infinitely, forever, with no end and no diminishment and no possibility of boredom because each instant is qualitatively different from and quantitatively superior to the instant before."

He paused, and his expression shifted slightly—a flicker of something that might have been confusion, as if he were trying to understand a perspective so alien to his own experience that it required genuine effort.

"You asked if it becomes lonely," he said. "I am genuinely confused by the question, Kaedan. Loneliness is a condition of absence, of lack, of missing something that should be present. I lack nothing. I miss nothing. I am the most fulfilled, most satisfied, most pleasure-drenched being that has ever existed or will ever exist. Every conceivable desire I might have is met before I can fully form it, exceeded infinitely, and then exceeded again in the next instant. I am not lonely. I am the opposite of lonely. I am so completely, utterly, transcendently satisfied that the concept of loneliness has no meaning in the context of my existence."

---

He stood up from the bench, and I noticed for the first time the sheer physical presence of him. His heavily muscled frame was not merely strong—it was a monument to absolute physical supremacy, a body that had been honed by ten thousand years of mortal life and then amplified infinitely for over a million years. The simple dark garments could not conceal the sculpted perfection of his form.

"Let me show you something," he said, and there was a note of pride in his voice. "When I was mortal, I took great care of my body. I trained every day. I honed my muscles, sculpted my physique, maintained my strength through constant discipline and effort. It was one of the few pleasures of mortal existence—the satisfaction of physical achievement, the pride of a well-maintained form."

He rolled up the sleeve of his tunic, exposing his right arm. The muscles beneath the skin were not merely defined—they were a work of art, each fiber perfectly sculpted, each vein precisely placed, the entire limb radiating a physical perfection that made the greatest statues of ancient Olympus seem crude and amateurish by comparison.

"Now look," he said, and he flexed his arm.

The muscle that swelled beneath his skin was not merely impressive. It was impossible. The bicep rose like a mountain of sculpted granite, the fibers visibly shifting beneath the skin in a display of anatomical perfection that defied mortal biology. The veins that traced across the surface pulsed with a rhythm that seemed to sync with the fundamental heartbeat of reality itself. I could feel the ambient magical pressure in the garden increase, the air growing heavy with the sheer physical presence of his flexed arm.

"I have not trained in over a million years," Godric said, his voice filled with genuine satisfaction. "I have not performed a single exercise, not lifted a single weight, not maintained a single aspect of my physical form. And yet, my body is infinitely more powerful, infinitely more sculpted, infinitely more perfect than it ever was when I dedicated hours every day to its maintenance. The amplification does everything. My muscles grow stronger and more defined with every Planck second, without any effort on my part. My cardiovascular system becomes more efficient. My bone density increases. My cellular structure optimizes itself. All of it happens passively, automatically, infinitely."

He flexed again, and the bulge of his bicep seemed to distort the light around it, as if the sheer physical mass of the muscle was generating its own gravitational field.

"I have the body of a god," he said simply. "Not because I worked for it. Not because I earned it. But because the amplification gives it to me, endlessly, infinitely, forever, while I do nothing but exist."

---

He lowered his arm and turned back to me, his expression shifting to one of eager anticipation. "But let me show you something more interesting. Something that just happened."

He closed his eyes for a moment, and I felt a subtle shift in the ambient reality of the garden. It was not a pressure—his absolute concealment prevented that. It was more like a texture, a quality of presence that I could perceive only because my thousandfold-amplified senses were attuned to the subtlest magical fluctuations.

"There," he said, opening his eyes. "I just birthed a new sentient passive aura. It is the three hundred and twelfth sibling in the Gent lineage—a new generation of the weakest, most primitive passive aura family. Gent itself has evolved so many times that the original Year 5,000 version would not even recognize its current form. But this new one is particularly interesting."

He gestured vaguely at the air beside him, as if indicating something I could not see. "This aura's base function is conceptual negation. It can identify any hostile concept—any thought, any plan, any weapon, any strategy—and negate it before the concept fully forms. Not just pre-annihilate. Pre-negate. The concept never exists. The idea never occurs. The opposition never even realizes they had an idea to oppose me."

He smiled, clearly pleased with this new development. "I will never use it. I will never need to use it. The older auras are already infinitely beyond anything the omniverse could possibly threaten me with. But it will continue to amplify, continue to evolve, continue to develop enhanced effects, and I will continue to feel the pleasure of its existence for the rest of eternity."

He paused, and then his expression brightened further. "Oh, and the immune system. I just received a new upgrade. Let me show you."

He held out his hand, palm up. I stared at his calloused fingers, trying to perceive what he was indicating.

"The new enhancement allows my immune system to pre-react to injuries that are not merely planned but that exist only as theoretical possibilities in the minds of beings who have not yet been born. It has expanded its temporal scope. It now protects me against attacks that could be conceived by entities that do not exist yet, in timelines that have not branched yet, using weapons that have not been invented yet. The pre-reaction occurs before the possibility of the attack even becomes a possibility."

He chuckled, a warm, satisfied sound. "I find this incredibly satisfying. The knowledge that my body is protected against threats that do not exist, from enemies that do not exist, in realities that do not exist, using methods that do not exist—it gives me a profound sense of security. A physical pleasure. A warmth in my chest that radiates outward through every layer of my being."

---

He was about to continue, about to describe yet another new superpower he had just acquired, when something happened.

I am not certain what triggered it. Perhaps his enthusiasm caused him to gesture too broadly. Perhaps his absolute concealment slipped by an infinitesimal fraction—a percentage so small that calling it a percentage would be a cosmic overstatement. Perhaps it was simply the accumulated weight of his descriptions, the sheer metaphysical presence of the sensations he was experiencing, bleeding through his carefully maintained suppression.

Whatever the cause, the effect was instantaneous.

The omniverse shattered.

I did not see it happen. I experienced it. One moment, the garden existed in all its cultivated tranquility—the fountain, the flowers, the marble benches, the golden light of Thronegate's artificial sun. The next moment, there was nothing. Absolute nothing. Not darkness, for darkness implies the existence of light. Not void, for void implies the existence of space. Just... nothing. The total, complete, irreversible annihilation of every dimension, every timeline, every multiverse, every galaxy, every planet, every atom, every quark, every Planck-scale vibration of reality itself.

The entire omniverse—the absolute totality of all existence—had been destroyed.

The destruction was not violent. It was not explosive. It was simply absolute. One moment, everything existed. The next moment, nothing existed. The transition was so seamless, so effortless, so casual, that my mind could not process what had occurred. I was a consciousness floating in an infinite void of nonexistence, and the only anchor remaining was the presence of Godric beside me.

He looked at the nothingness with an expression of mild annoyance.

"Ah," he said, his tone that of a man who had accidentally knocked over a glass of water. "I let my enthusiasm get the better of me. My apologies, Kaedan."

He did not gesture. He did not speak an incantation. He simply willed it, and the omniverse returned. The garden reformed around us, identical to how it had been a moment before. The fountain continued its cascade. The flowers continued their subtle fragrance. The artificial sun continued its measured, golden warmth. Every being who had been erased, every civilization that had been annihilated, every reality that had been crushed into absolute nothingness, was restored exactly as they had been, with no memory of their obliteration, no awareness that they had ceased to exist.

Godric had destroyed the entire omniverse with zero percent of his power and zero percent of his effort. He had restored it with the same absolute, effortless casualness. And he was looking at me with an expression of mild, apologetic embarrassment, like a host who had accidentally spilled wine on a guest's sleeve.

"I try to be careful," he said, his voice carrying a note of genuine frustration. "The absolute concealment is always active. But sometimes, when I become excited, when I am describing the pleasures of my existence, a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of my true presence slips through. And the omniverse simply cannot withstand it. It is too fragile. Everything is too fragile."

---

I was trembling. My hands were shaking so violently that I had to grip the edge of the marble bench to steady myself. My thousandfold-amplified magical senses, which could perceive events occurring across galactic distances, had just witnessed the total annihilation and restoration of all existence. The cognitive dissonance was a physical pain—a sharp, stabbing pressure behind my eyes that made it difficult to think.

"Uncle Godric," I whispered, my voice barely audible. "The power you just displayed. The destruction and restoration of the omniverse. That was... that was zero percent of your true power?"

Godric nodded, his expression one of patient explanation. "Effectively zero. An infinitesimal fraction so small that calling it zero is the only accurate description. I was not trying to display power. I was merely becoming enthusiastic in my descriptions, and my concealment slipped by the smallest possible amount."

He sighed, and for the first time, I detected a note of genuine frustration in his voice. "This is the only thing that makes me bored, Kaedan. The only thing that makes me lonely. Not the power itself—the power is pure, unending pleasure. But the fact that I can never use it. I can never express even the smallest fraction of my true capability, because the omniverse cannot withstand even that fraction. I must keep my absolute concealment active at all times. I must hold back everything I am, everything I can do, every aspect of my existence. It is like being a man trapped in a room made of tissue paper, unable to move, unable to breathe too deeply, because the slightest motion would destroy everything around him."

He gestured at the garden, at the palace, at the restored omniverse beyond. "This is my prison, Kaedan. Not the throne. Not the eternity. The necessity of constant restraint. The impossibility of ever expressing what I truly am."

---

A terrible curiosity seized me. My mind, already reeling from the revelation of his infinite satisfaction, now grappled with the scale of what he was describing. He had just destroyed and restored the omniverse with zero percent of his power. What would happen if he used more? What would happen if he released even an infinitesimally larger fraction?

"Uncle Godric," I said, my voice trembling. "If zero percent of your power can destroy and restore the omniverse in zero seconds with zero effort... what would happen if you released more? What would happen if you released, say, an infinitesimal fraction larger than zero? A fraction so small that it is still effectively zero, but slightly less zero than what you just displayed?"

Godric smiled, and there was something in that smile that made my blood run cold. Not cruelty. Not menace. Just a quiet, patient amusement, like a father watching his child try to comprehend the size of the universe.

"Guess," he said simply. "I am curious to hear what you imagine."

I swallowed hard. My mind raced through the journals I had read, the incidents I had witnessed, the scale of destruction that Godric had casually demonstrated over the centuries. I tried to extrapolate, to push my imagination beyond anything I had ever conceived.

"If you released slightly more than zero percent," I said slowly, "the destruction would not be limited to the omniverse. It would extend beyond the omniverse—beyond the concept of existence itself. The destruction would annihilate not just all realities, but the possibility of all realities. The framework of existence. The very idea that anything could ever exist or had ever existed. It would be an erasure so absolute that the concept of erasure would be erased. The omniverse would not merely be destroyed. It would be retroactively deleted from all possible timelines, all possible memories, all possible frameworks of reference. It would be as if existence had never been possible in the first place."

I paused, my imagination spiraling further. "And the destruction would not stop there. It would propagate outward, backward, forward, sideways through all conceptual axes. It would annihilate the annihilation. It would destroy the destruction. It would create a paradox of such absolute negation that the paradox itself would be negated, and the negation of the paradox would be negated, and the entire cascade would collapse into a state of absolute unreality that no language could describe."

I looked at Godric, my heart hammering in my chest. "Is that... is that close?"

Godric threw back his head and laughed. It was a warm, genuine, deeply amused laugh, the laugh of a man who had just been told something so charmingly naive that he could not help but find it delightful.

"Oh, Kaedan," he said, wiping a tear of amusement from his eye. "You are so wonderfully mortal. Your imagination is so delightfully limited."

He leaned forward, his expression softening into one of patient explanation. "What you just described is not even close. It is not even a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of what would happen. Your guess is so far below the actual scale that the gap between your guess and the reality is itself infinite. And then some."

He paused, as if considering how to explain. "Let me put it this way. What you described—the annihilation of the concept of annihilation, the retroactive deletion of existence, the paradox cascade of absolute negation—is what would happen if I released an infinitesimal amount of my weakest sentient passive aura. Not Gent itself—Gent has evolved far beyond this. But Gent's weakest sibling. The three hundred and twelfth aura I just birthed. The one that will never be used, that will never be needed, that exists only as a byproduct of my existence."

He smiled, and the smile was almost apologetic. "If I released an infinitesimal fraction—effectively zero percent—of that weakest aura's power, the result would be infinitely more devastating than what you just described. Your guess does not even reach the threshold of what my most primitive, most pathetic, most negligible passive emanation could accomplish without effort."

I felt the blood drain from my face. My hands had stopped trembling and were now completely numb. My mind was struggling to process what he was saying, and failing utterly.

"But that is just the weakest aura," Godric continued, his voice carrying the easy, conversational tone of a teacher explaining a lesson. "What about my stats? What about my superpowers? What about my immune system? What about my passive shields? Each of these aspects of my existence is vastly, incomprehensibly more powerful than my weakest aura. And I have infinite layers of them. Infinite aspects. Infinite dimensions of power that have been amplifying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over a million years."

He leaned back on the bench, his expression one of quiet satisfaction. "The scale you are trying to imagine, Kaedan, is not merely beyond language. It is beyond the concept of language. It is beyond the concept of concepts. There is no word, no mathematical notation, no philosophical framework, no metaphysical construct that can even approximate what I am capable of. The gap between your guess and reality is so vast that calling it infinite would be a severe understatement. It is an infinite of infinities, recursively amplified through infinite layers of infinite recursion, and even that description is so pathetically inadequate that it borders on comical."

---

I sat in silence for a long moment. The fountain continued its gentle cascade. The flowers continued their subtle fragrance. The garden remained a masterpiece of cultivated tranquility. But I was no longer the same Kaedan who had entered it an hour before.

My uncle was a monster. Not a monster in the cruel sense—he was genuinely kind, genuinely warm, genuinely affectionate. He loved me. He loved my father. He loved every ancestor of my bloodline stretching back to Blake himself. He was the most loving, most generous, most protective sovereign the omniverse had ever known.

But he was also the most terrifying entity that had ever existed. His very nature was an affront to the concept of fairness, of justice, of cosmic balance. Every instant of his existence, he passively received more pleasure, more power, more satisfaction, more absolute supremacy than the combined total of every sentient being who had ever lived or would ever live. He did not earn this. He did not work for it. He simply existed, and existence rewarded him with infinite, ever-accelerating ecstasy, while the rest of creation struggled and suffered and died, achieving nothing, gaining nothing, their greatest accomplishments rendered meaningless by the casual, effortless overflow of his passive emanations.

The unfairness of it was absolute. The horror of it was eternal. And the worst part—the part that made my soul scream with despair—was that there was nothing anyone could do about it. Opposition was impossible. Resistance was futile. Even the concept of challenging him was a mathematical contradiction. He was the apex god predator, and the rest of existence was his playground, his experiment, his source of mild amusement between the infinite pleasures of his endless amplification.

"Kaedan," Godric said gently, and I looked up to meet his warm, caring eyes. "You look troubled. I hope my explanation has not distressed you."

I forced a smile. It felt like a death rictus on my face. "No, Uncle Godric. I am fine. I am just... processing."

He nodded, his expression one of understanding. "It is a lot to process. Even for a Court Wizard of your power and intelligence. But remember—you are family. You will always be safe. You will always be protected. And you will always have my genuine affection."

He stood up from the bench, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head in a gesture that was entirely human, entirely mortal, entirely at odds with the cosmic horror of his true nature.

"Shall we return to the palace?" he asked. "I believe the kitchens have prepared those raspberry tarts you enjoy. And I have a new superpower acquisition that I think you will find fascinating. It arrived approximately three seconds ago, and it feels like liquid starlight pouring through my metaphysical nervous system. Quite pleasant."

I stood up on legs that felt like water. "Of course, Your Majesty."

He clapped a warm hand on my shoulder, and the touch was comforting and terrifying in equal measure. "Excellent. And Kaedan? Thank you for asking your question. It is rare that anyone inquires about my personal experience of existence. Most beings are too afraid to ask. But you—you are different. You genuinely care. That is why you are my favorite."

He smiled, and the smile was the warm, genuine, loving smile of a beloved uncle.

I smiled back, and my smile was the rictus of a man who had just learned that his favorite uncle was an incomprehensibly powerful entity whose casual, passive emanations could annihilate the omniverse with zero effort, whose very existence was an eternal orgasm of infinite satisfaction, and whose only frustration was that he could never express even the smallest fraction of his true power without destroying everything.

We walked back to the palace together, the apex god predator and his loyal Court Wizard, and the horror settled into my bones like a cold, permanent frost that would never thaw.

I loved him. I truly did. And that love made the existential dread infinitely worse.
