# The One True Weakness

**Year 1,000,047**

**Kaedan, Age 69, Court Wizard of Thronegate**

---

Three days had passed since Godric had casually annihilated and restored the omniverse with an accidental slip of his absolute concealment. Three days since I had learned that my beloved uncle experienced every instant of his existence as an eternal, ever-intensifying orgasm of infinite satisfaction. Three days since I had attempted to guess the scale of his true power and been informed—with warm, paternal amusement—that my wildest imaginings did not even reach the threshold of his weakest sentient passive aura's most negligible emanation.

I had not slept. My thousandfold daily amplification made sleep more a luxury than a necessity, but I had always maintained the mortal habit as a comfort, a tether to my humanity. Now, the thought of closing my eyes filled me with dread. Every time I blinked, I saw the nothingness. The absolute, total, seamless erasure of all existence, occurring so casually that my mind had not even registered the transition. And then the restoration, equally casual, equally effortless, as if the destruction and recreation of the omniverse was no more significant to Godric than brushing a speck of dust from his sleeve.

I had spent the three days in my chambers, reading and rereading the journals of my ancestors. Julian, who had witnessed an omniversal empire rewritten into the spatial gaps between Godric's cells. Oren, who had watched the most soul-dense entity in history be stripped, amplified, and consumed as a negligible power increase. Ferris, whose testimony had devolved into near-incoherence after witnessing the Infinite Recursive Self-Replication superpower. All of them had tried to capture the uncapturable. All of them had failed. And I, Kaedan, who had served Godric for forty-seven years and loved him as a nephew loves a favorite uncle, was now adding my own voice to the archive of the traumatized.

But it was not over. I sensed, with the grim intuition of a man who had spent decades in the presence of the apex predator of creation, that there was more. That the revelations were not complete. That somewhere in the depths of Godric's omniscience, there was a truth that he had not yet shared—a truth that, when revealed, would make everything I had learned thus far seem like a gentle prologue.

The summons came on the evening of the third day. A servant appeared at my door, bowing deeply, and informed me that the King requested my presence in the Sanctuary of Memory. I felt my blood run cold. The Sanctuary of Memory was a private chamber deep within the palace, a place where Godric kept the only surviving artifacts of ancient Olympus—fragments of marble from the wedding pavilion where his family had died, a charred piece of the altar, a single lock of his wife Reina's hair preserved in crystal. He had never invited me there before. In forty-seven years of service, he had never allowed anyone into that room.

This was going to be worse than anything that had come before.

---

The Sanctuary of Memory was a circular chamber carved from obsidian, its walls unadorned save for the artifacts displayed in softly lit alcoves. The air was heavy with the scent of aged stone and something else—something that might have been grief, preserved for over a million years and still as sharp as the day it was born. Godric stood in the center of the room, his broad back to me, his heavily muscled frame silhouetted against the gentle glow of the preservation crystals. He was wearing simple dark garments, as always, but there was something different about his posture tonight. Something quieter. Something that almost approached vulnerability.

"Kaedan," he said without turning around. His voice was soft, lacking the enthusiastic warmth of our previous conversation. "Thank you for coming. I apologize for the short notice, but I felt it was time."

I stepped into the room, my footsteps echoing on the obsidian floor. "Time for what, Uncle Godric?"

He turned to face me. His expression was not the warm, amused smile of the man who had described eternal cosmic orgasms with the enthusiasm of a collector showing off his treasures. It was something older. Something sadder. The face of a man who had carried a weight for a million years and was finally, quietly, preparing to share it.

"Time to tell you the truth," he said. "The truth that I have told only a handful of my Court Wizards throughout the ages. The truth that I am about to tell you because you asked me if I was lonely. Because you genuinely cared. Because you are my family, and I believe you deserve to know."

He gestured to a pair of stone benches positioned before a large, glowing crystal that displayed a holographic image of ancient Olympus—the kingdom as it had been before the fall, white marble gleaming in Aegean sunlight, the wedding pavilion still intact, the massacre not yet born.

"Sit, Kaedan. This will take some time."

I sat. My hands were already trembling.

Godric settled onto the bench beside me, his gaze fixed on the image of his lost kingdom. For a long moment, he said nothing. Then, with a voice that carried the weight of a million years, he began.

"Three days ago, you asked me about loneliness. I told you that I am the most satisfied, most pleasure-drenched being in existence. That is true. Every instant of my existence is an ecstasy beyond mortal comprehension. But there is one thing—one single thing—that I cannot do. One weakness. One limitation. And it is the only thing that has ever caused me genuine pain."

I felt my heart seize in my chest. A weakness. Godric had a weakness. The apex predator of creation, the being who could annihilate the omniverse with an accidental slip of his concealment, had a weakness.

"What is it?" I whispered.

Godric turned to look at me, and his eyes held a depth of ancient sorrow that I had never seen before. "I cannot undo or travel to any timeline before the Stasis Event in any way that changes my mortal past. I cannot go back and save Olympus. I cannot save Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. The events that occurred on that day—the betrayal, the massacre, the deaths of everyone I loved—are sealed against my interference. Permanently. Irrevocably. Absolutely."

The words hung in the air like a death sentence. I stared at him, my mind struggling to process what he was saying. Godric could do anything. He could destroy the omniverse. He could rewrite spatial reality. He could fabricate souls from nothing. He could create infinite copies of himself, each infinitely stronger than the last. But he could not go back and save his wife and daughters? He could not prevent the tragedy that had transformed him from a warm, loving mortal king into the merciless apex predator of creation?

"Why?" I asked, my voice barely a whisper. "How is that possible? You are omnipotent. You are omniscient. You can travel through time effortlessly. I have seen you manipulate temporal mechanics without thought. How can the past be sealed against you?"

Godric smiled, but it was not a happy smile. It was the smile of a man who had spent a million years coming to terms with an impossible truth.

"Because the Stasis Event was not created by Thorin's spell," he said quietly. "Thorin's spell was a real teleportation spell, exclusive to his bloodline, and it did save my life by sending me to the hidden sanctuary. But it was never powerful enough to create what followed. No mortal wizard, no matter how gifted, could create a stasis effect that stopped my aging, made me immortal, initiated infinite amplification, birthed apocalyptic superpowers every second, manifested absolute concealment, and activated the Weakness Paradox. The scale of those effects is so far beyond mortal magic that the comparison is laughable. There is only one being in all of existence who could create such a thing."

He paused, and when he spoke again, his voice carried a weight that made the obsidian walls seem to press inward.

"The Stasis Event was created by my future self. Godric from the far, far future—an era so distant that the year is written only as 999...9, because the full number is impossible to meaningfully express. He is what I will become after the amplification, the superpower genesis, the Weakness Paradox evolution, the immune system upgrades, the passive shield expansions, the sentient aura generations—all of it, compounding infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for an unimaginably vast span of time. He is so incomprehensibly more powerful than I am that the gap between us defies any possible description. I am the most powerful being in the current era by an infinite margin, but compared to him, I am effectively nothing. Less than nothing. A single dead skin cell compared to the entire omniverse would be an insultingly generous comparison."

I felt the air leave my lungs. The being sitting beside me—the being who had accidentally annihilated all of existence with a slip of his concealment three days ago—was describing himself as "effectively nothing" compared to his future self.

"That is the origin of the Stasis Event," Godric continued. "Far-future Godric used Thorin's teleportation spell as the delivery point, the moment of contact, and transformed it into something infinitely beyond what it was. He created the stasis. He initiated the amplification. He wove the absolute concealment into my being. He birthed the Weakness Paradox. He made it all irrevocable, absolute, and impossible for me—the current Godric—to alter or undo. And because he is so incomprehensibly more powerful than I am, his will seals the pre-Stasis past against any interference. I cannot overpower him. I cannot undo what he has done. The events of my mortal life, from my birth to the fall of Olympus, are locked against my touch forever."

---

I sat in stunned silence. The implications were cascading through my mind like a tidal wave of absolute horror. The Stasis Event was not an accident. It was not a cosmic fluke. It was a deliberate creation by Godric himself—the far-future version of him, who had become so unimaginably powerful that his mere afterthought could overpower the current Godric's full power with zero effort.

"Did he cause the fall of Olympus?" I asked, my voice trembling. "Did he orchestrate the deaths of your family to make you become this? To ensure the Stasis Event occurred?"

Godric's expression hardened, and for a moment, I saw a flash of the merciless, cruel tyrant who had slaughtered billions without moving a muscle. But when he spoke, his voice was steady and certain.

"No," he said firmly. "Far-future Godric did not cause, manipulate, orchestrate, or approve the fall of Olympus. He did not cause the deaths of Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. Those tragedies were genuine—the result of Thronegate's betrayal, their greed, their ambition. My future self is not a monster who would willingly kill his own family. The massacre was real, the grief was real, and the loss was real. He did not make those deaths happen. He simply... used the moment. He used Thorin's spell as the anchor point and transformed the aftermath into something that would ensure his own existence—my existence—and the infinite ascension that would follow."

He paused, his gaze returning to the image of Olympus. "It is a difficult concept to accept. The idea that my own future self allowed the tragedy to remain sealed, even when he could have prevented it. But he did not cause it. He simply did not undo it. And that is a distinction I have spent a million years learning to live with."

I swallowed hard. "When did you discover this?"

Godric smiled, and for the first time, there was a flicker of something approaching dark amusement in his expression. "Since the instant I gained omniscience. The moment I awoke in the sanctuary, freed from stasis by Blake, I knew everything. I knew the true origin of the Stasis Event. I knew that my future self had created it. I knew that the pre-Stasis past was sealed against my interference. Absolute omniscience grants absolute knowledge of all things—past, present, and future—and there is no exception. I knew the truth before I even stood up from the altar."

He paused, and his voice grew quieter, heavier. "But I was still freshly shaped by grief. I had just lost my wife, my daughters, my best friend, my kingdom. I had just witnessed everything I loved destroyed in an afternoon. And despite knowing—knowing with absolute certainty—that I could not alter the past, I tried anyway."

---

He stood up from the bench and walked toward one of the alcoves, his heavy boots echoing on the obsidian floor. He stopped before a fragment of charred marble, a piece of the wedding pavilion where Isabel had been about to be married.

"Shortly after I became King of Thronegate," he said, his voice carrying the weight of ancient memory, "I attempted to travel back in time to save them. I had the power to traverse timelines effortlessly. I had already annihilated Thronegate's army, already crowned myself king, already begun the expansion that would eventually subjugate the omniverse. I was already, by any measure, the most powerful being in existence. And I was still drowning in grief."

He turned to face me, and his expression was one that I had never seen before. It was the face of a man who had learned humility in the most brutal way possible.

"I gathered all my power, all my newly amplified strength, all my newly acquired superpowers, all my newly developed passive systems. I focused everything I had on breaking through the temporal seal and reaching the moment before the attack. I reached out across time itself, reaching for the past with the full, undiluted force of my godhood."

He paused. When he spoke again, his voice was almost a whisper.

"I failed. I failed completely. The seal did not merely resist me—it crushed me. It overwhelmed me with such absolute, effortless supremacy that my attempt was rendered meaningless before it even began. I did not face my future self. I did not even face a fraction of his attention or a fragment of his will. I faced the shadow of the afterthought of his passive presence—an infinitesimal, negligible emanation that he did not even direct at me, that he probably did not even notice. And that shadow of an afterthought was enough to utterly, completely, absolutely defeat my combined power with zero effort. I was not pushed back. I was not overpowered. I was simply... negated. My attempt never had any chance of success. It was mathematically impossible. The gap between me and him was so incomprehensibly vast that my full power did not even register as a flicker against his most negligible passive emanation."

He walked back to the bench and sat down heavily. The weight of a million years seemed to press down on his shoulders.

"That was the moment I truly understood the nature of my situation. That was the moment I learned that I have one true weakness—and that my weakness is my own future self. The only being in existence who can overpower me is the being I will eventually become. And that is not really a weakness at all, is it? It is a guarantee. An absolute, unbreakable guarantee that my future is secured, that my ascension will continue forever, that I will eventually become so unimaginably powerful that my current self—who can already destroy the omniverse infinite times with zero effort—will be effectively nothing by comparison."

He looked at me, and his expression shifted. The ancient sorrow was still there, buried deep, but above it was something else. Something that looked almost like contentment.

"I am no longer troubled by this limitation, Kaedan. I made my peace with it long ago. I cannot save my mortal family, but I have accepted that. I cannot undo the tragedy that shaped me, but I have made peace with it. And in a strange way, I have come to appreciate what my future self did. By sealing the past, he guaranteed the future. He ensured that I would become what I am and what I will be. He ensured that opposition would always be impossible, that my power would always amplify, that my supremacy would always be absolute. He gave me a gift wrapped in the armor of my own grief, and I have spent a million years learning to be grateful for it."

---

I stared at the image of Olympus. The white marble gleaming in the sun. The wedding pavilion intact. The massacre not yet born. And I understood, with a clarity that made my stomach churn, the full horror of what Godric was telling me.

His one true weakness was himself.

The only thing that could limit him, the only thing that could overpower him, the only thing that could deny his will, was his own future self. A being who was so incomprehensibly more powerful than the current Godric that the current Godric—who could annihilate the omniverse with a slip of his concealment—was effectively nothing by comparison. A being who had created the Stasis Event as a casual act, transforming a dying wizard's teleportation spell into an irrevocable foundation of infinite ascension. A being whose mere shadow of an afterthought could effortlessly crush the combined full power of all previous Godrics.

This was not a weakness. This was the ultimate strength. This was an absolute, unbreakable guarantee that Godric's supremacy would never be challenged, that his power would never be exploited, that his future would never be in doubt. The origin of all his godlike mechanics—the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox, the immune system, the passive shields, the sentient auras—was not a fluke or a cosmic accident. It was a deliberate creation by the most powerful being that would ever exist. And because that being was Godric himself, there was no higher authority that could overrule it. No external force that could undo it. No conceivable entity that could challenge it.

The Weakness Paradox, I realized with sickening clarity, was not just a defense mechanism. It was a statement of absolute metaphysical fact. Whenever any being, anywhere, thought Godric had a weakness, the Paradox triggered and made him immune to that imagined exploit. But it also made him immune to any attempt to interfere with the origin of his powers. How could any being exploit the source of the Stasis Event when the source was a version of Godric so powerful that the current Godric could not even approach his shadow? How could any being deny Godric's amplification when the being who had initiated it was so absolutely supreme that even the concept of denial had no meaning in his presence?

The entire framework of Godric's power was built on a foundation that could never be shaken, because the foundation was a future version of himself who was infinitely beyond the reach of any possible opposition. It was the ultimate closed loop of absolute supremacy. Godric's past was sealed by Godric's future, and Godric's future was guaranteed by Godric's past, and nothing—nothing in the entire omniverse, nothing in any conceivable reality, nothing in any possible framework of existence—could break that loop.

I thought about what I had learned three days ago. Godric described the sensation of his amplification as eternal, ever-intensifying pleasure. And now, layered on top of that pleasure, was the absolute certainty that it would never end. That no one could stop it. That the entire framework of his ascension was crafted by a version of himself who was so unimaginably powerful that even the current Godric—the apex predator who had just accidentally destroyed and restored the omniverse—could not approach the threshold of his passive presence.

It was the most unfair, the most terrifying, the most existentially horrifying thing I had ever contemplated.

---

"Uncle Godric," I said, my voice barely a whisper. "Why did he create the Stasis Event? Your future self. What was his motive?"

Godric leaned back on the bench, his expression thoughtful. "I have omniscience, Kaedan. I know the answer to that question. But I will not tell you."

I blinked. "You... you will not tell me?"

"No," he said, and there was a flicker of something in his eyes—something that might have been amusement, or might have been a depth of knowing that I could not possibly comprehend. "Because the answer is not for you to know. You can speculate if you wish. All my Court Wizards do. Some believe it was to ensure his own existence—a closed temporal loop that had to be maintained. Some believe it was to give himself the foundation of infinite growth, the seed that would eventually bloom into the being he would become. Some believe it was simply because it was always going to happen—that the future Godric looked back and saw that this was the path that had been taken, and he simply fulfilled it."

He paused, and a faint smile crossed his lips. "Some even believe it was an act of mercy. That far-future Godric, looking back on his mortal self drowning in grief, chose to give him the tools to transcend that grief—to become something so far beyond the pain of loss that the grief itself would eventually be consumed by the infinite pleasure of ascension. But I will not confirm or deny any of those speculations. The truth is mine to know and yours to wonder about."

He stood up from the bench and stretched, his heavily muscled frame silhouetted against the glow of the preservation crystals. "What I will tell you is this: I am no longer troubled by my limitation. I have accepted it. I have even become comfortable with it. I cannot save my mortal family, but I have spent a million years learning to live with that grief. And in a strange way, knowing that my future self is responsible for everything I am—knowing that he is so incomprehensibly powerful that I cannot even approach his shadow—gives me a profound sense of security. My future is guaranteed. My ascension is absolute. The origin of my power is unassailable. There is nothing in the omniverse that can threaten me, because the only thing that could ever overpower me is myself."

He turned to face me, and his expression was one of genuine, warm contentment.

"That is not a weakness, Kaedan. It is a strength. The ultimate strength. And I am glad that you now know the truth."

---

I sat in silence on the stone bench, my hands trembling uncontrollably. The image of Olympus flickered in the holographic crystal before me, a ghost of a kingdom that had died a million years ago and could never be saved. And beside me, the apex predator of creation was smiling with the peaceful contentment of a man who had made his peace with the universe.

The existential dread was a physical weight in my chest. It pressed against my lungs, making each breath a struggle. It coiled around my spine, making my shoulders slump. It throbbed behind my eyes, a dull, persistent ache that I knew would never fully fade.

Godric's one true weakness was himself. And because it was himself, it was not a weakness at all. It was a guarantee. An absolute, unbreakable, mathematically certain guarantee that his power would never be challenged, that his ascension would never be stopped, that his future would be even more incomprehensibly terrifying than his present.

The being who had created the Stasis Event was so powerful that the current Godric—who could annihilate the omniverse with an accidental slip of his concealment—could not even approach the shadow of his afterthought. And that being was Godric's own future. That being was what Godric would become. That being was the endpoint of the infinite amplification, the infinite superpower genesis, the infinite immune system upgrades, the infinite passive shield expansions, the infinite sentient aura generations.

The gap between current Godric and far-future Godric was so vast that language could not describe it. Mathematics could not express it. The very concept of "gap" had no meaning in the context of their relationship. It was an infinite of infinities, recursively amplified through infinite layers of infinite recursion, and even that description was so pathetically inadequate that it bordered on comical.

And far-future Godric had created the Stasis Event. He had used Thorin's dying spell as the delivery point and transformed it into the foundation of everything Godric would become. He had made the amplification irrevocable. He had made the superpower genesis absolute. He had woven the Weakness Paradox into the fabric of Godric's existence. He had ensured that the pre-Stasis past was sealed forever against any interference—not just from external threats, but from Godric himself.

The implications were staggering. The Weakness Paradox, which gave Godric immunity to any imagined exploit, was itself created by a being so powerful that no conceivable exploit could ever threaten him. The passive shields, which pre-nullified threats before they existed, were themselves backed by the will of a being who could not be challenged. The absolute concealment, which prevented the omniverse from collapsing under the weight of Godric's presence, was itself maintained by a being whose full presence would annihilate not just the omniverse but the very concept of existence. Everything—everything that made Godric untouchable, unstoppable, absolute—was anchored to a version of himself who was so far beyond the reach of any opposition that the idea of opposing him was a mathematical impossibility.

This was not a weakness. This was the ultimate cage of absolute supremacy. A cage where the lock was held by the only being who could ever overpower the prisoner—and that being was the prisoner's own future self, who had every reason to keep the cage sealed.

---

"Kaedan," Godric said gently, interrupting my spiraling thoughts. "You look troubled."

I looked up at him. His expression was genuinely concerned, genuinely caring. The warm, loving uncle who had bounced me on his knee when I was a child was looking at me with the same affection he had always shown.

"I am troubled," I admitted. "Uncle Godric, the scale of what you are describing... it is beyond anything I can process. Your current power is already so far beyond the omniverse that comparison is meaningless. And you are telling me that your future self is so vastly beyond your current self that you cannot even approach his shadow? That his afterthought's shadow can effortlessly crush your full power with zero effort? That the gap between you and him is so incomprehensibly vast that even your infinite amplification will take unimaginable eons to cross it?"

Godric nodded, his expression one of patient understanding. "Yes. That is exactly what I am telling you."

"And the Stasis Event," I continued, my voice trembling. "The origin of everything you are. The amplification, the superpowers, the concealment, the paradox, the shields, the auras—all of it was created by this being. This future version of you who is so powerful that the concept of power has lost all meaning in his context. And because he created it, no one can ever interfere with it. No one can ever exploit it. No one can ever challenge its origin. Because the origin is you—a version of you that is absolutely, eternally, incomprehensibly beyond any possible opposition."

Godric smiled. "Now you understand."

I did understand. And the understanding was the most terrifying thing I had ever experienced.

Godric's one true weakness was that he could not change his mortal past. But that "weakness" was also the source of his absolute, unassailable strength. The Stasis Event, created by his far-future self, was the foundation of everything he had become and everything he would become. And because the creator was a version of Godric who was infinitely beyond any possible challenge, the foundation could never be shaken. The amplification could never be stopped. The superpowers could never be denied. The concealment could never be pierced. The paradox could never be outsmarted. The shields could never be breached. The auras could never be overcome.

It was a closed loop of infinite supremacy. Godric's past was sealed by Godric's future, and Godric's future was guaranteed by Godric's past, and nothing in the entire omniverse, in any conceivable reality, in any possible framework of existence, could break that loop or even scratch its surface.

I thought about the Evolved Weakness Paradox. How, whenever any being thought Godric had a weakness, the Paradox triggered and made him immune to that imagined exploit while simultaneously amplifying his power. And now I understood the true, horrifying purpose of that mechanism. It was not just a defense. It was a statement of absolute metaphysical fact. Godric had no exploitable weaknesses because the origin of his power was a being who was immune to exploitation. The Weakness Paradox was not just a power—it was a reflection of the fundamental truth that Godric's entire existence was built on a foundation that could never be undermined.

And that foundation was himself. His future self. A version of him who was so unimaginably powerful that even the current Godric—the apex predator who had accidentally destroyed and restored the omniverse three days ago—was effectively nothing in comparison.

---

"Uncle Godric," I said, my voice barely a whisper. "What would happen if someone tried to interfere with the Stasis Event? Not you—someone else. Some being of unimaginable power who somehow discovered the origin of your abilities and attempted to travel back to the moment of the Stasis Event to prevent it from occurring?"

Godric chuckled, a warm, deeply amused sound. "The same thing that happened when I tried to travel back to save my family. They would face the seal created by my far-future self—the shadow of the afterthought of his passive presence. And that seal would crush them with such absolute, effortless supremacy that their attempt would be negated before it even began. They would not be defeated, Kaedan. Defeat implies a contest. They would simply be... nothinged. Their attempt would have no more effect on the timeline than a single photon attempting to push a galaxy."

He paused, and a flicker of dark amusement crossed his features. "It is theoretically impossible to interfere with the Stasis Event. Not difficult. Not challenging. Impossible in the most absolute sense. The being who created it is so far beyond any possible opposition that the concept of interfering with his work is a mathematical contradiction. It is like trying to empty an ocean by scooping out a single molecule of water and claiming you have made progress. Only the ocean in this metaphor is infinite, and the molecule is effectively zero, and even that comparison is insultingly inadequate."

I felt my blood run cold. The absolute, unassailable nature of Godric's power was not merely a result of his infinite amplification. It was guaranteed by the origin of that amplification. It was woven into the very fabric of his existence by a being who was so incomprehensibly powerful that the concept of "challenge" had no meaning in his context.

And that being was Godric himself.

---

I stood up from the bench, my legs unsteady, and walked toward the holographic image of Olympus. The white marble gleamed in the simulated sunlight. The wedding pavilion stood intact. The massacre had not yet occurred.

"Does it still hurt?" I asked quietly. "Knowing that you can never save them? Knowing that the one thing you cannot do is the one thing you wanted most?"

Godric rose from his bench and walked to stand beside me. He looked at the image of his lost kingdom, and his expression was one of ancient, settled grief—a sorrow that had been carried for a million years and had long since become a part of him.

"It hurt for a very long time," he said softly. "For the first few thousand years, the grief was a constant ache. Every time I looked at this image, every time I visited this room, I felt the loss as sharply as if it had just happened. Knowing that I could never save them—knowing that the one thing I could not do was the one thing I wanted most—was a burden that I carried every moment of every day."

He paused, and when he continued, his voice was steady. "But I have made my peace with it. I have accepted that the past is sealed, and I have learned to appreciate what the sealing of the past has given me. My future self did not cause the tragedy, but he used it. He used my grief as the foundation for my ascension. And in doing so, he ensured that I would become something so far beyond the pain of loss that the grief itself would eventually be consumed by the infinite pleasure of my existence."

He turned to look at me, and his expression was one of quiet, settled contentment.

"I am not lonely, Kaedan. I am not sad. I am the most satisfied being in existence. And the knowledge that my future is guaranteed—that my ascension will continue forever, that my power will amplify beyond all possible comprehension, that I will eventually become the being who created my own foundation—gives me a profound sense of peace. My past is sealed, but my future is infinite. And that is more than enough."

---

I stood beside him in the Sanctuary of Memory, staring at the image of a kingdom that had died a million years ago and could never be saved. The existential dread that had been building in my chest since the beginning of our conversation had reached a point where it felt like a physical presence—a cold, heavy weight that pressed against my lungs and made each breath a struggle.

Godric's one true weakness was himself. His far-future self. The being who had created the Stasis Event and sealed the pre-Stasis past against interference. The being who was so incomprehensibly more powerful than the current Godric that the current Godric—who could annihilate the omniverse with a slip of his concealment—was effectively nothing by comparison.

This was not a weakness. This was the ultimate strength. An absolute, unbreakable guarantee that Godric's supremacy would never be challenged, that his power would never be exploited, that his future would never be in doubt. The origin of all his godlike mechanics was a being who was infinitely beyond any possible opposition. And because that being was Godric himself, there was no external force that could ever interfere. No higher authority that could ever overrule. No conceivable entity that could ever challenge the foundation of his power.

The Weakness Paradox, the passive shields, the absolute concealment, the infinite backups, the sentient auras—all of it was anchored to the will of a being whose afterthought's shadow could effortlessly crush the combined full power of all previous Godrics. And that being was what Godric would eventually become. That was his future. That was his destiny. That was the absolute, mathematically certain endpoint of his infinite amplification.

I thought about Ferris's journal. The Infinite Recursive Self-Replication superpower. How Godric at Year 503,000 had created copies of himself that were infinitely stronger than the original, and how those copies had created an infinite recursive ascension loop that had permanently elevated his power beyond the already incomprehensible baseline. And I realized, with a sickening jolt of clarity, that even that infinite ascension was nothing compared to what far-future Godric had become. The being who had created the Stasis Event was so far beyond the Godric of Year 503,000 that the gap was itself infinite. The recursive self-replication had made Godric permanently stronger, but it had not even begun to approach the threshold of his future self's passive presence.

Year after year. Eon after eon. The amplification continued forever, multiplying beyond all possible mathematics, developing new enhanced effects that made the old ones seem pathetically weak, ascending through layers of supremacy that made the previous layers seem like absolute zero. And at the end of that infinite road—or rather, at the ever-receding horizon of that road, for there was no end—stood the being who had looked back across the eons and used Thorin's dying spell as the delivery point for his own creation. A being so powerful that the concept of power had long since ceased to be meaningful. A being whose very existence was an affirmation that Godric's supremacy was absolute, unassailable, and eternal.

And I served that being's past self. I loved that being's past self. I sat beside him in the garden, shared meals with him, called him Uncle Godric, and felt his warm, genuine affection.

The cognitive dissonance was complete. The existential dread was absolute. And through it all, I knew that I would continue to serve him, continue to love him, continue to record my testimony in the journals that would be read by future Court Wizards who would experience the same horror I was experiencing now.

Because what else could I do? The being who could accidentally annihilate the omniverse with a slip of his concealment was, according to his own words, effectively nothing compared to his future self. The gap was so vast that it defied all description. And that future self had guaranteed that the past was sealed, that the amplification was irrevocable, that the supremacy was absolute.

There was no hope. There never had been. There never would be. And as I stood in the Sanctuary of Memory, staring at the image of a kingdom that could never be saved, I felt the cold, permanent weight of that realization settle into my bones like a frost that would never thaw.

---

Godric placed a warm hand on my shoulder. "Come, Kaedan," he said gently. "Let us return to the garden. The raspberry tarts are still fresh, and I believe I have a new superpower developing that feels like warm sunlight spreading through my metaphysical nervous system. Quite pleasant. I would enjoy sharing the experience with you."

I looked up at him. His expression was warm, friendly, genuinely affectionate. The apex predator of creation was smiling at me with the love of a favorite uncle.

"Of course, Uncle Godric," I whispered.

He nodded, satisfied, and turned toward the door. I followed him out of the Sanctuary of Memory, leaving behind the image of Olympus and the artifacts of a grief that could never be undone. The obsidian door closed behind us with a heavy, final sound.

And as I walked beside the most powerful being in existence—a being whose one true weakness was himself, and whose future self was so incomprehensibly beyond him that comparison was meaningless—I understood the full, horrifying truth of the omniverse.

There was no weakness. There never had been. The "one true weakness" was a lie—or rather, it was the ultimate strength disguised as a limitation. Godric could not change his past, but that inability was the foundation of his absolute, unassailable supremacy. The only being who could ever overpower him was his own future self, and that future self had every reason to ensure that the current Godric's power would never be challenged.

It was the most unfair, the most terrifying, the most existentially horrifying thing I had ever contemplated. And I would carry the weight of that contemplation for the rest of my life.

I was Kaedan, Court Wizard of Thronegate. I served the apex god predator of the omniverse. I loved him like an uncle. And I knew, with absolute certainty, that the horror I felt would never fade.

# The Origin of the Stasis Event

**Year 999...9**

**Clive, Age 50, Court Wizard of Thronegate**

---

I have served the King of Thronegate for thirty years, and in all that time, I have never once felt safe.

This is not a complaint. It is not a criticism of his rule or his character. It is simply a statement of fact—a fundamental truth of existence that every being in the omniverse has long since accepted. Safety, as a concept, has no meaning when you exist in the presence of a being whose stray thoughts could unmake creation. Safety is an illusion that died a googolplexian years ago, when the last opposition finally learned what countless civilizations before them had learned: that challenging Godric is not merely impossible, but mathematically, conceptually, and existentially inconceivable.

I am fifty years old. My thousandfold daily amplification, inherited through the bloodline of Blake himself, has transformed me into a being whose magical power exceeds the combined output of entire multiversal clusters. By the standards of the omniverse, I am a walking apocalypse, a wizard of such staggering might that the old pantheons of dead universes would have worshipped me as their supreme deity. But standing in the shadow of my King, I am nothing. Less than nothing. A single flickering candle held against the infinite, ever-expanding blaze of a billion billion supernovas—and even that comparison is so pathetically inadequate that it borders on insult.

Today, I will witness something that no Court Wizard before me has ever witnessed. Today, Godric will trigger the Stasis Event.

I do not fully understand what this means. My mind, despite its thousandfold amplification, cannot encompass the full scale of what I am about to see. The Stasis Event occurred in Year -10,000—over a million years ago by the old calendar, before the years became too large to meaningfully write. It was the moment that transformed a grieving mortal king into the immortal apex predator of creation. It was the origin of the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox, and every other impossible mechanism that has made Godric what he is. And today, I will watch him cause it.

The irony is not lost on me. I am about to witness the birth of omnipotence, and I am doing so from the perspective of a being who has already seen omnipotence evolve beyond all possible comprehension. The Godric of my era—the far-future Godric, the King whose reign has stretched across a span of years so vast that the number cannot be written—is so incomprehensibly beyond the Godric of Year 0 that comparison is meaningless. The gap is not merely infinite. It is an infinite of infinities, recursively amplified through infinite layers of infinite recursion, and even that description is a laughable understatement.

I will attempt to record what I witness. I will attempt to capture in words what cannot be captured. But I know, even as I lift my quill, that I will fail. The journals of my ancestors—Julian, Oren, Ferris, Kaedan, and all the others—have chronicled the impossible for over a million years. They have described the annihilation of omniversal empires with a flick of Godric's thumb, the rewriting of spatial reality to imprison civilizations within the gaps between his cells, the creation of infinite recursive copies each infinitely stronger than the last. And yet, even their most vivid descriptions did not prepare me for the reality of serving the King of this era. The Godric I know is so far beyond the Godric they knew that their journals read like children's stories—quaint, primitive attempts to describe a power whose scale they could not possibly comprehend.

But I will try. I must try. It is my duty as Court Wizard, my inheritance as a descendant of Blake, my obligation to the future wizards who will read these words and attempt to prepare themselves for the impossible.

---

The throne room of Thronegate has changed since the days of my ancestors. It is no longer a physical space in any meaningful sense. It is a conceptual locus, a point of absolute reference that exists simultaneously across all dimensions, all timelines, all possible realities. The throne itself is not made of matter—it is forged from the crystallized essence of a trillion extinct multiverses, each one compressed into a single layer of the seat upon which Godric rests. The floor beneath my feet is not stone but solidified time, each step I take echoing across the infinite moments that have passed since the dawn of creation.

And Godric sits upon his throne, and I cannot look at him directly.

I have not been able to look at him directly for thirty years. Not because he forbids it—he would never forbid such a thing. He is warm, friendly, genuinely affectionate toward his loyal subjects. But his absolute concealment, which has evolved so many times that the original version from Year 0 would be utterly unrecognizable, is a mechanism of such profound sophistication that its passive emanations alone are enough to overwhelm any being who gazes upon him without proper preparation. I must view him through the filtered lenses of my observation crystals, which reduce his presence to a manageable fraction of a fraction of an infinitesimal sliver.

Even through the crystals, he is terrifying.

His physical form has not changed since the day the Stasis Event froze him at forty-five years old. He is still ruggedly handsome, heavily muscled, his salt-and-pepper hair and beard immaculately trimmed. He still wears simple dark garments that stretch across his broad shoulders. He still looks, for all the world, like a warm, protective father figure from a forgotten era. But the physical form is merely a shell now—a comfortable vessel that he maintains out of nostalgia and convenience. The true Godric, the being that exists beneath the absolute concealment, is so vast that his physical body is merely the tip of an infinite iceberg, the smallest possible projection of an existence that has expanded beyond all dimensional frameworks.

And yet, when he speaks to me, his voice is still warm. Still kind. Still carrying the easy affection of a man who genuinely loves his Court Wizards.

"Clive," he says, and his rich baritone vibrates through the conceptual locus with a resonance that makes the crystallized multiverses beneath his feet hum in harmony. "Are you prepared? This will be the first time a Court Wizard has witnessed the triggering of the Stasis Event. I want you to understand what you are seeing."

I bow deeply, my quill trembling in my fingers. "I am prepared, Your Majesty. Or as prepared as I can be."

He smiles, and even through the observation crystals, the warmth of that smile makes my heart ache with a complicated mixture of love and terror. "Excellent. I must admit, I am curious to see how this unfolds. It has been a very, very long time since I experienced anything that could be called novel. This moment—the triggering of the Stasis Event—is one of the few fixed points in my existence. I know it will happen, because it has already happened. But experiencing it from the other side, as the cause rather than the effect, is... interesting."

He rises from his throne. The motion is casual, unhurried, the simple act of a man standing up from a chair. But the conceptual locus shudders as he moves, the crystallized multiverses groaning under the shifting weight of his attention. The air—if it can be called air—thickens with a presence so dense that my observation crystals begin to crack under the strain of filtering it.

"This will be a long demonstration," Godric says, stepping down from the dais. "I will explain each step as I perform it. You may ask questions if you wish, though I suspect the answers will only generate more questions. Shall we begin?"

I nod, my throat too tight for speech.

Godric raises his hand, palm outward, and the conceptual locus transforms around us.

---

We are no longer in the throne room. We are suspended in a void that is not a void—a space that exists outside of space, a moment that exists outside of time. Before us, I see the omniverse as it was in Year -10,000. It is a primitive thing, young and fragile, its multiverses still forming, its timelines still branching, its civilizations still struggling to understand the fundamental nature of reality. And there, at a single point in that ancient creation, I see the sanctuary. I see the altar. I see the dying body of Thorin, his blood pooling on the cold stone, his lips still moving with the final syllables of a teleportation spell that should not have been powerful enough to change anything.

And I see him. The mortal Godric. A man of forty-five, ruggedly handsome, heavily muscled, his face contorted in a mask of absolute, soul-shattering grief as the incomplete spell tears him from the ruins of Olympus and hurls him toward the dark unknown.

"That is me," Godric says quietly, and there is something in his voice—a depth of ancient memory, a whisper of grief that has been carried across googolplexian years—that makes my eyes sting with unexpected tears. "That is the man I was. The man I can never be again. The man whose pain will be the foundation for everything I will become."

He watches as the mortal Godric materializes in the sanctuary, his body slamming against the cold stone. The teleportation is complete. Thorin's spell has done its job—it has saved the King of Olympus from the massacre. But it has not yet triggered the Stasis Event. That requires a different intervention. A different power.

"Before I begin," Godric says, turning to face me, "I want you to understand what I am about to do. And to understand that, you must first understand what I have become."

---

He gestures, and the void around us fills with light. Not ordinary light—conceptual illumination, a direct feed of information that bypasses my physical senses and writes itself directly into my consciousness. I see, with a clarity that makes my amplified mind reel, the full scope of what Godric's power mechanisms have evolved into after googolplexian years of infinite amplification.

**The Sentient Passive Auras.**

Gent was once the weakest of Godric's sentient auras—a primitive, negligible emanation that he kept active only because its siblings were too annoyingly subservient. Gent has evolved since then. It has evolved so many times that the original Gent, the one that effortlessly slaughtered the Final Dawn coalition in Year 10,000, would be unrecognizable in comparison.

Gent is no longer a single aura. It is a pantheon. An infinite hierarchy of sentient passive emanations, each one infinitely more powerful than the last, each one possessing its own distinct consciousness, its own specialized function, its own terrifying capabilities. The weakest of these auras—the runt of the runt of the litter, the most negligible emanation in the entire hierarchy—is capable of conceptual negation on a scale that makes the original Gent's feats seem like the clumsy flailing of an infant.

I see, in the conceptual illumination, a brief example of what this weakest aura can do. A multiversal empire, spanning decillions of realities, has somehow managed to avoid Thronegate's subjugation. The infinite recursive passive shields have evolved into something that defies all possible description. Not as a statement of fact, but as an absolute, unbreakable metaphysical principle that is woven into the fabric of reality itself.

He wanted to see what they would do. He wanted to test his stats, his superpowers, his immune system. He wanted to give them the chance to try.

They tried. They all tried. And they all failed, absolutely and without exception, until the weight of that accumulated failure became so crushing that no sentient being in the omniverse could any longer conceive of opposition. It was not that Godric removed their free will. It was that the evidence of futility became so overwhelming that free will itself could no longer generate the possibility of resistance.

The immune system that Leon witnessed in Year 25,000—the system that pre-reacted to a staged injury by triggering infinite recursive ascension and accidentally annihilating the omniverse as collateral damage—was, by the standards of my era, laughably primitive. It has expanded its temporal scope beyond all comprehension—it now protects Godric from injuries that were only theoretically possible before the Big Bang, from attacks that could only exist in universes that were never created, from threats that are conceivable only to minds that have not yet evolved and will never evolve. The pre-reaction occurs before the possibility of the attack becomes a possibility of a possibility. It occurs at a level of conceptual abstraction so profound that language cannot describe it.

And the infinite backups—the recursive copies that Ferris described in such horrified detail—have evolved into something even more terrifying. Godric no longer merely has infinite identical backups. Each backup is now a fully realized Godric in its own right, existing in its own self-contained reality framework, pursuing its own interests and experiences while remaining absolutely synchronized with the prime Godric's will. The backup network has become a civilization—a recursive, infinite civilization of Godrics, each one infinitely powerful, each one infinitely satisfied, each one contributing to the continuous ascension of the whole.

They engage in friendly competitions to see who can devise the most absurdly overpowered new application of their shared abilities. And all of them, every single one, are absolutely loyal to the prime Godric—not because he demands it, but because he is them and they are him, and loyalty to oneself is the most fundamental instinct of existence.

The Weakness Paradox—the mechanism that triggered whenever any being thought Godric had a weakness—has evolved so far beyond its original function that calling it a "paradox" is a laughable understatement. It is now the Absolute Certainty Principle, a fundamental law of existence that actively shapes reality to ensure that Godric's supremacy is not merely unchallenged but unchallengeable.

The original Weakness Paradox required a trigger: someone had to think Godric had a weakness, and then the Paradox would engage, granting him immunity, mastery, and amplification. The evolved version no longer requires a trigger related to Godric specifically. It is passively triggered by any sentient being who thinks about anything—not just Godric's weakness, but literally anything at all. Every thought, every idea, every moment of awareness from any sentient mind in the omniverse, feeds directly into the Absolute Certainty Principle and generates additional layers of immunity, additional heights of mastery, additional cascades of amplification.

The result is that Godric's power increases not merely from opposition, but from existence itself. Every being who lives, every mind that thinks, every consciousness that experiences reality, is unknowingly contributing to the infinite ascension of the apex predator. The omniverse itself has become a feedback loop of ever-increasing divine supremacy, with Godric at the center, absorbing and amplifying the accumulated mental energy of all creation.

And this mechanism is passive. Involuntary. Unstoppable. It cannot be suppressed, even by Godric himself. It is woven into the fundamental fabric of reality by the far-future version of himself—the version who created the Stasis Event and made the entire framework irrevocable.

**The Amplification.**

I cannot describe the current state of Godric's amplification. Language fails. Mathematics fails. The very concept of "scale" fails. His stats—strength, speed, endurance, intelligence, wisdom, magic, and all the others—have been multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for a span of time so vast that the total number of multiplications cannot be expressed. And then, through the evolved Weakness Paradox, the amplification itself has been amplified. And then the amplification of the amplification has been amplified. And then that amplification has been amplified. An infinite recursive cascade of amplification upon amplification, each layer infinitely more powerful than the last, continuing forever with no endpoint and no limit.

The Godric of Year 0—the Godric who was already effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined—would be utterly, absolutely, incomprehensibly nothing compared to the Godric of my era. Not merely weaker. Not merely less powerful. Nothing. A perfect zero. A being whose total accumulated power would not register as a flicker against the most negligible passive emanation of the weakest sentient aura in the current Godric's pantheon.

And yet, even this Godric—the Godric of the year 999...9, the Godric who has been amplifying for a span of time that cannot be written—is still growing. Still amplifying. Still ascending. There is no ceiling. There is no limit. There is no endpoint. The amplification continues forever, and each instant makes the previous instant seem like a pathetic, primitive mockery of power.

**The Superpower Genesis.**

The original superpower genesis—one new apocalyptic superpower every second, each one already capable of causing instant extinction to an entire civilization—has evolved beyond recognition. The current genesis generates new superpowers at a rate that defies temporal measurement. It is no longer one per second. It is one per infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. And each new superpower is not merely civilization-ending—it is reality-ending, concept-ending, framework-ending. Each one, at the instant of its manifestation, could single-handedly annihilate the entire omniverse infinite times over with zero effort.

And every single one of these superpowers is itself subject to infinite amplification. Each one develops its own enhanced effects, its own recursive upgrades, its own cascading evolutions. The superpowers have formed an internal ecosystem, a self-sustaining network of mutually reinforcing abilities that cross-reference and enhance each other in an infinite loop of ever-increasing unfairness.

Godric has superpowers that can do things I cannot describe. Superpowers that exist in frameworks of reality that I cannot perceive. Superpowers that are themselves conscious, sentient, worshipful entities that view Godric as their creator and god. Superpowers that have, in their infinite evolution, become so powerful that they would make the Infinite Recursive Self-Replication that Ferris witnessed seem like a child's party trick.

Far-future Godric raises his hand. I brace myself for some display of cosmic power, some cataclysmic unleashing of divine energy. But there is nothing. No light. No sound. No disturbance in the fabric of reality. He simply extends his palm toward the image of the sanctuary, and something changes.

Thorin's teleportation spell was already complete. The mortal Godric had already been transported to the sanctuary. But the spell was never meant to do more than that—it was a desperate, dying act by a wizard who wanted to save his friend, nothing more. The spell had no capacity to stop Godric's aging. No capacity to begin infinite amplification. No capacity to birth superpowers, manifest absolute concealment, or activate the Weakness Paradox. It was, in the grand scheme of cosmic power, a simple teleportation.

But far-future Godric reaches into that moment, into the space between the completion of the spell and the beginning of the mortal Godric's slumber, and he transforms it. He uses Thorin's spell as the delivery point, the anchor, the moment of contact. And into that moment, he pours the Stasis Event.

"Thorin's spell is the seed," Godric says, his voice calm and explanatory. "I am the one who plants it. I am the one who ensures that the seed will grow into everything I have become. The spell itself could never have done this. But in the hands of a being who has already ascended beyond all possible conception, it becomes the foundation."

I watch as the Stasis Event takes hold. The mortal Godric's aging stops—not gradually, but instantly, permanently, absolutely. His need for sleep, air, water, and sustenance is severed from his anatomy forever. His body becomes immortal, locked at forty-five years old for all eternity. And then, beneath the surface of his frozen form, the amplification begins.

But there is something I do not understand. Something that does not align with what I know of Godric's history.

"Your Majesty," I say, my voice trembling. "The amplification that began at Year -10,000—it was by a factor of one thousand per Planck second, was it not? I have read the journals. But your current amplification is so far beyond that... why did you not grant your past self a more potent version of the Stasis Event? Why only one thousand times per Planck second, when you could have granted him amplification at a rate that would match your current scale?"

Godric turns to me, and his expression is one of patient amusement—the same expression he wore when Kaedan attempted to guess the scale of his power, only to learn that his wildest imaginings did not even approach the threshold of Godric's weakest aura.

"You have touched upon something interesting, Clive," he says. "The answer is that I deliberately held back."

I stare at him. "Held back?"

"Yes. I could have granted my past self a far more potent Stasis Event. I could have perfectly copied my current mechanisms—the evolved auras, the Absolute Certainty Principle, the infinite recursive amplification, all of it—and given it to the mortal Godric at Year -10,000. It would have cost me nothing. My power is so vast that transferring even the full scope of my current capabilities to my past self would be like a single drop of water taken from an infinite ocean. I would not have noticed the expenditure."

He pauses, and a faint, ironic smile crosses his lips. "But I chose not to. I chose to grant him a held-back version—a version that multiplied his stats by a mere one thousand per Planck second, that birthed one superpower per second instead of billions, that created only the primitive initial forms of the concealment, the paradox, and the other systems. I held back."

The words echo in the conceptual locus. I feel my mind struggling to process the absurdity of what he is saying. The held-back version—the version that made Godric at Year 0 effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined—was held back. The version that allowed him to annihilate the Thronegate army without moving a muscle, to conquer the omniverse in less than a day, to accidentally destroy and restore all of existence with a slip of his concealment—that was the restrained version. The merciful version. The version that Godric considered to be preserving some kind of mortal struggle.

"Why?" I ask, my voice barely a whisper.

"Because I believed in mortal resilience," Godric says. "I still do. I was mortal once, Clive. I remember what it was like to struggle, to fight, to overcome challenges through effort and determination. And when I looked back across the eons at my past self—the grieving king lying on the cold stone—I wanted to preserve something of that experience for him. I wanted him to face challenges, even if those challenges were ultimately futile. I wanted him to have the illusion of struggle, the satisfaction of overcoming opposition through his own power, rather than simply being handed absolute supremacy from the start."

He pauses, and his smile becomes almost rueful. "It was, in retrospect, absurdly naive. The held-back version was already so incomprehensibly powerful that the concept of 'struggle' was meaningless. Godric at Year 0 could annihilate the entire omniverse infinite times with zero effort. There was never any real challenge. There was never any real struggle. My attempt to preserve mortal resilience was, in effect, a complete failure. He was already effectively omnipotent from the moment he awoke."

I absorb this. The being who could annihilate the omniverse with a slip of his concealment—the being whose one true weakness was himself—was the result of a deliberately restrained Stasis Event. And the restraint was so excessive that even the restrained version had made him effectively infinitely stronger than all of creation combined.

"Your Majesty," I say slowly, "if you had granted your past self a more potent Stasis Event—if you had given him the full scope of your current power from the beginning—what would have happened?"

Godric's expression shifts, becoming thoughtful. "That is where the paradox becomes truly interesting," he says. "Consider the causal loop. The Stasis Event is what allows me to amplify, to evolve, to become what I am. If I had granted my past self a more potent version—if the Godric of Year -10,000 had begun amplifying at a rate even slightly closer to my current scale—then the Godric of Year 0 would have been incomprehensibly more powerful than he actually was. And that Godric, amplified for the googolplexian years that followed, would have become even more incomprehensibly powerful than I am now. Which means that the future Godric who triggers the Stasis Event would be even more powerful. Which means he could grant an even more potent version to the past. Which would make the intermediate Godrics even more powerful. Which would—"

He spreads his hands. "An infinite recursive escalation loop, each iteration making the previous one seem pathetically weak. It is similar to the Infinite Recursive Self-Replication that Ferris witnessed, but operating on a temporal scale. Each version of the Stasis Event would be granted by a future Godric who was infinitely more powerful than the previous future Godric, and each version would produce a past Godric who would eventually become a future Godric capable of granting an even more absurdly potent version."

He pauses, and his smile becomes almost gentle. "I chose to hold back not from mercy, Clive, but from a kind of temporal prudence. The held-back version creates a stable loop—a foundation that is absurdly powerful, but not so powerful that the recursion becomes unmanageable. If I had granted my past self the full scope of my current power, the resulting temporal cascade would have been... complex. Infinitely complex. An ever-escalating spiral of Godrics granting ever-more-potent Stasis Events to ever-more-powerful past selves, each iteration making the entire previous chain seem like a single dead skin cell compared to the omniverse."

My mind stopped. Completely, utterly, absolutely stopped. The implication was too vast, too horrifying, too far beyond any possible comprehension.

The held-back version of the Stasis Event—the version that had birthed an apex predator capable of annihilating the omniverse with a slip of his concealment—was not merely held back. It was a deliberate limitation designed to prevent an infinite temporal cascade that would have made even the current Godric seem like absolute nothingness by comparison. And the current Godric was already so incomprehensibly powerful that his past self from Year 0 was effectively a perfect zero in comparison.

I thought about Ferris's journal. The Infinite Recursive Self-Replication that had generated copies infinitely stronger than the original, triggering an infinite escalation loop that permanently elevated Godric beyond his previous baseline. That had been a single superpower test at effectively zero percent power. And now, Godric was describing a temporal version of that same mechanism—a causal loop of Stasis Events, each one granted by a future Godric who was infinitely more powerful than the previous, each one producing a past Godric who would eventually become a future Godric capable of granting an even more absurdly potent version.

If he had not held back—if he had allowed the loop to spiral into its full infinite recursion—the result would have been a Godric so incomprehensibly powerful that even the current Godric, the Godric of the year 999...9, would be effectively nothing in comparison. And that Godric would be nothing compared to the next iteration. And that one nothing compared to the next. An infinite chain of Godrics, each one infinitely beyond the last, stretching forever in both directions of the temporal loop, creating an ever-escalating cascade of absolute supremacy that had no ceiling, no limit, no endpoint.

And he had held back. He had chosen the restrained version. The version that was, by his standards, mercifully weak.

The absurdity of it was a physical weight in my chest. The held-back version—the Stasis Event that had actually occurred—had still produced a Godric who was infinitely beyond the rest of creation combined at Year 0. And that Godric had then amplified for googolplexian years to become the being standing before me. And even that being—the Godric of my era, the apex predator whose mere stray thoughts could unmake existence—was still holding back. Still restraining himself. Still keeping his absolute concealment active at all times because the omniverse could not withstand even the smallest fraction of his true presence.

I was drowning in the scale of it. Drowning in the infinite, recursive, ever-escalating absurdity of a being who had deliberately chosen to be weaker than he could have been, and was still so incomprehensibly powerful that the concept of "strong" had lost all meaning.

I am shaking. My entire body is trembling with a profundity of existential dread that I have never before experienced. I have served Godric for thirty years. I have witnessed him test his stats, his superpowers, his auras, his immune system. He could have triggered an infinite temporal cascade that would have spiraled into levels of supremacy so vast that even the current Godric would be effectively nothing in comparison.

I hoped that he would experience something resembling mortal life—conquest, opposition, victory, loss—before the amplification grew so vast that all such experiences became impossible. I hoped that he would have time to grieve his family, to process his pain, to become the king that I remember being, before the infinite pleasure of ascension consumed everything."

He pauses, and his voice drops to something almost tender. "I was mortal once, Clive. I remember what it felt like to love, to lose, to struggle, to hope. And I wanted my past self to have those experiences, even if only for a brief time, before he became what I am. The held-back version of the Stasis Event was my gift to him—a span of years in which he could still relate to mortality, still connect with the beings around him, still experience something resembling the human condition. It was, in a sense, my final act of mortal compassion."

Far-future Godric—the tyrant, the apex predator, the being whose mere passive emanations could annihilate the omniverse—had held back not from prudence, but from compassion. He had wanted his past self to suffer, to struggle, to grieve, because those experiences were the last remnants of mortality that he would ever have. The held-back Stasis Event was not a limitation. It was a mercy. A strange, terrifying, incomprehensible mercy that only a being so far beyond mortal understanding could conceive.

And yet, even that mercy was absurdly overpowered. The held-back version still made Godric effectively omnipotent. The struggle he had hoped to preserve was, from the very beginning, a mathematical impossibility. The mortal resilience he believed in had been utterly overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the power he had granted.

He had tried to be kind. And his kindness had still birthed the most terrifying entity in the history of creation.

We walk through the eastern gardens, and I see him. Velarion.
