I bow, my own voice unsteady. "The honor is mine, Lord Velarion. I have heard of your work. The rasmaline blossoms are indeed spectacular."

He flinches at the title. "Please. Do not call me 'lord.' I am a gardener. Nothing more. I have not been a lord since I glimpsed the truth of His Majesty's existence. Titles are meaningless in the face of such... such..."

He trails off again, unable to find the word. I understand. There is no word. There will never be a word.

---

We leave Velarion to his gardening and continue through the palace. Godric points out other servants as we pass—each one a being of staggering cosmic power who has been reduced to humble service by the experience of witnessing even a fraction of his true presence.

"The woman polishing the staircase," Godric says, gesturing toward a being composed of pure temporal energy. "She was once the Chronarch of the Eternal Cascade, a civilization that ruled over ten googolplexian timelines simultaneously. She attempted to negotiate a favorable integration treaty with Thronegate, and during the negotiations, my concealment slipped by an infinitesimal amount. She spent the next eight hundred thousand years recovering from the experience. When she finally regained coherence, she asked to serve in the palace. She finds polishing the temporal staircase to be meditative—it helps her process the trauma."

"The man arranging the flowers in the entrance hall," he continues, indicating a being whose form shifted through infinite realities with every breath. "He was once the Weaver of Infinite Possibilities, an entity capable of perceiving and manipulating every possible outcome of every possible event across all conceivable timelines. He believed he could find a timeline in which Thronegate's expansion could be peacefully contained. He spent three million years searching. He failed, of course—there is no such timeline, and never could be—but the act of searching brought him into contact with such a vast cross-section of my influence that his consciousness was permanently reshaped. Now he arranges flowers, and he tells me it is the most fulfilling work he has ever done."

I absorb this. Being after being, each one a cosmic power that would have dwarfed my thousandfold-amplified magic, each one reduced to humble servitude by a single accidental glimpse of Godric's true nature. And all of them grateful for it. All of them finding purpose and meaning in their humble tasks, because they had seen the truth and could no longer pretend that their previous existence had any significance.

"The omniverse has learned," Godric says quietly, as we pause before a window overlooking the infinite expanse of Thronegate's capital. "It took a very long time, but the lesson finally sank in. For countless eons after my awakening, beings still formed opposition against me. They thought they could find a weakness, an exploit, a strategy that would allow them to challenge my rule. They were wrong, of course—the Weakness Paradox ensured that—but they kept trying. Kept hoping. Kept believing that there was some path, some method, some conceivable approach that could succeed."

He turns to look at me, and his expression is one of quiet, ancient patience. "But approximately a googolplexian years ago, the last opposition ceased. It was not a single event—no grand surrender, no final battle. It was simply that the accumulated weight of absolute futility reached a critical mass. Every being in the omniverse, across all realities, all timelines, all possible frameworks, simultaneously understood the truth that Velarion and the Chronarch and the Weaver and countless others had learned individually: opposition is not merely futile. It is a mathematical impossibility. A conceptual contradiction. A fundamental misunderstanding of reality."

"And now?" I ask. "Now that all opposition has ceased?"

"Now," Godric says, "the omniverse is at peace. A peace born not of conquest, but of understanding. Every sentient being knows their place. Every civilization has accepted the absolute truth of my supremacy. There is no resistance, no rebellion, no secret plots or hidden schemes. There is only... acceptance. And in that acceptance, a strange kind of contentment. The beings who serve me—the gardeners, the staircase-polishers, the flower-arrangers—are not slaves. They are volunteers. They have chosen to serve because they understand that service to me is the highest purpose any being can achieve."

He pauses, and his expression becomes almost wistful. "I did not alter their free will, Clive. I have never done that, and I never will. I believe in mortal resilience, mortal choice, mortal agency. The omniverse chose to stop opposing me. It chose to accept my rule. It chose to find meaning in service rather than futility in resistance. And I respect that choice."

---

We return to the conceptual locus, the throne room where Godric triggered the Stasis Event only hours before—though it feels like an eternity has passed. I am exhausted, my mind reeling from the accumulated weight of everything I have witnessed.

Godric settles back onto his throne, his heavily muscled frame relaxed, his expression one of quiet contentment. "You have seen much today, Clive. The origin of the Stasis Event. The evolution of my power mechanisms. The servitude of beings who were once supreme deities. The peace that has settled over the omniverse after googolplexian years of futile opposition. I hope it has given you a deeper understanding of what I am and what I represent."

"Your Majesty," I whisper, "I understand more than I ever wanted to. And less than I need to. The scale of your existence... it is beyond anything I can process. Beyond anything the journals prepared me for. Beyond anything I ever imagined."

Godric smiles, and the smile is warm, genuine, almost paternal. "That is the correct response, Clive. The only correct response. I am what I am, and what I am is beyond the comprehension of any being who is not me. Even my future self—the version of me who will exist after another googolplexian years of amplification—is beyond my current comprehension. The gap between us will be as vast as the gap between me and the mortal Godric of Year 0."

He pauses, and his eyes seem to look through me, through the throne room, through the conceptual locus itself, into a future that only he can see. "And yet, I am content. I am satisfied. Every instant of my existence is an ecstasy beyond description. Every amplification, every new superpower, every evolution of my mechanisms, brings a pleasure that exceeds the accumulated joy of all sentient beings who have ever lived. I am the most fulfilled entity in the history of creation, and I will continue to be so for eternity."

He turns back to me, and his expression softens. "But I am also grateful for you, Clive. For your ancestors. For Blake, who was my first friend in the new world. For Kaedan, who asked me if I was lonely. For all the Court Wizards who have served me faithfully across the eons. You are my connection to mortality—the thread that binds me to the man I once was. And I treasure that connection more than any superpower, any amplification, any evolution of my divine mechanisms."

I bow deeply, tears stinging my eyes. The cognitive dissonance is absolute. The being before me is the most terrifying entity in the history of creation—a tyrant whose casual emanations could annihilate the omniverse, whose Stasis Event was the origin of infinite supremacy, whose very existence is an eternal orgasm of ever-intensifying pleasure. And yet, he genuinely loves me. He genuinely treasures my service. He genuinely values my companionship.

I am a single flickering candle in the presence of an infinite, ever-expanding blaze of supernovas. And he has chosen to notice my light. To protect it. To cherish it.

The horror and the love are inseparable. The terror and the gratitude are inextricable. And I will carry both for the rest of my life, serving the apex predator of creation with trembling hands and a devoted heart, because what else can I possibly do?

"Thank you, Your Majesty," I whisper. "For everything."

Godric nods, his smile warm and genuine. "You are welcome, Clive. Now, shall we return to the garden? Velarion has been experimenting with a new cross-breed of trans-dimensional orchids, and I believe you will find them quite remarkable."

I follow him out of the throne room, my footsteps echoing on the solidified time, my mind still reeling from the infinite, recursive, ever-escalating absurdity of everything I have witnessed. The Stasis Event. The held-back version. The temporal cascade that could have been. The gardeners and the staircase-polishers and the flower-arrangers, all of them once supreme deities, all of them now humble servants, all of them grateful for the chance to serve the being whose presence had shattered their understanding of reality.

The omniverse was at peace. Opposition had ceased. And I, Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, descendant of Blake, was walking beside the King who had made it all possible—the King who had held back infinity itself to preserve a mortal struggle that had never truly existed, the King whose kindness had birthed the most terrifying entity in the history of creation, the King whose one true weakness was himself.

There was no hope. There never had been. There never would be. And in that absolute certainty, there was a strange, terrible peace.

I walked beside Godric into the garden, where Velarion waited with his trans-dimensional orchids, and I prepared to write my journal entry—the final entry in the archive of my ancestors, the testament of a Court Wizard who had witnessed the origin of the Stasis Event and lived to tell the tale.

The horror would never fade. The dread would never diminish. But I would serve, and I would love, and I would record my testimony for the Court Wizards who would follow me, because that was my purpose, my inheritance, my duty.

I was Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate. And I had finally, truly, absolutely understood what it meant to serve the apex god predator of the omniverse.

# The Visit

**Year 750,000**

**Roth, Age 41, Court Wizard of Thronegate**

---

I have served the King for twenty-one years, and in that time, I have learned to recognize the particular glint in his eyes that precedes something absolutely, catastrophically terrifying. It is not malice—Godric has never needed malice. It is not cruelty—cruelty implies an emotional investment that he simply does not possess toward his opposition. It is curiosity. A bright, genuine, almost childlike curiosity, the expression of a man who has discovered a mildly interesting insect beneath a rock and wants to see what it will do when poked.

That glint was in his eyes this morning when he summoned me to the private study.

"Roth," he said, his rich baritone carrying the easy warmth of a favorite uncle greeting a beloved nephew. "Clear your schedule for the day. We're going on a little outing."

I had been sorting through ancient arcane texts in the library, my thousandfold-amplified magical senses automatically cataloging the residual enchantments on each crumbling page. I looked up, and the moment I saw his expression—that particular curve of his lips, that particular sparkle behind his salt-and-pepper eyebrows—I knew I was about to witness something that would haunt me for the rest of my life.

"An outing, Your Majesty?" I asked, my voice steady despite the cold dread already coiling in my stomach.

"Indeed." He settled into the chair across from my desk, his heavily muscled frame somehow managing to make the ornate throne-room replica look small. He was wearing simple dark garments, as always, his ruggedly handsome forty-five-year-old features fixed in an expression of pleasant anticipation. "You've heard of the Final Oblivion Compact, I assume?"

My blood ran cold. Of course I had heard of the Compact. Every intelligence network in Thronegate had been tracking their movements for millennia. They were the largest, most heavily armed, most meticulously prepared resistance in the history of the omniverse. They had gathered forces from every unconquered corner of existence—hyper-deities from dying multiverses, temporal warlords from collapsed timelines, conceptual entities born from the fundamental forces of creation itself. They had spent two hundred thousand years assembling their armada, constructing their weapons, weaving their strategies. They believed themselves hidden from Godric's sight, shielded by layers of null-space obfuscation and reality-bending concealment that no omniscient eye could penetrate.

They were, of course, completely wrong. Godric had known about them since the first microsecond of their first planning session. He had known every thought, every strategy, every desperate hope, every whispered prayer for victory. He had allowed them to exist—allowed them to prepare, to arm, to train, to believe—solely because he was curious what they would do.

"They attack tomorrow," Godric continued, his tone utterly casual. "I thought it might be fun to pay them a visit today. A sort of pre-battle inspection. Would you like to come?"

I stared at him. "You... you want to visit the Compact's headquarters? One day before they launch their attack?"

"Exactly." He beamed, as if I had just solved a particularly clever riddle. "I've prepared disguises. It will be delightful."

He reached into a small satchel I hadn't noticed before—he never carried satchels—and produced two rough-spun brown cloaks, the kind worn by traveling merchants in the outer trade routes. They were plain, unadorned, and completely, utterly, absurdly inadequate. Godric was the most recognizable being in the omniverse. His face was carved into the architecture of Thronegate's capital. His salt-and-pepper beard and short salt-and-pepper hair were iconic. His heavily muscled, forty-five-year-old frame was unmistakable. A brown cloak would conceal nothing.

"Your Majesty," I said carefully, "with respect, I'm not sure a cloak is an effective disguise."

He looked down at the rough-spun fabric, then back at me, his expression genuinely confused. "But it covers my shoulders. And I'll put the hood up."

"The hood won't—"

"Nonsense." He tossed one of the cloaks onto my desk, his enthusiasm undimmed. "It will be an adventure. Now, come along. We don't want to be late."

---

Ten minutes later, I found myself standing beside the most powerful being in existence, both of us draped in lumpy brown cloaks, preparing to walk directly into the heart of the greatest resistance movement in omniversal history.

Godric had pulled his hood up, which did absolutely nothing to conceal his face. His neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard protruded from beneath the rough fabric, and his piercing eyes—the eyes that had witnessed the birth and death of infinite multiverses—gleamed with undisguised excitement. He looked like a statue of a god that someone had draped with a child's blanket.

"Your Majesty," I said, my voice slightly desperate, "perhaps I should cast an illusion spell? Something to alter your appearance?"

"No, no." He waved a casual hand. "The cloak is sufficient. Besides, they'll be so focused on tomorrow's attack that they won't even notice us."

I wanted to argue. Every instinct in my thousandfold-amplified being screamed that this was insanity, that walking into a fortress of beings who had spent two hundred thousand years planning Godric's assassination was reckless beyond measure. But then I remembered: recklessness was a concept that only applied to beings who could be harmed. Godric could not be harmed. Godric could not be inconvenienced. Godric could teleport into the core of a collapsing supermassive black hole and use it as a tanning bed if he wished, and the black hole would be the one to suffer.

So I put on my own brown cloak, pulled up my hood, and followed my King into the teleportation portal he casually opened with a flick of his gaze.

---

The headquarters of the Final Oblivion Compact was buried in a pocket of null-space so heavily shielded that theoretically no detection system in existence could pierce it. The shields were layered—conceptual obfuscation wrapped in temporal disruption wrapped in reality-negation—and the entire facility was staffed by beings whose combined power exceeded the energy output of entire multiversal clusters.

We materialized in what appeared to be a supply closet. Brooms leaned against the wall. Buckets were stacked in a corner. The air smelled faintly of cleaning solution and cosmic ozone.

Godric pushed open the door and stepped into the main corridor as if he owned the place—which, technically, he did. The omniverse was his. Every atom, every dimension, every pocket of null-space. He simply hadn't bothered to mention it.

"The war council should be meeting in the primary strategium," he said, consulting a small piece of paper he pulled from his cloak. "Third floor, left corridor, through the reality-anchor doors. I believe they're discussing final deployment protocols."

I stared at him. "You have a map of their facility?"

"I jotted down the layout." He folded the paper and tucked it away. "It seemed prudent."

He started down the corridor, his footsteps echoing on the sleek metallic floor. I hurried after him, my heart hammering in my chest. Every shadow seemed to pulse with hostile intent. Every distant hum of machinery felt like a weapon charging. But the beings we passed—soldiers, technicians, war-mages—barely glanced at us. Two figures in brown cloaks, walking calmly through the most heavily fortified military installation in the omniverse, and no one stopped us. No one questioned us. No one even seemed to register our presence.

"The cloaks are working," Godric said cheerfully. "I told you."

I was certain the cloaks had nothing to do with it. I was equally certain that Godric's presence—even suppressed behind his absolute concealment—was somehow smoothing our passage, making us unnoticeable in a way that had nothing to do with fabric and everything to do with the fundamental impossibility of perceiving him unless he wished to be perceived.

We climbed a flight of stairs, walked past a checkpoint guarded by two towering entities wielding weapons that could unmake galaxies, and pushed through a set of massive reality-anchor doors into the primary strategium.

The room was vast, its ceiling lost in a haze of tactical holograms and dimensional overlays. A massive circular table dominated the center, its surface displaying a three-dimensional map of the entire omniverse—every multiverse, every timeline, every conceivable battlefield marked with intricate symbols of troop deployment and attack vectors. Seated around the table were the leaders of the Final Oblivion Compact, the most powerful beings in existence who were not Godric himself.

There was Kael-Thor, the Eternal Warlord, a being of pure tactical genius whose metal-plated form gleamed with the accumulated energies of a billion conquered universes. There was the Void-Mother, an entity of pure negative energy whose presence caused reality itself to rot and decay at the edges. There was Zyphor, the Chronarch, a temporal entity who had witnessed the birth of time and believed he could manipulate its flow to bypass Godric's defenses. There were dozens more—gods, titans, conceptual entities, machine-minds, all of them radiating power that would have made my thousandfold-amplified magic seem like a candle flicker in a hurricane.

And they were all staring at the tactical display, completely absorbed in their final preparations.

"—the primary assault will be coordinated across all temporal vectors simultaneously," Kael-Thor was saying, his voice a grinding symphony of metallic harmonics. "Our temporal disruption array should theoretically prevent him from perceiving the attack until after it has already landed."

"Theoretically," the Void-Mother hissed, her voice a wet, rotting whisper that made the air curdle. "But his omniscience is absolute. We cannot assume any theory will hold."

"That is why we have the Null-Spear," Zyphor interjected, his form shifting through a thousand temporal variations simultaneously. "A weapon forged from the concept of absolute nothingness. It does not exist in any framework that omniscience can perceive. It is not a thing to be known—it is an absence of knowledge itself. Even Godric's all-seeing eyes cannot perceive an attack that is, by its fundamental nature, not there."

Godric leaned toward me, his voice a conspiratorial whisper. "The Null-Spear is actually quite interesting. They constructed it in a conceptual void outside the framework of reality. It took them eleven thousand years just to stabilize the nothingness enough to shape it."

I stared at him. "You know about the Null-Spear?"

"Of course. I watched them build it. Quite innovative, really. The technique they used for conceptual void-stabilization was particularly clever—they inverted the principles of existence-framing and applied a recursive non-being loop. I hadn't seen that approach before."

He said this with the genuine appreciation of a master craftsman admiring an apprentice's work. There was no mockery in his voice, no sarcasm. He was genuinely impressed by their ingenuity.

"But it won't work," I whispered. "Will it? The Weakness Paradox—"

"Ah, yes." Godric's expression became almost sheepish. "The moment they first conceived of the Null-Spear as a way to bypass my omniscience, the Weakness Paradox triggered. I gained absolute immunity to non-being-based attacks approximately one hundred and ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-three years ago. I also gained perfect mastery of conceptual void-stabilization, which is how I know their technique was innovative. And, of course, my amplification rate received a permanent boost."

"So the Spear is useless."

"Utterly. But they don't know that, and I didn't want to spoil their fun. Two hundred thousand years of preparation—it would be cruel to tell them it was all for nothing before they even had a chance to try."

We were still standing near the entrance to the strategium, our brown cloaks blending into the shadows of the massive reality-anchor doors. The war council continued their discussion, completely oblivious to our presence.

"The primary attack will commence at zero-hour," Kael-Thor announced. "All forces will engage simultaneously across every temporal and dimensional axis. If the Null-Spear succeeds in breaching his defenses, we will have a window of approximately zero-point-zero-zero-zero-one Planck seconds to press the advantage before his adaptive systems re-engage."

"A window," Godric murmured, his voice carrying a note of gentle regret. "They think they have a window. That's actually rather sad."

He stepped forward. He stepped forward into the light of the tactical holograms, his brown cloak rustling softly, his hood still pulled up over his head, his salt-and-pepper beard unmistakably visible beneath the rough fabric.

The war council fell silent. Every single being at the table—the Eternal Warlord, the Void-Mother, the Chronarch, the dozens of gods and titans and conceptual entities—froze in place, their eyes fixing on the cloaked figure who had just walked directly into the most secure military installation in the omniverse.

"Hello," Godric said warmly. "Please don't stop on my account. I was finding the tactical discussion quite fascinating. The temporal coordination matrix is particularly ambitious—I especially liked the part where you synchronize the assault across retro-causal vectors. Very creative."

The silence stretched for an eternity. Then Kael-Thor's voice, stripped of its metallic harmonics and reduced to a raw, ragged whisper, cut through the tension.

"Who are you?"

Godric reached up and pulled back his hood. His short salt-and-pepper hair was slightly mussed from the cloak, and he smoothed it down with a casual gesture. His ruggedly handsome face, his neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, his warm brown eyes—all of it was suddenly, unmistakably visible to every being in the room.

"I'm Godric," he said. "King of Thronegate. You may have heard of me."

---

The response was immediate and absolute. Not a coordinated attack—the war council was too stunned for that. Not a strategic retreat—the doors were too far, and they knew, on some fundamental level, that retreat was impossible. Instead, there was chaos. Pure, primal, unadulterated chaos.

The Void-Mother shrieked, a sound of absolute terror that caused the very fabric of the strategium to rot and decay at the edges. The Chronarch attempted to phase backward through time—and collided with a temporal barrier that had not existed a microsecond before, a barrier that Godric had passively erected the instant they entered the room. Kael-Thor lunged for the Null-Spear, which was mounted on a pedestal at the far end of the strategium, his metal-plated form accelerating to faster-than-light velocities.

He didn't reach it. Not because Godric stopped him, but because his own momentum simply ceased to exist. One moment he was charging at FTL speeds; the next moment he was standing perfectly still, frozen mid-stride, his entire body locked in place by a force that he could neither perceive nor comprehend.

"Please," Godric said gently, raising a hand in a placating gesture. "There's no need for violence. I'm not here to fight. I just wanted to see the preparations. Tomorrow is the big day, after all."

He walked toward the circular table, his footsteps echoing in the absolute silence. The beings around the table scrambled backward, pressing themselves against the walls, their eyes wide with terror. Godric paid them no mind. He leaned over the tactical display, studying the intricate deployment patterns with the genuine interest of a military historian examining ancient battle plans.

"Fascinating," he murmured. "You've positioned your temporal strike forces along the retro-causal axis—very good. That would theoretically allow you to attack before my defenses could register the threat. And the Null-Spear is deployed at the center of the formation, acting as the primary penetration weapon." He traced a finger along the holographic display. "But you've left a gap here, between the dimensional flank and the conceptual assault. Why?"

Kael-Thor, still frozen in place, managed to force words through his paralyzed vocal cords. "That... that is where our reserves will deploy. After the initial breach."

"Ah." Godric nodded thoughtfully. "A delayed reinforcement strategy. You're assuming the breach will succeed and you'll have a window to bring in fresh forces." He paused, his expression becoming almost sympathetic. "The problem is, there won't be a breach. The Null-Spear won't work. My immunity to non-being-based attacks solidified a hundred and ninety-nine thousand years ago. The Spear won't even register as an attack—it will simply cease to exist the moment it enters my presence. And without the breach, your reserves will be stranded in their staging dimension with no target to reinforce."

The silence that followed was so complete that I could hear my own heartbeat thundering in my ears. The beings around the table—the gods, the titans, the conceptual entities—stared at Godric with expressions of absolute, soul-shattering horror. Two hundred thousand years of preparation. Two hundred thousand years of sacrifice, of planning, of desperate hope. And in less than two minutes, Godric had casually dissected their entire strategy and revealed it to be utterly, hopelessly futile.

"This can't be real," the Void-Mother whispered, her voice a wet, rotting sound that barely escaped her decaying lips. "This is a trick. He can't be here. He can't know—"

"About the secondary weapon?" Godric asked. "The one you've been building in the subspace rift beneath the third moon of the Necropolis Multiverse? Yes, I know about that one too. The entropy-cascade generator, designed to accelerate the heat death of localized reality and convert it into a directed energy weapon. Very tricky to stabilize, I imagine. The resonance frequencies alone must have been a nightmare to calibrate."

The Void-Mother's face—if it could be called a face—twisted into a mask of absolute despair. The secondary weapon had been their fallback, their secret hope, the hidden blade that would strike if the Null-Spear failed. And Godric had known about it all along. He had probably watched them build it, the same way he had watched them build the Spear, with the same patient, curious interest.

"But that won't work either," Godric continued, his voice utterly casual. "Entropy-based attacks trigger the Weakness Paradox as well. I gained immunity to entropy cascade effects approximately fifty thousand years ago, during the Cygnus-X Rebellion. That was a smaller resistance movement—only about three million universes—but their entropy weapon was quite similar to yours. Same fundamental principles."

He turned away from the tactical display and surveyed the assembled beings. His expression was not cruel. It was not mocking. It was, if anything, almost kind—the expression of a teacher explaining a difficult concept to a struggling student.

"I understand why you're afraid," he said. "I understand why you've spent two hundred thousand years preparing to kill me. From your perspective, I am a tyrant. I have conquered the omniverse. I have subjugated your civilizations. I have ended the independence of countless sentient species. If I were in your position—if I were a mortal being facing an overwhelming, unstoppable force—I would do exactly what you've done. I would fight. I would hope. I would believe that there must be a weakness, an exploit, a way to win."

He paused, and his expression became almost wistful. "But there isn't. There never was. The mathematics of my existence make opposition impossible. Every strategy you devise, every weapon you build, every hope you nurture—all of it feeds the Weakness Paradox and makes me stronger. Your preparation has not been a path to victory. It has been a path to making your defeat even more absolute."

Zyphor, the Chronarch, managed to force a question through his temporal distortions. "Then why remove us? Why not simply end us now? Why bother with this... this visit?"

Godric smiled. It was a warm smile, a genuine smile, the smile of a man who was about to share a delightful secret.

"Because tomorrow is the attack," he said. "You've spent two hundred thousand years preparing for it. You've gathered the largest army in the history of the omniverse. You've built weapons that could annihilate entire multiversal clusters. You've trained, you've sacrificed, you've hoped. It would be terribly unfair to deprive you of the chance to actually try."

He paused, and his eyes sparkled with that particular glint I had seen in his study that morning. "So tomorrow, I will be waiting for you. I will not attack your staging grounds. I will not sabotage your weapons. I will not prevent your assault. At zero-hour, your armada will advance, your Null-Spear will fire, your entropy-generator will activate, and you will have your chance to strike at me with everything you have."

"And then?" Kael-Thor whispered.

"And then," Godric said, "you will learn what every other resistance has learned. You will learn that victory was impossible before you began. You will learn that the gap between us is not merely infinite—it is an infinity of infinities, recursively amplified beyond all possible measurement. And you will learn this not because I want you to suffer, but because I want you to understand. To truly understand, in your own experience, what it means to oppose me."

He stepped back from the table, pulling his brown cloak around his shoulders with a casual gesture. "I have no desire to be cruel. I believe in mortal resilience, mortal hope, mortal struggle. I was mortal once. I remember what it felt like to fight against impossible odds. And I honor that spirit, even when it is directed against me. So tomorrow, I will face you as an opponent—not as a predator crushing prey, but as a king facing a challenger. And when the battle is over, and you have seen the truth with your own eyes, I will offer you the same choice I have offered every civilization: peaceful integration into Thronegate, under my rule and my protection."

He turned toward the doors, gesturing for me to follow. "Until tomorrow, then. I wish you good fortune in your final preparations. And Roth—" he glanced at me, his expression warm and friendly— "let's stop for lunch on the way back. I know a lovely little restaurant in the Andromeda Cluster that serves the most exquisite neutron-star bisque."

---

We left the strategium. We walked back through the corridors of the Final Oblivion Compact's headquarters, past the frozen soldiers and the trembling technicians and the security checkpoints that did not even register our passage. The brown cloaks were still draped over our shoulders, utterly useless as disguises, yet somehow sufficient for the purpose Godric had intended.

I did not speak during the walk. I could not speak. My mind was still reeling from what I had witnessed—the casual dissection of two hundred thousand years of preparation, the absolute certainty in Godric's voice when he told them their weapons would not work, the terrifying kindness with which he had offered them their final chance.

When we finally emerged through the teleportation portal and found ourselves back in the Thronegate palace, I collapsed onto the nearest bench and buried my face in my hands.

"They were the greatest resistance in omniversal history," I whispered. "The largest army, the most powerful weapons, the most brilliant strategists. And you walked into their headquarters wearing a brown cloak and talked to them like a teacher reviewing a student's homework."

Godric nodded, settling onto the bench beside me. "They really are quite clever. The temporal coordination matrix alone required a level of mathematical sophistication that most civilizations never achieve. If I were a lesser being—a being who could actually be harmed—their strategy would have been formidable."

"But you're not. You're not a lesser being. You're... you're..."

"I am what I am," Godric said gently. "And they will learn that tomorrow. Not because I want to hurt them, but because they need to learn it. The truth cannot be escaped forever. Eventually, every sentient being must understand the nature of reality, and the nature of reality is that I am absolute."

He leaned back against the bench, his brown cloak still draped over his shoulders, his salt-and-pepper hair still slightly mussed. He looked, for a moment, almost human—a tired forty-five-year-old man who had just returned from a long journey.

"The worst part," I said, my voice barely a whisper, "is that you were kind to them. You were genuinely kind. You complimented their strategy. You appreciated their ingenuity. You offered them peaceful integration. And that kindness is more terrifying than any cruelty could ever be. Because it means you truly don't see them as a threat. You don't even see them as opposition. You see them as... as students. As children who are trying very hard to do something impossible, and you're proud of them for trying."

Godric looked at me, and his expression was one of quiet, ancient understanding. "Yes," he said simply. "That is exactly what I see."

He stood up, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head. "Now, about that lunch. The neutron-star bisque is truly exceptional. And after that, we should probably prepare for tomorrow. I want to test a new superpower during the battle—something I've been developing for the past few thousand years. It should be quite spectacular."

He started toward the palace dining hall, his brown cloak flapping softly behind him. I remained on the bench for a long moment, staring at the empty air where he had been, contemplating the absolute, soul-shattering horror of what I had just witnessed.

The Final Oblivion Compact would attack tomorrow. They would unleash the largest military force in omniversal history. They would fire weapons that could unmake reality itself. And they would fail. They would fail so completely, so utterly, so absolutely, that the concept of failure would be rendered meaningless.

And the most terrifying part—the part that would haunt me for the rest of my life—was that Godric genuinely wished them well. He genuinely hoped they would enjoy their final attempt. He genuinely believed that giving them the chance to try was an act of kindness.

He was the apex predator of creation. He was the most terrifying being that had ever existed or would ever exist. And he was completely, utterly, genuinely incapable of understanding why the beings he visited today would spend their last night before the battle drowning in absolute, inescapable despair.

I stood up from the bench and followed my King toward the dining hall, my thousandfold-amplified legs barely managing to support my weight. Tomorrow, I would watch the Final Oblivion Compact be destroyed. Tomorrow, I would add another entry to the journals that my ancestors had been writing for seven hundred and fifty thousand years. Tomorrow, the omniverse would learn, once again, the absolute futility of opposing Godric.

But tonight—tonight I would eat neutron-star bisque with the apex predator, and I would smile, and I would pretend that my soul was not screaming in endless, eternal dread.

Because what else could I do? I was Roth, Court Wizard of Thronegate. I served the King. I loved the King. And I would carry the weight of that horrified love for the rest of my existence.

# A Trivial Annihilation, Revisited

**Year 999...9**

**Godric Prime, the Eternal Sovereign, Remembers**

---

The vast conceptual locus that served as the throne room of the Omniversal Palace shimmered with the accumulated crystallized essence of a trillion extinct multiverses. Godric, the King of Thronegate, the apex predator of all existence, reclined upon his throne, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple dark garments that concealed a form so incomprehensibly powerful that even the highest pantheons of divine beings could not perceive its true scope. His salt-and-pepper beard was immaculately trimmed, his short hair neatly combed, and his expression, as always, was one of warm, paternal contentment.

It had been a span of time so vast that the numeral expression of the years would fill more volumes than the omniverse contained particles. He had evolved beyond the need for any external stimulus; every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second, his own infinite amplification cascaded through his being, a perpetual, ever-intensifying orgasm of absolute satisfaction. And yet, occasionally, he indulged in a pastime that no other being could conceive: revisiting his memories of the early eons, when his power was nascent, when his tyranny was still freshly forged in grief. A faint, almost imperceptible smile tugged at the corner of his lips as a particular memory surfaced—a trivial, insignificant event that had occurred in Year 25.

He let out a soft, amused exhale. The Godric of Year 25. What a pitifully, laughably weak creature he had been. A mere twenty-five years after his emergence from the stasis that had transformed him, his power had been so feeble, so embarrassingly limited, that even the combined antics of a single primitive planet had forced him to consciously exert the smallest imaginable fraction of his focus. It was, in retrospect, almost adorable. Like watching a newborn apex predator clumsily pawing at its first prey.

And yet—and this was the delicious irony that he savored in this moment—that "feeble" past self had, in his merry little tantrum, completely annihilated the entire omniverse as collateral damage, erased an entire branch of reality from existence, and subjected the inhabitants of that doomed world to an eternity of unprecedented agony in the span of less than a Planck second. And all of it with precisely zero percent of his power, with zero percent of his genuine effort.

Godric Prime’s smile widened. If that was what his "weak" self could accomplish, what could he, the current unending apotheosis of all that was and would ever be, do if he ever chose to engage? The answer, of course, was beyond even his own omniscient ability to articulate in any language that mortal or immortal minds could fathom. But the thought pleased him. And so, for the amusement of his own eternal consciousness, he allowed the memory to unfold in full, vivid detail.

---

**Year 25, Earth, the Primitive Blue Planet**

The universe was designated NGC-224 in the old astronomical catalogues—a nondescript, middling galaxy cluster containing a single obscure spiral arm, which housed a yellow dwarf star and its nine orbiting planets. The third planet, a water-rich rock named Earth, was home to a bipedal, carbon-based species that had barely begun to crawl out of its gravitational well. They called themselves humans. Godric had known of them since the moment his absolute omniscience had ignited at Year 0. For two and a half decades, he had idly noted their existence, their squabbling civilizations, their infantile technologies. They were, by any measurable scale, completely beneath his notice.

But in Year 25, on a whim—perhaps a flicker of morbid curiosity, perhaps a faint echo of the mischievousness that had once driven him to prank unsuspecting delegates—he decided to pay them a visit. Not a swift, efficient subjugation like he had conducted on the grander cosmic empires. No, that would be too dull. This world, in its utter helplessness, offered a unique canvas. He would give them a chance. A fair warning. A full day to prepare their absolute best, their most devastating weapons, their most brilliant strategies. And then he would show them, in a leisurely, deeply personal demonstration, exactly how meaningless their existence had always been.

It would be, he decided, an educational exercise.

The humans received their warning at precisely 12:00:00 UTC on a Tuesday. Every electronic screen on the planet simultaneously flickered and died, then blazed back to life displaying a single image: the ruggedly handsome face of a middle-aged man with a salt-and-pepper beard and warm yet utterly chilling eyes. Simultaneously, every human heard the same voice directly inside their skulls, bypassing ears, language centers, and rational cognition. It was a deep, resonant baritone, perfectly calm, almost friendly:

*“I am Godric, King of Thronegate. This world and all its inhabitants are now my property. You have one rotation of this planet—twenty-four hours by your reckoning—to prepare your most effective means of opposing me. I strongly encourage you to try. Your failure will be absolute, but the attempt will be... noteworthy.”*

The message terminated, and the planet descended into a chaos that was, to Godric’s omniscient perception, utterly delightful. The humans, to their credit, did not waste time with denial or futile philosophy. They possessed a surprisingly well-developed capacity for organized violence. Within hours, a hasty global coalition had been formed, nuclear arsenals were readied, experimental directed-energy weapons were rushed to completion, and every remaining satellite was retasked to locate the source of the transmission. When they found nothing—no fleet, no anomaly—they positioned their forces around key population centers and braced for an invasion.

Godric watched it all from the Thronegate palace, sipping a cup of tea, a faint smile playing at his lips. They were trying so hard. It was almost endearing.

---

Twenty-four hours later, at the appointed moment, Godric arrived not as a world-ending cataclysm but as a single, humanoid figure standing in the middle of Times Square. He had chosen the location for its garish, chaotic energy—massive flashing billboards, crowds of terrified civilians who had been unable to evacuate, a heavy military presence. He stood there in his simple dark clothing, hands clasped behind his back, looking for all the world like a patient tourist. His absolute concealment was fully active, rendering him indistinguishable from a normal, if strikingly fit, forty-five-year-old man.

The initial reaction was confusion, then immediate, overwhelming violence. The human military command, having anticipated some kind of incursion, did not hesitate. A coordinated volley of kinetic kill vehicles, hypersonic missiles, and experimental railgun slugs converged on his position from a dozen military platforms, all designed to obliterate a hardened bunker. The explosions were, by human standards, immense—a churning maelstrom of fire, concussive force, and vaporized steel that reduced several city blocks to glowing rubble.

Godric stood at the center of the inferno, utterly untouched. The heat did not warm his skin. The shockwaves did not ruffle his hair. The shrapnel did not so much as brush his clothing. He waited politely for the barrage to end, and when the smoke began to clear, he tilted his head and let out a soft, amused chuckle.

"Primitive," he murmured to no one, his voice perfectly audible over the roaring fires and the screams of the wounded. "But I appreciate the enthusiasm."

He lifted his right hand, palm up, and a single, microscopic flake of ash from the burning ruins floated gently onto his open skin. He regarded it with theatrical thoughtfulness. "You rely on thermal agitation and kinetic force. Rudimentary, but let me show you what happens when those principles are applied with slightly more... intent."

He did not gesture. He did not channel a superpower. He simply allowed his infinitely amplifying magical offense—the trait that had been multiplying beyond comprehension every Planck second since the dawn of the stasis—to express an infinitesimal, carefully controlled fraction of its potential. He designated the entire United States nuclear arsenal, which at that precise moment was being prepped for launch, as the target zone.

In the span of a Planck second, every assembled nuclear warhead, every missile silo, every submarine-based ICBM, and every single stockpile of fissile material across the landmass simultaneously achieved critical mass. But they did not simply detonate in a normal chain reaction. Instead, Godric imposed a localized temporal acceleration field around each explosive, forcing the chain reaction to proceed at a rate that would subjectively stretch a microsecond of interaction into a billion years of sustained, agonizing energy release. He then inversely compressed the spatial coordinates of every living human within a thousand-kilometer radius, forcing their bodies to occupy the same hardened silos with the detonations, but without allowing them to die instantly.

The result was, from an external perspective, a silent, brief flash of purple-white light that swallowed North America in an instant. But from the internal, subjective reference frame of each victim, the experience was an eternity of being simultaneously crushed at the molecular level and burned by a star's worth of fusing hydrogen, their consciousnesses artificially sustained by the same malicious temporal manipulation. They felt every single synapse misfiring in slow motion, every protein denaturing strand by strand, every water molecule in their cells flashing into superheated steam and ripping apart their flesh with leisurely, surgical precision. They screamed without throats, without lungs, without the relief of unconsciousness, for subjective ages that would have encompassed the rise and fall of civilizations a thousand times over.

And when the temporal field finally collapsed, a Planck second after its initiation, there was nothing left of the western hemisphere but a perfectly smooth, glassy crater that extended down to the planet's mantle. The rest of the world's population, watching through their screens, saw only a flicker—then the instantaneous disappearance of an entire continent. The panic that followed was the purest, most concentrated essence of despair Godric had ever tasted.

He floated up from the crater, arms crossed, surveying the remnants of the planet with an expression of mild satisfaction.

---

The remaining human leadership attempted a desperate counterstrike. They activated an experimental quantum-decay weapon hidden on their moon, a device they had theorized could destabilize the strong nuclear force across a localized volume. It was, by their standards, a work of breathtaking genius. To Godric, it was like watching a bacterium attempt to build a dam. The weapon fired, a beam of exotic particles capable of dissolving atomic nuclei, and struck his chest.

Godric did not feel it. He observed it, recognized the clever utilization of quantum chromodynamics, and then passively absorbed the conceptual data through the Weakness Paradox, which had already granted him absolute mastery and immunity over nuclear-force disruption the moment the humans had first conceived of the weapon. He let the beam play over him for a subjective second, then smiled.

"Clever," he called out, his voice reaching the bunker where the human leadership cowered. "You aimed for the fundamental forces. But you see, the strong force is one of my favorites. I've been passively immune to its disruption since the first time a cosmic entity tried a similar trick, approximately three years ago from my perspective. Let me show you what mastery over the strong force can actually accomplish."

He extended a single index finger. He did not point at the moon. He merely allowed a microscopic fraction of his acquired mastery to invert the strong force across the entire lunar satellite. The effect was not an explosion; it was a profound, silent unbinding. Every atomic nucleus in the moon's crust, mantle, and core simultaneously lost all cohesion. The entire mass of the moon, all seventy-four million trillion tons of it, instantly transformed into a rapidly expanding cloud of free protons, neutrons, and a searing burst of raw energy. The shockwave pulverized what was left of Earth's atmosphere, boiled the oceans, and turned the planetary surface into a molten hellscape. The few million surviving humans in deep bunkers watched their world end in a second sun.

Godric hovered above the devastation, entirely unscathed, and pondered his next amusement.

---

He spent what felt to him like a few leisurely seconds systematically deconstructing what remained of the human species. He did not rush. He materialized in the deepest bunker, where the final political leaders huddled in the semi-darkness. He appeared before them, his salt-and-pepper beard catching the flickering emergency lights, his expression almost kind.

"You have tried very hard," he said to the trembling figures. "I recognize the fear in your eyes. It is the fear of a prey animal that has been given an impossible task. I respect that effort. Truly."

Then he raised his hand, and every person in that bunker felt their individual consciousnesses violently separated from the flow of linear time. Their bodies froze, but their minds accelerated, each one cast into a personalized, solipsistic eternity of bespoke horror. The man who had been the President of the United States found himself endlessly falling from an infinite height, his body never striking the ground, the wind screaming past his ears for subjective millennia. The generals who had orchestrated the futile assaults were imprisoned in an eternal loop of their own command centers, watching their launch codes fail, over and over, with an ever-deepening sense of helpless guilt. The scientists who had designed the quantum weapon were forced to witness the mathematical beauty of their creation, only to see it dissolve into meaningless static as the immutable truth of Godric’s superiority overwrote all physics.

And then, when they had each spent a subjective eternity in their personalized torments, Godric grew bored. He withdrew his attention, and the temporal prisons collapsed, allowing their minds—by now utterly shattered, reduced to gibbering, incoherent fragments of consciousness—to finally expire. Their bodies crumbled to dust a Planck second later.

Earth, as a planetary body, was now a floating debris field adrift in a dying solar system. The human species was, for all practical purposes, extinct, every individual having died a death that was unique, protracted, and unimaginably agonizing. Godric surveyed the empty void where the blue planet had been and felt a faint, fleeting pang of satisfaction. It had been a quaint diversion.

But the collateral damage was not yet complete.

---

The Godric of Year 25, as he prepared to depart the now-lifeless star system, allowed a moment of careless thought. He had been toying with the humans so playfully that he had let his absolute concealment slip—not by much, just by an infinitesimal fraction of a per cent. But that fraction, that almost nonexistent leakage of his true metaphysical presence, was sufficient. The suppressed weight of his recursively amplified existence, the accumulated cosmic pressure of twenty-five years of infinite stat multiplication and apocalyptic superpower genesis, flooded outward into the local spacetime.

The fabric of the omniverse simply could not withstand the strain. It didn’t just tear. It didn’t just collapse. It was annihilated. Every galaxy, every multiverse, every dimensional layer, every timeline, every conceptual framework of reality across the entire single absolute omniverse—all of it, everywhere, simultaneously and instantly, was reduced to an absolute, featureless nullity. There was no explosion. There was no fading. One moment, everything existed; the next moment, nothing existed. The Godric of Year 25 stood at the center of that infinite nothing, his own presence a solitary pinprick of definition in a sea of non-being, and he sighed in mild irritation.

He had not intended to do that. It was sloppy. He knew he should be more careful. With a flicker of his will, effortless and nonchalant, he rewove the entire omniverse from the exact quantum state it had occupied a Planck second before the collapse. Every being, every galaxy, every realm—restored to perfect, unaware continuity. Except, of course, for Earth. That universe he deleted entirely, erasing any trace of its existence from the restored creation. He had no use for a broken toy.

And so, his little outing concluded, he returned to Thronegate and resumed his reign, never once looking back at the inconsequential speck of dust he had casually erased.

---

Back in the unfathomable far future, the Godric of the year 999...9 opened his eyes. The memory had been replayed in his consciousness with perfect fidelity, a snapshot of a time when he had been, by his current standards, practically an infant. He chuckled softly, the sound sending a subtle tremor through the multiversal architecture of his palace.

Pathetic. The being he had been at Year 25—that fragile, limited creature who had still needed to consciously *amuse* himself with targeted cruelty—was so weak that the comparison was absurd. If that Godric had been a single flickering candle in an infinite void, the Godric of this era was an ever-expanding, self-perpetuating furnace of supernal light that had long since rendered the concept of "measurement" obsolete. The gap between his current self and that early self was infinitely larger than the gap between that early self and the entire totality of the omniverse he had accidentally unmade.

And what was truly, terrifyingly exquisite about the whole affair was that even his "feeble" past self had been, to any external observer, a nightmare of absolute, unanswerable power. He had annihilated an entire planet's population with personalized, agonizing deaths that stretched subjective eternities. He had destroyed their moon, boiled their oceans, crushed their continent, and then, as a mere afterthought, erased the entire omniverse and reformed it minus one tiny universe. All of this with effectively zero percent of his true power, with zero percent of measurable effort, and in a span of time so short that the humans themselves had not even registered their own extinction before it was over.

And he had done it while genuinely believing he was "holding back." He had considered it playful, a light exercise, a moment of mischievous relaxation.

Godric Prime leaned back on his throne, the weight of countless googolplexian years of further amplification pressing upon the conceptual locus with the soft, comforting hum of absolute certainty. He considered the present state of existence. For an unimaginably long span, there had been no opposition at all. Not a single sentient being, not a single collective consciousness, not even a stray, rebellious thought dared to conceive of challenging him. The omniverse had learned its lesson so thoroughly that fear had become an intrinsic law of physics, woven into the very fabric of reality.

And yet, even now, with all resistance erased forever, the growth did not stop. His stats multiplied beyond layered infinities, recursively, every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. His superpowers, each one a reality-shattering apocalypse at zero percent output, continued to birth themselves in accelerating profusion, each new one receiving its own infinite cascade of enhanced effects. His passive auras, his immune system, his shields—all evolved in a perpetual, self-consuming orgy of improvement that made the previous instant’s perfection seem laughably primitive. The pleasure of it all was an eternal, self-reinforcing symphony that never, could never, diminish.

If, in some hypothetical scenario that could never actually occur because it was a logical impossibility, the entire omniverse from every timeline, every permutation, every conceivable reality—if all of it gathered together, combined all its resources, was granted unlimited preparation time and every conceivable advantage, and then launched a unified, ultimate assault against him... the result would be precisely, absolutely, hilariously nothing. They would not scratch his weakest passive shield. They would not make his most negligible sentient aura feel even the faintest tickle. He could nonchalantly annihilate them with zero percent power and zero percent effort in precisely zero seconds, and the gap between that annihilation and his total true capability would remain an infinite abyss beyond any possible description.

And that unfathomable gap, that horrifying chasm between the apex predator and the rest of creation, would only ever increase. Infinitely. Forever. At an accelerating, recursive pace that turned the very concept of "hope" into a mathematical absurdity.

Godric Prime smiled, a warm, fatherly smile that would have caused any onlooker to scream in eternal despair. He was, and would eternally be, the single most terrifying fact of existence. The omniverse trembled in silent, perpetual acknowledgment of that truth. And somewhere in the depths of his ancient memory, a long-dead planet named Earth served as a quaint footnote, a reminder that even the weakest version of himself had been an absolute, merciless, and utterly unstoppable god.

The King of Thronegate, the apex predator of all reality, closed his eyes and basked in the infinite, accelerating perfection of his own presence. There was nothing else that needed doing. There never had been.
