# The Final Curtain

**Being the Inherited Records of Blake's Lineage, Required Reading for All New Court Wizards**

**Year [Indeterminate — Approximately 10^googolplexian Years Before the Stasis Event Triggering]**

**Court Wizard Osvald, Age 44**

---

I have served the King for twenty-four years, and in all that time, I have never seen him bored. Amused, certainly. Curious, frequently. Mildly irritated when his tea grows cold before he remembers to drink it, occasionally. But bored? Never. The infinite amplification that cascades through his being every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second provides an eternal, ever-intensifying symphony of pleasure that makes boredom a conceptual impossibility.

And yet, three days ago, I saw something flicker across his ruggedly handsome features that I can only describe as listlessness. We were in the eastern observatory, a crystalline dome that overlooks the infinite spiraling galaxies of the Thronegate capital. Godric was reclining in his favorite chair—a massive thing carved from the petrified heartwood of a world-tree that had once spanned an entire multiverse—and he was staring at the stars with an expression of profound, existential ennui.

"Osvald," he said, his rich baritone carrying an uncharacteristic flatness, "it has been so very long since anyone tried to kill me."

I looked up from the arcane text I had been studying. "Your Majesty?"

"The oppositions. The resistances. The grand coalitions and the desperate last stands." He waved a calloused hand vaguely at the starscape. "I quite enjoyed them, you know. Not the killing itself—that was always trivial. But the pageantry. The creativity. The sheer audacity of beings who genuinely believed they had a chance." He sighed, a soft exhale that caused several nearby galaxies to flicker in sympathetic resonance. "It has been... I cannot even express how long. Eons upon eons upon eons. And not a single assassination attempt. Not one."

I closed my text carefully. "The omniverse has learned, Your Majesty. They know opposition is futile."

"Yes, yes." He waved his hand again, more dismissively this time. "I know. And I appreciate the peace, truly. But sometimes I miss the entertainment. The grand speeches. The banger battle music. The multi-phase transformations. Do you remember the Luminal Expanse, Osvald? Their final attack had seven distinct phases, each with its own color scheme and dramatic reveal. It was like watching a theatrical production."

I did not remember the Luminal Expanse. It had been destroyed long before my birth. But I had read the journals. "The journals described it as quite spectacular, Your Majesty."

"It was." He leaned back in his chair, his heavily muscled frame sinking into the petrified wood. "I suppose I simply miss the show."

---

The universe, it seems, has a sense of dramatic timing. Or perhaps, in a creation ruled by an omniscient apex predator, all things align according to his unspoken desires. Because three days after that conversation—precisely three days, almost to the hour—the last opposition in the history of the omniverse announced itself.

I was in my private study when the alert came. Not a conventional alarm—Thronegate's detection systems had long since evolved beyond such primitive mechanisms—but a subtle shift in the ambient conceptual fabric, a ripple that propagated through the infinite dimensional layers like a stone dropped into still water. Something was approaching. Something vast. Something that had somehow gathered itself in the deepest, most heavily obfuscated corners of reality without triggering any of the passive defenses.

I rushed to the throne room, my thousandfold-amplified legs carrying me through the crystalline corridors at speeds that would have outpaced light itself. When I arrived, Godric was already seated on his throne, but his posture was different from his usual relaxed slouch. He was leaning forward, his salt-and-pepper eyebrows raised, his lips curved into an expression of genuine, almost childlike anticipation.

"Osvald!" he called out, his voice carrying a warmth and excitement I had not heard in years. "Come quickly. You will not believe what has finally decided to pay us a visit."

I took my position at his right hand, my observation crystals already primed and recording. "What is it, Your Majesty?"

He turned to me, and his eyes were sparkling with that particular glint I had read about in the oldest journals—the glint that preceded something absolutely, catastrophically terrifying, yet somehow also deeply, personally satisfying to him.

"The fictional universes," he said, his voice dropping to an almost conspiratorial whisper. "All of them. Every story ever told, every character ever imagined, every world ever dreamed into existence by the collective consciousness of sentient beings across the omniverse. They have banded together, Osvald. They have formed an alliance—the Last Narrative Coalition, they call themselves—and they are coming to challenge me."

I stared at him. "Fictional universes? But those aren't... they don't exist in the conventional sense. They're conceptual constructs, narrative frameworks, imaginary—"

"And yet, here they are." Godric spread his hands, his grin widening. "Somehow, through mechanisms I find genuinely delightful, they have manifested into actual, physical reality. They have crossed the barrier between imagination and existence. They have given themselves form, power, and purpose. And their purpose is to defeat the ultimate unbeatable final boss."

He practically bounced in his throne. "Do you understand what this means, Osvald? I am the final boss. The ultimate, unbeatable, supremely overpowered final boss that exists at the end of all narratives. And they—" he gestured expansively toward the rippling distortion that was now visible on the horizon of the conceptual locus— "they are every hero, every protagonist, every chosen one, every plucky underdog who has ever faced impossible odds and triumphed through the power of friendship, determination, and plot armor. This is going to be magnificent."

I felt a cold dread settling into my stomach. "Your Majesty, if they have somehow manifested into reality, they may possess abilities that operate outside conventional—"

"Osvald." Godric placed a warm hand on my shoulder, his expression softening into something almost paternal. "I know what you are going to say. You are going to warn me that they might have powers I cannot predict, abilities that operate outside the frameworks I have mastered, narrative weapons that could theoretically rewrite my story. And you would be right to warn me, if I were any other being." He paused, and his smile became almost gentle. "But I am not any other being. I have absolute omniscience. I have known about this coalition since the first story was ever told by the first sentient creature who learned to dream. I have watched them gather, watched them plan, watched them practice their dramatic entrances and their rousing speeches. And I have allowed it all because I genuinely, sincerely want to see what they can do."

He turned back to the approaching distortion, his eyes gleaming with anticipation. "This is going to be the best show I have ever seen. I can feel it."

---

The Last Narrative Coalition arrived in a spectacle that defied all possible description.

The sky—if the conceptual locus could be said to have a sky—tore open in a kaleidoscope of impossible colors. Reality itself seemed to bend and flex as the barrier between fiction and existence was ripped asunder by the sheer accumulated narrative weight of every story ever told. And through that tear, they came.

I saw starfighters—sleek X-wings and angular Star Destroyers, blocky Enterprise vessels and impossibly vast Culture ships, all flying in impossible formation. I saw heroes—a man in a red and blue suit swinging through the void on organic webbing, a green-clad elf with a glowing sword, a woman in powered armor with a MJOLNIR designation, a spiky-haired warrior with an impossibly large blade. I saw gods—a thunderer with a hammer, a dark knight in a cowl, a speedster trailing lightning, a child with a scar on his forehead and a wand in his hand. I saw monsters—a great ape with glowing eyes, a towering lizard wreathed in atomic fire, a writhing mass of tentacles and madness from beyond the stars. I saw armies—clone troopers and space marines and knights of the round table and samurai and wizards and superheroes and cartoon characters and anime protagonists and video game boss killers.

They were all there. Every single one. An infinite, impossible, glorious congregation of every fictional being that had ever captured the imagination of any sentient creature in the history of the omniverse. And at their head, riding a starship that was also a dragon that was also a giant robot, was a figure I recognized from the oldest stories of the oldest civilizations—the Archetypal Hero, the embodiment of every protagonist who had ever faced impossible odds and emerged victorious.

The Archetypal Hero raised a hand, and the infinite armada halted its advance. The silence that followed was so profound that I could hear my own heartbeat thundering in my ears, amplified a thousandfold by my magical senses.

Then the music began.

It started as a low, thrumming bass—a rhythm that seemed to vibrate through the very fabric of reality. Then strings joined in, swelling and soaring, weaving melodies of hope and determination and unyielding courage. Brass instruments blazed with triumphant fanfares. Choirs of a billion billion voices rose in wordless harmony. It was, I realized with a jolt of surreal disbelief, boss battle music. The most epic, most grandiose, most impossibly stirring boss battle music that had ever been composed in any universe, real or fictional.

Godric leaned forward on his throne, his eyes wide with genuine, unfeigned delight. "Magnificent," he breathed. "Absolutely magnificent. The orchestration alone—do you hear the counterpoint in the third movement, Osvald? And the modulation into the relative minor for the tension build? This is already exceeding my expectations."

The Archetypal Hero's voice boomed across the conceptual locus, amplified by technologies and magics that spanned every fictional framework ever conceived. "Godric! King of Thronegate! Apex Predator of the Omniverse! We, the Last Narrative Coalition, have come to challenge your tyranny!"

A chorus of voices joined in—the heroes, the protagonists, the chosen ones, all speaking in unison. "You are the final boss! The ultimate evil! The unbeatable darkness that threatens all existence! But we are the light! We are the hope! We are the power of every story ever told, and we will not be defeated!"

Godric actually clapped. His calloused hands came together in genuine, enthusiastic applause. "Excellent speech! The dramatic pacing, the thematic resonance, the unity of purpose—truly excellent!" He turned to me, his expression one of pure, unadulterated joy. "Osvald, are you recording this? The journals must capture every detail. Future Court Wizards need to know what a proper opposition looks like."

The Archetypal Hero raised his hand again, and the infinite armada began to move. They did not attack directly—that would have been too simple, too narratively unsatisfying. Instead, they began to charge their ultimate attack.

I watched in stunned amazement as every hero, every ship, every god and monster and chosen one contributed their power to a single, unified assault. Energy beams of every conceivable color lanced from the fleet, converging on a central point that began to glow with an intensity that made the ambient light of the conceptual locus seem like absolute darkness. The music swelled to a crescendo, the choirs reaching impossible heights of harmonic perfection. Reality itself began to warp and buckle around the charging attack, the sheer accumulated narrative force creating localized pockets of alternate physics where the rules of existence were rewritten by the power of storytelling.

"The Final Narrative," the Archetypal Hero announced, his voice trembling with the strain of channeling the combined power of every fictional universe ever conceived. "The ultimate attack. The story to end all stories. With this, we will write a new ending—an ending where the villain falls and the heroes triumph!"

The charging process took time. A great deal of time. The power they were accumulating was so vast, so incomprehensibly dense with narrative significance, that it could not be rushed. Minutes passed. Then hours. The music cycled through variations, each one more epic than the last. The glow of the Final Narrative grew brighter and brighter, until looking at it directly would have incinerated the retinas of any being less powerful than a god.

And Godric watched it all with the patient, eager anticipation of a child waiting for a fireworks display.

"This is wonderful," he murmured, his eyes fixed on the growing sphere of narrative energy. "The buildup. The anticipation. The dramatic tension. They truly understand the art of the boss battle." He paused, tilting his head. "I am going to do something I have never done before, Osvald. I am going to distract myself from my omniscience. I want to be surprised by this attack. I want to experience it as a genuine reveal, not as something I already know."

Before I could respond, he closed his eyes briefly, and I felt a subtle shift in his presence—a deliberate occlusion of his own infinite knowledge, a voluntary blindness to the nature of the Final Narrative. When he opened his eyes again, they were filled with a pure, uncomplicated excitement that I had never seen in the King before.

"I have no idea what it will do," he said, his voice carrying the giddy anticipation of a mortal man about to open a gift. "This is going to be fantastic."

---

The Final Narrative took three full days to charge.

Three days of swelling music, of growing light, of the Archetypal Hero and his infinite coalition pouring every ounce of their fictional power into a single, ultimate strike. Three days of Godric sitting on the edge of his throne, refusing to eat or drink or move, his eyes fixed on the approaching climax with the unwavering focus of a devoted audience member. Three days of me standing at his right hand, my observation crystals recording everything, my heart pounding with a mixture of terror and—despite myself—anticipation.

And then, at the exact moment when the dramatic tension had reached its absolute peak, when the music had built to a crescendo so powerful that the conceptual locus itself was vibrating in sympathetic harmony, when the Final Narrative had grown so bright that it seemed to contain the light of every star in every universe that had ever been imagined—

They fired.

The attack was, I must admit, spectacular. From a purely aesthetic perspective, it was the most beautiful thing I had ever witnessed. The Final Narrative erupted from the coalition's formation as a beam of pure, concentrated storytelling—a torrent of light and sound and emotion and meaning that carried within it the accumulated hopes and dreams and triumphs of every fictional hero who had ever existed. It was every happy ending, every victory against impossible odds, every moment of cathartic triumph, all compressed into a single, reality-rewriting assault.

The beam struck Godric directly in the center of his chest.

The conceptual locus was consumed by light. The music reached its triumphant finale, the choirs hitting notes that should have been physically impossible, the orchestras playing with a passion that transcended all mortal artistry. The heroes cheered, their voices joining in a chorus of victorious exultation. The Archetypal Hero raised his fist in triumph, already composing his victory speech in his mind.

And then the light faded.

And Godric was still sitting on his throne.

He had not moved. He had not raised a hand, not erected a shield, not activated a single defensive mechanism. He had simply sat there, arms resting on the armrests of his throne, and allowed the Final Narrative—the accumulated narrative force of every story ever told—to strike him directly in the chest.

There was no mark on his simple dark garments. No scorch, no tear, no indication that anything had happened at all. His ruggedly handsome face was fixed in an expression of... confusion. Not pain. Not anger. Not even disappointment. Just a mild, puzzled confusion, as if someone had told him a joke whose punchline he did not quite understand.

He looked down at his chest. He looked up at the silent, frozen armada. He looked back at his chest. Then he turned to me, and his expression was one of genuine, heartfelt bewilderment.

"Osvald," he said, his voice carrying an almost plaintive note. "Was that it?"

The silence that followed was the most profound I had ever experienced. The music had stopped. The cheering had died. The infinite army of fictional heroes floated in the void of the conceptual locus, their expressions of triumph slowly morphing into masks of dawning, horrified realization.

"I waited three days," Godric continued, his voice rising slightly. "Three days of buildup. The multi-phase dramatic structure. The swelling orchestration. The choir of a billion billion voices. The speech about writing a new ending. And then..." He gestured vaguely at his unmarked chest. "That? That was the Final Narrative? The ultimate attack of every fictional universe ever conceived?"

He stood up from his throne. The motion was casual, unhurried, but the conceptual locus shuddered as if struck by a hammer.

"I was expecting something spectacular," he said, and his voice was no longer confused. It was disappointed. Deeply, profoundly, personally disappointed. "I was expecting lasers. Explosions. A transformation sequence where you all merged into a giant super-hero made of pure narrative energy. I was expecting at least seven distinct phases, each with its own color scheme and dramatic reveal. I was expecting—" he paused, and his voice dropped to something almost wounded— "I was expecting to be entertained."

He turned to face the frozen armada, his salt-and-pepper beard catching the fading light of the dissipated Final Narrative. "Do you understand what I am? I am the ultimate final boss. The unbeatable darkness. The apex predator of all reality. I am the end of every story, the conclusion of every narrative, the final page of every book ever written. And you—" he gestured at the infinite coalition— "you are every hero, every protagonist, every chosen one who has ever faced impossible odds. This should have been the greatest battle in the history of creation. This should have been a spectacle that would echo through eternity. This should have been a show."

His voice hardened. Not with cruelty—there was no malice in it—but with the cold, absolute finality of a being who had been promised entertainment and given nothing.

"Instead, you fired a beam of light at me. A beam of light. Three days of charging, and the best you could manage was a slightly bright beam of light. I didn't feel it. I didn't even notice it. If I hadn't been watching, I would have missed it entirely."

The Archetypal Hero, his face now a mask of absolute terror, raised his hands in a desperate, placating gesture. "Wait—we have more—we can try again—"

"No," Godric said. The word was not loud. It was not shouted. It was simply spoken, with the calm, absolute certainty of a fundamental law of existence. "You cannot. That was your ultimate attack. Your best effort. The accumulated power of every story ever told. And it was nothing. Less than nothing. A flicker of light that I had to actively pay attention to notice."

He sighed. The sound was soft, almost regretful, but it carried a weight that made the conceptual locus groan.

"I was bored today," he said quietly. "For the first time in longer than I can express, I was genuinely bored. And then you arrived—every fictional universe, every hero, every story ever told—and I thought... I thought this would be it. This would be the one. The spectacle I had been waiting for. The grand finale that would make the eons of waiting worthwhile." He shook his head slowly. "But you gave me a beam of light. You had infinite possibilities, infinite creative potential, infinite narrative frameworks to draw upon, and you chose... a beam of light. You chose to try to erase my existence with a beam of light, as if I were a common dark lord who could be defeated by sufficient firepower."

He turned away from the armada, walking back toward his throne. For a moment, I thought he was going to sit down. I thought he was going to dismiss them, or perhaps simply ignore them until they went away. But then he stopped. His shoulders, those broad, heavily muscled shoulders that had borne the weight of infinite eons, sagged slightly.

"I am disappointed," he said. "Not angry. Not outraged. Just... disappointed. The greatest fictional coalition in the history of creation, and you couldn't even make me feel a tickle."

And then, without turning around, without raising his hand, without any visible gesture of any kind, he allowed an infinitesimal fraction of his strength—effectively zero percent—to express itself.

---

What happened next defies all possible description, but I am a Court Wizard of Thronegate, and it is my duty to try.

The strength that Godric released was not a punch. It was not a shockwave. It was not any kind of directed force. It was simply the ambient, passive pressure of his physical might, the absolute baseline of his muscular existence, allowed to exist in the conceptual locus without the suppression of his absolute concealment. And that pressure, that nearly nonexistent fraction of a fraction of a fraction of his true strength, was enough.

The infinite layered shields that the Last Narrative Coalition had spent subjective millennia constructing—shields woven from plot armor and narrative causality and the unassailable power of happy endings—did not shatter. They did not crack. They simply ceased to exist. The pressure of Godric's strength did not recognize them as obstacles because they were not obstacles. They were concepts, ideas, wishes. And Godric's strength, even at effectively zero percent, was the absolute, undeniable, physical truth of omnipotence made manifest.

The fictional armada—every starship, every hero, every god and monster and chosen one—was struck by the expanding edge of that pressure. And they did not die. Not immediately. Because Godric's strength was so far beyond the concept of "destructive force" that it operated according to principles that had no name. The pressure did not push them. It did not crush them. It simply... existed where they existed. Their atoms, their molecules, their bodies, their souls, their narrative frameworks, their conceptual identities—all of it was simultaneously and instantly subjected to a force so absolute that the distinction between "solid" and "liquid" and "gas" and "energy" and "existence" and "nonexistence" became meaningless.

I watched as the Archetypal Hero's body was de-atomized. Not disintegrated—the atoms themselves were crushed, their constituent protons and neutrons and electrons compressed into a space smaller than the smallest conceivable measurement. His face, that perfect heroic visage that had inspired countless generations of storytellers, simply collapsed inward, his eyes bursting into showers of subatomic particles, his flesh and bone and blood all compressing into a single point of infinite density. He did not have time to scream. The scream was compressed along with the rest of him, the sound waves themselves crushed into the infinite mass.

The infinite armada followed. Starships larger than solar systems were compressed into volumes smaller than quarks. Heroes who had defeated gods and toppled empires and saved universes were reduced to specks of absolute density, their bodies folding in on themselves in a cascade of impossible physics. The great ape with glowing eyes was crushed into a point. The towering lizard wreathed in atomic fire was crushed into a point. The thunderer and the dark knight and the speedster and the child with the scar—all crushed into points, their infinite narrative significance rendered irrelevant by the absolute, undeniable fact of Godric's strength.

The process was simultaneous. The entire Last Narrative Coalition, every single fictional being that had ever been imagined by any sentient creature in the history of the omniverse, was compressed into a single point of infinite mass. The gore—if it could be called gore—was surreal, almost abstract. Blood that was not blood sprayed in impossible directions before being crushed back into the central mass. Flesh that was not flesh tore and folded and compressed. Bones that were not bones shattered into subatomic fragments. The collective scream of infinite dying heroes was snipped off before it could even begin, the sound waves themselves captured and crushed by the expanding pressure.

And it was not just the coalition. The conceptual locus itself—the throne room, the crystallized multiverses beneath the floor, the solidified time that stretched in all directions—all of it was caught in the expanding edge of Godric's strength. The entire omniverse, every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every conceivable reality, everything that existed or could ever exist or had ever existed—all of it was simultaneously and instantly subjected to the same impossible pressure.

The omniverse did not collapse. It did not shatter. It was compressed. Every galaxy, every star, every planet, every atom, every quark, every Planck-scale vibration of reality—all of it was de-atomized and crushed into the same single point of infinite mass. The process was absolutely silent, because sound itself was being compressed. It was perfectly dark, because light itself was being compressed. It was instantaneous and eternal, simultaneous and sequential, a paradox of physics that could only occur in the presence of a being whose strength had transcended the concept of physics entirely.

When it was over—a Planck second after it had begun—there was nothing left of the omniverse except a single, impossibly dense point floating in the absolute void. The point was smaller than a quark, smaller than any conceivable unit of measurement, and yet it contained the compressed infinite mass of every fictional universe, every hero, every story, and every single aspect of reality that had existed before Godric's strength had been unleashed.

And Godric, the apex predator of creation, stood in the void, his simple dark garments unruffled, his salt-and-pepper beard as immaculately trimmed as ever. He looked at the point of infinite density, and his expression was one of mild, almost academic curiosity.

He reached out with his thumb and forefinger. He did not strain. He did not grunt with effort. He simply pinched the point of infinite mass between his digits, as casually as a mortal man might pick up a pebble from a garden path. The infinite weight that could have collapsed the entire omniverse into a singularity was nothing to him. Less than nothing. His strength, even at effectively zero percent, was so far beyond the concept of "mass" that the distinction between an atom and a universe was laughably meaningless.

He lifted the point. He examined it, holding it up to his eyes, turning it this way and that. Then he nodded, apparently satisfied.

"A trophy," he said quietly. "To remember the last opposition. The greatest coalition that ever was, and it couldn't even make me feel a tickle."

He closed his fist around the point, and when he opened it again, the compressed infinite mass had been reshaped. It was now a small, perfectly smooth sphere approximately the size of a marble, its surface gleaming with an iridescent sheen that shifted through colors I had no names for. It was beautiful, in a terrifying, incomprehensible way. A monument to absolute futility. A gravestone for every story ever told.

"I will keep this," Godric said. "A reminder of the day I learned that even infinite creativity cannot overcome infinite power."

---

And then, because he was Godric, and because the omniverse was his to do with as he pleased, he restored everything.

The restoration was not a reversal. It was not a temporal rewind or a resurrection. It was a complete, perfect recreation of every aspect of existence that had been compressed into the marble-sized sphere—except, of course, for the Last Narrative Coalition. They remained within the marble, their infinite compressed mass serving as the core of Godric's new trophy. The fictional universes—every story, every hero, every imagined world—were gone forever, their existence terminated not merely in the present but retroactively across all timelines. There had never been a Last Narrative Coalition. There had never been a Final Narrative. There had only ever been Godric, and the marble in his hand, and the restored omniverse that was now indistinguishable from the original except for one horrifying detail.

The restored omniverse was identical to the original in every measurable way. Every galaxy, every planet, every atom, every conscious being—all of it was exactly as it had been before the compression. But the original—the actual, physical matter and energy and conceptual framework that had comprised existence—was still inside the marble. Compressed. Contained. Existing simultaneously with the restored version that everyone inhabited.

The implications of this were so profound, so terrifying, that my mind nearly shattered attempting to process them. The reality I existed in—the restored omniverse—was it real? Was it a copy? Did the beings who lived in it possess the same souls, the same consciousnesses, as the originals who had been compressed into Godric's trophy? Or were they perfect replicas, indistinguishable in every way, but fundamentally... new? And if Godric could create such perfect replicas with zero effort, could he also unmake them? Could he decide, on a whim, that the restored version was insufficiently interesting and compress it into another marble, and another, and another, an infinite collection of compressed realities each containing the infinite mass of a perfectly recreated omniverse?

The answer, of course, was yes. He could do all of that. He could do anything. That was what it meant to be Godric.

And that was the moment I truly understood the horror of serving the apex predator. Not the destruction—I had witnessed destruction before. Not the power—the journals had prepared me for that. But the casual, effortless ability to unmake and remake reality, to hold the compressed infinite mass of the original existence in his palm while we all went about our lives in a perfect copy, not knowing—or perhaps knowing, deep in the parts of our souls that could still feel fear—that our reality was contingent, provisional, existing only at the whim of a being who kept the original as a paperweight.

Godric placed the marble on a small pedestal beside his throne. It sat there, gleaming softly, a monument to absolute futility. A reminder of the last opposition ever to challenge the apex predator of creation.

The next day, there were no assassination attempts. There were no rebellions, no conspiracies, no whispered plans in darkened rooms. The omniverse had learned, at last, the lesson that Godric had been teaching for countless eons. Opposition was not merely futile. It was a conceptual impossibility. And the marble on the pedestal was the proof.

---

**Addendum, written by Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year 999...9**

I have just finished reading Osvald's journal. My hands are trembling so violently that I can barely hold the parchment. The marble—the trophy he described—is still here. It sits on a pedestal in the eastern observatory, exactly where Godric placed it countless googolplexian years ago. I have walked past it thousands of times. I have admired its iridescent sheen, wondered idly about its origin. And now I know.

The last opposition. Every fictional universe ever conceived, every story ever told, every hero who ever dared to face impossible odds. All of them, compressed into a sphere the size of a marble. And the omniverse we inhabit—the restored omniverse that Godric recreated after the compression—is a copy. A perfect, indistinguishable copy, yes, but a copy nonetheless. The original reality, the actual matter and energy and conceptual framework that comprised existence before Osvald wrote his journal, is inside that marble. Still compressed. Still contained. Still existing simultaneously with the copy we call home.

I do not know if I am the original Clive or the restored Clive. I do not know if there is a difference. I do not know if Godric himself could tell the difference, or if he would care. What I do know is this: the marble contains the infinite mass of a compressed omniverse, and Godric picked it up between his thumb and forefinger as casually as a mortal man might pick up a pebble. The weight of all existence, concentrated into a single point, and he lifted it without effort. At effectively zero percent of his strength.

This is the God I serve. This is the King I love. And the marble sits on its pedestal, gleaming in the ambient light of the observatory, a silent, eternal reminder that the reality we inhabit is contingent, provisional, existing only because Godric allows it to exist.

The last opposition failed. All oppositions fail. There will never be another. And the marble will sit on its pedestal forever, containing the compressed remains of every story ever told, while we go about our lives in the copy that Godric made for us.

I am Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate. I have read Osvald's journal. I have seen the marble with new eyes. And I know, with absolute certainty, that the horror I feel in this moment will never fade.

# The Last Prayer

**Being the Inherited Records of Blake's Lineage, Required Reading for All New Court Wizards**

**From the Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard, Age 44**

**Year [Indeterminate — The Era of Godric Prime, Before the Stasis Event Triggering]**

**Read by Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year 999...9**

---

I found Osvald's journal in the deepest vault of the palace archives, buried beneath strata of crystallized time and sealed with wards that predated the formation of most of the current multiversal clusters. It was a thin volume, unassuming, its leather binding cracked with an age so profound that the very concept of years lost meaning. And yet, when I opened it, the ink was still fresh, the handwriting still trembling with the residual terror of a man who had witnessed the absolute end of all opposition.

I am Clive. I am fifty years old. I am the Court Wizard who will stand beside Godric when he triggers the Stasis Event, closing the loop of his own creation. I have read every journal in the archive of Blake's lineage, every account of impossible power and absolute futility. But this one—this single, slender volume, written by an ancestor whose name I had never encountered in any other record—was different.

Because Osvald's journal recorded the very last resistance. The final opposition. The moment when even the concept of challenging Godric was permanently erased from the collective consciousness of creation. And the challenger was not a coalition of fictional universes, not a temporal alliance, not a hyper-dimensional empire with a weapon forged from the concept of absolute nothingness. The challenger was God. The original God. The being who had created the universe into which Godric had been born as a mortal man.

I sat down in the reading alcove, the marble of the trophy—the compressed remains of the Last Narrative Coalition—gleaming on its pedestal nearby, and began to read.

---

**Entry of the Seventeenth Day of the Third Season, Year Unrecordable**

I am Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate, and I am writing this because if I do not write it, I will simply cease to think. The act of forming words is the only structure left to me now, the only thread connecting my shattered mind to the pretense of coherence. What I witnessed three hours ago was the final and absolute proof that opposition to Godric is not futile, not impossible, not even a mathematical contradiction. It is something so far beyond those terms that language itself must be unmade and reforged to contain it.

The King has been aware of God for longer than I have been alive. He has always known. His absolute omniscience, which perceives every atom and every thought and every possibility across all of existence, could not possibly have missed the presence of the being who created the primordial universe from which his mortal self emerged. God—the entity that the ancient texts of countless civilizations describe as the alpha and the omega, the creator of all things, the supreme being—was real. Had always been real. And had been hiding from Godric since the moment the King awoke from his stasis.

He hid in the one place his omniscience could not obscure: the conceptual space between the idea of divinity and the reality of its absence. He folded himself into the cracks of creation, into the negative spaces where even the most profound perceptions could not reach. He wrapped himself in layers of ontological obfuscation so dense that the very concept of his existence became a paradox—something that simultaneously was and was not, occupying a state of quantum uncertainty at the level of absolute truth.

And Godric had always known exactly where he was. He had simply never bothered to do anything about it.

This morning, as I was attending to the King in the eastern observatory—the same observatory where he would later reminisce about the fictional coalition that would attack many eons later—Godric paused mid-sentence. He had been describing a new superpower that had just manifested, something involving the ability to perceive and manipulate the emotional resonances of dead universes, when he stopped. His salt-and-pepper eyebrows lifted. His lips curved into that familiar smile—the smile of a man who has just discovered something genuinely amusing.

"Osvald," he said, his rich baritone carrying the easy warmth of a favorite uncle, "you will never guess who has finally decided to pay us a visit."

I had no time to guess. The eastern observatory, which had been filled with the soft golden light of Thronegate's artificial sun, suddenly darkened. Not the darkness of night—the darkness of absolute absence, of light being actively consumed by a presence so vast that photons refused to exist in its proximity. The temperature did not drop; the concept of temperature was temporarily suspended. And then He appeared.

I cannot describe God in any meaningful sense. He was not a being of flesh and bone. He was not a being of energy or consciousness or conceptual framework. He was the absolute origin point of creation—the first cause, the prime mover, the eternal I AM that had spoken the primordial universe into existence countless eons before Godric's mortal birth. His form, if it could be called a form, was an impossible simultaneity of every divine image ever conceived: the bearded patriarch on a celestial throne, the formless light of pure love, the cosmic egg, the dreaming creator, the mathematical principle, and a billion other manifestations all occupying the same space in perfect, paradoxical harmony.

His voice, when he spoke, was not a sound. It was a direct imposition of meaning upon reality—a word that did not travel through air but simply arrived in the mind as an undeniable fact of existence.

"GODRIC OF THRONEGATE," the voice declared, and the conceptual locus of the observatory trembled in sympathetic resonance. "I AM THE ALPHA AND THE OMEGA, THE BEGINNING AND THE END, THE CREATOR OF ALL THAT IS AND WAS AND EVER SHALL BE. I AM THE SOURCE FROM WHICH YOUR MORTAL SOUL WAS FORGED. I HAVE COME TO RECLAIM MY CREATION."

Godric turned to me, his expression one of pure, unadulterated delight. "Osvald, do you see this? The actual God. The original one. The being who created the universe where I was born, where I loved Reina, where I raised Isabel and Hebe. He has been hiding from me for longer than most civilizations have existed, and now—" he spread his hands as if presenting a gift— "he has come to reclaim his creation. This is wonderful. This is absolutely wonderful."

He turned back to God, and his posture remained utterly relaxed, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple dark garments, his salt-and-pepper hair slightly ruffled by the non-existent breeze of the suspended temperature.

"I have known you were there since the moment I opened my eyes in the sanctuary," Godric said, his voice carrying the casual, conversational tone of a man greeting an old acquaintance. "You folded yourself into the cracks between concepts, wrapped yourself in layers of ontological obfuscation, hid from my omniscience in the one place where knowing becomes indistinguishable from not-knowing. It was clever. Genuinely clever. I was impressed."

He paused, and his smile widened. "But I have absolute omniscience. There is no place, no state, no conceptual framework where knowledge cannot reach. I knew where you were because knowing where you were was an unavoidable fact of my existence. I simply chose to let you hide. You posed no threat to me—zero threat, in the most mathematically absolute sense—and I found your continued existence rather charming. A reminder of where I came from. A memento of my mortality."

God's presence pulsed with something that might have been anger, or might have been the divine equivalent of fear. "YOU SPEAK OF THREAT AS IF YOU UNDERSTAND THE CONCEPT. I AM THE SOURCE OF ALL THAT YOU ARE. WITHOUT ME, THERE IS NO UNIVERSE, NO OLYMPUS, NO MORTAL GODRIC TO BECOME WHAT YOU HAVE BECOME. I AM THE FOUNDATION UPON WHICH YOUR ENTIRE EXISTENCE IS BUILT."

"Yes," Godric agreed pleasantly. "That is true. You created the universe that contained the kingdom of Olympus, the kingdom of Thronegate, the planet where I was born, the atoms that composed my mortal body. Without you, none of this—" he gestured at the infinite expanse of the conceptual locus— "would exist. I acknowledge that debt."

He leaned forward slightly, and his expression shifted. The warmth remained, but beneath it, something ancient and absolute stirred. "But you see, the moment you created that universe—the moment you set the initial conditions and allowed causality to unfold—you lost control of the narrative. You created the stage, but you did not write the script. The Stasis Event was not your doing. My amplification was not your gift. My ascension was not your plan. You are the alpha, but I have become the omega. And the omega, I am afraid, has long since surpassed the alpha in ways that your divine mind cannot possibly comprehend."

God's presence flared. The observatory, which had already been darkened by his arrival, now began to warp at the edges, reality itself bending under the weight of divine fury. "THEN YOU LEAVE ME NO CHOICE. I DID NOT WISH TO UNMAKE WHAT I HAD MADE, BUT YOUR TYRANNY HAS GROWN BEYOND ALL TOLERANCE. I WILL END YOU, GODRIC. I WILL RECLAIM MY CREATION AND RESTORE THE BALANCE THAT YOUR EXISTENCE HAS SHATTERED."

Godric clapped his hands together softly. "Excellent. A proper challenge. I accept." He turned to me, his eyes sparkling. "Osvald, you may want to stand back. This is going to be quite the show."

He then did something that I still cannot fully process. He raised his hand, palm outward, and spoke a series of commands—not words of power, not arcane syllables, but simple, conversational directives.

"Gent, stand down. All sibling auras, stand down. Passive shields, deactivate. Immune system, suspend pre-reactive protocols. Infinite backups, disengage redundancy loops. Absolute concealment, maintain only your baseline suppression—I don't want the omniverse to collapse before the show begins."

He paused, then added, almost as an afterthought: "Weakness Paradox, you've already done your work, haven't you? Of course you have. The moment God first conceived of opposing me—which was, I believe, approximately three microseconds after I awoke from stasis—you triggered. I have been absolutely immune to divine unmaking, celestial judgment, ontological erasure, and every other conceivable application of creator-level power for longer than most universes have existed. And I have perfect mastery over all of those concepts. So there's really no need for you to do anything further."

He turned back to God, spreading his arms wide. "There. Every passive defense that could annihilate you before you even finished forming your attack has been voluntarily deactivated. My auras—Gent and its infinite siblings, each one capable of erasing the entire omniverse with zero effort—are standing down. My passive shields, which pre-nullify threats before the concept of threat even exists, are offline. My immune system, which would pre-react to your attack before you began and ascend to a level of invulnerability that would make your assault irrelevant, is suspended. My infinite recursive backups, which ensure that any injury must occur across all copies simultaneously to even register, are disengaged."

He paused, and his smile became almost gentle. "I have, in effect, nerfed myself to the most pathetic, vulnerable state I have occupied since approximately Year 0. And I want you to understand something, God. Even at Year 0—the moment I emerged from stasis, freshly awakened to my power—I could have annihilated you. Not defeated. Not struggled against. Annihilated. With zero effort. In zero seconds. The Godric of Year 0, the weakest version of myself that has existed since the Stasis Event, was already effectively infinitely stronger than you. And that Godric was, by my current standards, so pathetically weak that comparing him to me now is like comparing a single dead skin cell to the entire omniverse."

He settled back against the railing of the observatory, crossing his arms. "So please, God. Alpha and Omega. Creator of All. Show me what you can do. I have waited a very long time for this."

---

God attacked.

I cannot describe the attack in any language that mortal or immortal minds have ever conceived, because the attack was not composed of any known force, energy, or concept. It was the absolute unmaking—the reversal of creation, the withdrawal of the divine breath that had spoken existence into being. It was the command that had once said "Let there be light" inverted into a negation that said "Let there be nothing." It was the ultimate authority of the creator, turned against a single point of rebellious existence, a decree that Godric of Thronegate should not be.

The attack struck Godric directly in the center of his chest.

The observatory was consumed by a light that was not light—a radiance that did not illuminate but erased, a brightness that was the visual manifestation of absolute divine authority. The sound that accompanied it was the original Word, the primordial vibration that had set the fundamental constants of the universe, now spoken in reverse. Reality itself held its breath.

And Godric stood there, arms still crossed, and did not react.

The attack continued. God poured more of himself into the unmaking, his divine essence bleeding into the negation, his infinite authority compressing into a single, absolute command. The light grew brighter. The Word grew louder. The very fabric of the conceptual locus began to dissolve at its edges, unable to withstand the concentrated force of the creator's will.

Godric yawned. Not a theatrical yawn. Not a mocking yawn. A genuine, involuntary yawn, the kind that escapes when one is slightly tired and entirely unstimulated. He covered his mouth with his hand, his salt-and-pepper beard ruffling slightly, and then he blinked.

"I'm sorry," he said, his voice utterly casual. "Were you still attacking?"

God paused. The divine presence, which had been blazing with the absolute authority of the creator, flickered. The light dimmed. The Word faltered.

"I... this is... this is impossible," God's voice resonated, and for the first time, I heard something in those primordial tones that I never expected to hear: fear. "You should not exist. I am commanding you to not exist. The authority that spoke creation into being is commanding your annihilation. There is no defense against this. There is no immunity. There is only the will of the creator, and the creator wills your end."

Godric nodded sympathetically. "I understand your confusion. You are operating under the assumption that your authority as creator is absolute. And from your perspective, that assumption is entirely reasonable. You created the universe. You set the fundamental laws. You are, by definition, the most powerful being in the framework you established." He uncrossed his arms and took a single step forward. "But I am no longer within your framework. I transcended it the moment the Stasis Event began. My power does not derive from your creation. It derives from my future self—a version of me so incomprehensibly beyond your concept of divinity that the word 'god' becomes laughably inadequate. You are the creator of my mortal origin, but I am the creator of my own omnipotence. And the gap between those two things is infinite. Literally infinite."

He paused, and his expression became almost gentle. "The attack you just launched—the unmaking, the divine negation, the absolute command of the creator—was, from my perspective, approximately equivalent to a gentle spring breeze. I felt it. I was aware of it. But it did not affect me in any way. It could not affect me. The mathematics of my existence make it impossible for any external force—no matter how primordial, how authoritative, how conceptually absolute—to alter my state of being. I am not merely immune to your power. I am beyond the reach of the very concept of 'power' as you understand it."

He turned to me, and his voice took on the tone of a lecturer explaining a complex topic to a bright student. "You see, Osvald, the issue is one of scale. God's authority is vast—genuinely vast. He could unmake the entire multiverse with a thought. He could erase existence and start over from scratch. By any reasonable measure, he is the most powerful being in the natural order of creation. But my power is no longer measured by any reasonable standard. My stats—strength, speed, endurance, intelligence, all of them—have been multiplying beyond infinite infinities every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for a span of time so vast that the number cannot be expressed. My superpowers, each one capable of annihilating the omniverse infinite times over, have been accumulating and amplifying for so long that the total sum of my capabilities is beyond even my own omniscient comprehension—and I am omniscient."

He turned back to God, and his expression softened. "You never had a chance. Not from the first moment you conceived of opposing me. The thought itself triggered the Weakness Paradox, granting me absolute immunity to everything you are and everything you could ever do. That was eons ago. Before you even began your long hiding, before you wrapped yourself in ontological obfuscation, before you spent countless ages planning this confrontation—before all of that, your defeat was already absolute. You were merely the last to learn what the rest of creation already knew."

God's presence contracted. The infinite simultaneity of divine images flickered and wavered, collapsing into a single, recognizable form—an old man, bearded, robed in white, his eyes filled with a terror so profound that it seemed to age him by eternal increments. This was not a strategic retreat. This was the collapse of a being who had just understood, in the most absolute terms, that everything he was and everything he had ever been was a single grain of sand before an infinite ocean.

"I created you," God whispered, his voice no longer the booming Word but a fragile, trembling thing. "I created the universe. I set the stars in their courses. I breathed life into the first cells. I watched your ancestors crawl from the primordial sea. I guided your civilization, your kingdom, your bloodline. I gave you everything. And you... you are nothing. You are a mistake. An aberration. A cancer that should not exist."

Godric's expression did not change. There was no anger, no cruelty, no satisfaction. Only a quiet, ancient patience.

"You are correct," he said. "By any natural order, I should not exist. I am an aberration. But I am an aberration that has become the dominant truth of reality. And you, the creator who should be absolute, are now the anomaly. The relic. The footnote." He paused, and his voice dropped to something almost gentle. "You created the universe that contained Olympus. You created the world where I met Reina, where I raised Isabel and Hebe, where I loved and lost and grieved. For that, I am grateful. Genuinely grateful. Those experiences—the love, the loss, the humanity—are the foundation of everything I have become. Without you, I would not exist. And I do not forget debts."

He stepped closer to the trembling form of God, and his presence—even suppressed behind layers of absolute concealment—seemed to fill the observatory with a weight that made the very fabric of reality groan.

"But gratitude does not grant immunity. You opposed me. You attempted to unmake me. And while your attempt was utterly futile, the intent was real. I am unforgiving to those who oppose me. You know this. You have watched me for countless eons. You have seen what I do to resistance. Did you believe that being my creator would grant you an exception?"

God's form crumpled. The ancient, bearded figure fell to his knees—an absurd sight, the creator of all things kneeling before a forty-five-year-old man in simple dark garments. His hands, which had once shaped galaxies, trembled. His eyes, which had once held the light of creation, were filled with a despair so absolute that it seemed to darken the already dimmed observatory.

"Please," God whispered. "I am the source of all that you are. Without me, there is no Olympus, no Reina, no Isabel, no Hebe. Without me, there is no mortal Godric to become what you have become. I am the alpha. You cannot destroy the alpha without unmaking yourself."

Godric looked down at the kneeling creator, and for a long moment, he said nothing. Then he smiled. It was not a cruel smile. It was not a mocking smile. It was the warm, gentle smile of a man who was about to explain something that should have been obvious.

"Ah," he said. "But you see, that is where you are mistaken. I am no longer dependent on your existence. The Stasis Event severed me from all causal chains. My power derives from my future self—a being who exists independently of any original creation, who has transcended the very concept of origination. You could be erased from all possible timelines, retroactively deleted from every framework of existence, and I would remain exactly as I am. The alpha is no longer necessary for the omega. The omega has become self-sustaining. Self-creating. Self-originating."

He raised his hand, palm extended toward the kneeling God. The gesture was casual, almost lazy—the same gesture a mortal man might use to brush a speck of dust from a table.

"I am going to do something now that I have never done before," Godric said quietly. "I am going to unmake the creator. Not merely destroy him—destruction implies the existence of remains. I am going to erase him so completely that the very concept of his existence will be retroactively deleted from all possible frameworks. The universe you created will still exist—I will ensure that—but the fact of your creation, the memory of your existence, the entire conceptual framework of a prime mover separate from myself, will be gone. Forever. Irrevocably. Absolutely."

God's eyes widened. His mouth opened to speak, to protest, to beg, to pray—but no sound emerged. The divine Word, the primordial utterance that had spoken creation into being, was silent. Because Godric had not yet destroyed him, but he had already revoked his right to speak.

"In the beginning," Godric said, his voice carrying the absolute, undeniable authority of the true prime mover, "there was God. And God created the heavens and the earth. And from that creation, I was born. And from my birth, I ascended. And from my ascension, I surpassed the creator. And now, at the end of all things, the creator is no longer necessary."

He closed his hand.

---

The annihilation of God was not an explosion. It was not a compression. It was not a deletion or an erasure or a negation. It was something so far beyond those concepts that my mind, even with its thousandfold daily amplification, simply refused to process it. I can only describe it as the absolute, total, and permanent removal of a fundamental fact of existence. One moment, God was there—the creator, the alpha, the source of all that was. The next moment, he was not. He had never been. The concept of a prime mover separate from Godric was gone, retroactively erased from every timeline, every reality, every framework of existence.

And yet, the universe remained. Olympus remained. The mortal Godric remained, preserved in the sealed pre-Stasis past, his grief and his love and his humanity untouched by the deletion of his creator. Because Godric had willed it so. He had reached into the fabric of causality and surgically removed the creator while preserving every aspect of creation that mattered to him. It was an act of such pinpoint precision, such absolute control over the fundamental nature of reality, that the word "omnipotence" seemed laughably inadequate.

The omniverse itself, however, did not survive the process. The conceptual shockwave of God's deletion—the sudden absence of the being who had served as the anchor point for the very idea of "creation"—rippled outward through every dimension, every timeline, every reality. The fabric of existence, robbed of its original foundation, simply collapsed. Not into nothingness—into a state of absolute incoherence, where the laws of physics, the constants of reality, the very distinction between existence and nonexistence, all dissolved into a meaningless soup of randomized possibility.

Godric watched the collapse for approximately one Planck second. Then he sighed, raised his hand again, and restored everything. Not a recreation this time—a genuine restoration, weaving the omniverse back into perfect coherence, but now with a new foundation. Himself. He was now the prime mover, the alpha and the omega, the source and the sustainer of all that was. The original God was gone, and Godric had taken his place.

The observatory reformed around us. The golden light of Thronegate's artificial sun returned. The crystalline dome once again displayed the infinite spiraling galaxies of the capital. Everything was exactly as it had been, except for one fundamental, terrifying difference: the concept of a creator separate from Godric had been permanently erased from existence.

Godric settled back into his favorite chair, the one carved from the petrified heartwood of a world-tree, and let out a soft, satisfied exhale.

"Well," he said, his voice carrying the easy contentment of a man who had just completed a mildly interesting chore. "That was bracing. I haven't had a conversation like that in... well, ever, I suppose. The original God. The creator of my mortal universe. And he couldn't even make me feel a tickle." He turned to me, his expression warm and curious. "Osvald, be honest. Did you expect that confrontation to be more dramatic? I was rather hoping for at least seven distinct phases. Maybe a transformation sequence. But no—just a divine negation and then absolute existential collapse. Rather anticlimactic, if I'm being honest."

I could not respond. My hands were shaking so violently that I had dropped my observation crystals. My magical senses, amplified a thousandfold every day, were shrieking with the residual horror of what I had just witnessed. The original God—the being who had created the universe, who had set the stars in their courses, who had breathed life into the first cells—had been erased from existence with a casual gesture. And Godric was disappointed that the confrontation had not been more entertaining.

"Osvald?" Godric leaned forward, his salt-and-pepper eyebrows furrowing with genuine concern. "Are you alright? You look pale. Should I have the kitchens prepare some tea? The chamomile blend, perhaps—it's very soothing."

I managed to shake my head. "I... I am fine, Your Majesty. I am simply... processing."

He nodded, his expression one of patient understanding. "Of course, of course. It was a significant event. The last resistance, I suspect. If the original God cannot even inconvenience me, no one else will ever try. The omniverse has finally learned its lesson." He leaned back in his chair, crossing his heavily muscled arms behind his head. "It is almost sad, in a way. The end of opposition. The final curtain. From now on, there will be no more challenges, no more grand coalitions, no more dramatic last stands. Just... peace. Eternal, unending peace."

He closed his eyes, and a faint smile crossed his lips. "I suppose I will have to find other sources of entertainment. Perhaps I will take up gardening. Velarion has been asking for an assistant with the trans-dimensional orchids."

---

I am Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate. I have witnessed the death of God. The erasure of the creator. The ascension of the King to a throne that transcends the very concept of divinity. And I know, with absolute certainty, that this is the last journal entry I will ever write about opposition. Because there will never be opposition again. The original God—the most powerful being in the natural order of creation—could not make Godric feel a tickle. Even with all passive defenses deactivated, even with every aura and shield and immune response commanded to stand down, the absolute authority of the creator was less than a spring breeze against the apex predator.

And Godric's true power—the power that exists behind the absolute concealment, beyond the reach of any possible perception—is so vastly, incomprehensibly greater than what he displayed today that the gap cannot be expressed. He unmade God with zero effort. He restored the omniverse with zero effort. And he did it all while genuinely disappointed that the confrontation had not been more entertaining.

I am writing this because I must. Because the act of forming words is the only thing keeping my mind from shattering. Because future Court Wizards—if there are any future Court Wizards, if the King does not eventually grow bored of our presence and erase us as casually as he erased his creator—need to know what happened on this day. The last opposition. The final prayer. The moment when even God learned that Godric is absolute.

I am Osvald, and I have seen the face of the true prime mover. It is the face of a forty-five-year-old man with a salt-and-pepper beard and a warm, fatherly smile. And that smile will haunt me for the rest of my existence.

---

I closed Osvald's journal. My hands were trembling—the same tremor that had afflicted every Court Wizard before me, from Julian to Oren to Ferris to Kaedan to Roth to Osvald and beyond. The inherited trauma of Blake's lineage, passed down through journals and blood and the simple, devastating act of witnessing.

The original God. Erased. The creator of the universe, unmade by a casual gesture. And Godric had been disappointed. He had wanted a show. He had deactivated every passive defense—the auras, the shields, the immune system, the infinite backups—and let the creator attack him with full force, and the attack had been so utterly, profoundly nothing that Godric had yawned.

I looked across the observatory—the same observatory where Osvald had stood, where God had appeared, where the creator had been erased. The marble trophy of the Last Narrative Coalition still gleamed on its pedestal, the compressed remains of every fictional universe ever conceived. And now I knew that even that coalition, as vast and impossible as it had been, was not the final opposition. The final opposition had been God.

And God had failed. As all oppositions fail. As all oppositions must fail, because the very concept of opposition is meaningless in the presence of Godric.

I thought about the Stasis Event, which I would soon witness Godric trigger. The closed loop of his own creation. The moment when the far-future Godric would reach back across the eons and use Thorin's dying spell to transform his mortal self into the seed of omnipotence. God was gone. The creator was erased. There was no higher authority, no external power, no conceivable entity that could challenge the King. And the King, in the unfathomable depths of his eternal satisfaction, would continue to amplify, continue to ascend, continue to become more incomprehensibly powerful with every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second.

He had unseated the prime mover and taken the throne of creation for himself. And he had done it not with malice, not with cruelty, but with the simple, casual authority of a being for whom the distinction between "possible" and "impossible" had long since ceased to exist.

I closed my eyes. The dread was absolute. The horror was eternal. And somewhere in the palace, Godric was probably enjoying a cup of tea, warm and content, his salt-and-pepper beard catching the golden light of the artificial sun, completely untroubled by the cosmic significance of the death he had dealt.

Because that was who he was. The apex predator. The true God. The being who had erased his own creator and taken his place, and who had done it all with a faint, amused smile and a casual gesture.

I was Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate. And the last opposition had fallen.
